(Surah Maryam)
(It has ninety-eight verses and is Meccan.)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad.﴾

Before entering into the readings (qira'at), three preliminaries are necessary:

The First Preliminary: The letters of the alphabet (huruf al-mu'jam) are of two kinds: two-letter (thunna'i) and three-letter (thulathi). It is the custom of the Arabs to pronounce the two-letter ones in a cut-off manner with imalah (inclination of the vowel), so they say: "ba, ta, tha," and similarly others of their kind; and to pronounce the three-letter ones in which there is an alif in the middle with a fully extended fatha, so they say: "dal, dhal, sad, dad," and similarly their forms. As for the letter zay alone among the letters of the alphabet, both practices are common regarding it: whoever makes its ya' clearly audible in pronunciation until it becomes three-letter does not apply imalah to it, and whoever does not make its ya' clearly audible in pronunciation until it resembles the two-letter form applies imalah to it.

The Second Preliminary: It should be known that prolonging the fatha (ishba' al-fatha) in all positions is the original form, and imalah is a derivative branch of it. For this reason, it is permissible to prolong every inclined vowel, but it is not permissible to incline every prolonged fatha.

The Third Preliminary: For the readers, in the readings specific to this position, there are three methods:

The first: to adhere to the original, which is prolonging the fatha of the ha' and the ya'.

The second: to incline the ha' and the ya'.

The third: to combine between the original and the derivative, so that a difference occurs between the ha' and the ya': they make one of them fatha, whichever it may be, and the other kasra. Regarding the reason that necessitates this difference, they have two opinions:

The first: that the prolonged fatha is the original, and imalah is a well-known derivative that is frequently used; so one of them is prolonged and the other is inclined, so that it combines observance of both the original and the derivative, and this is better than observing one of them and neglecting the other.

The second opinion: that the two-letter letters of the alphabet, when they are cut off (maqti'ah), are with imalah, and when they are connected (mawsulah), are with prolongation. Ha and Ya in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾, are cut off in pronunciation and connected in writing; so one of them is inclined and the other is prolonged, so that both sides observe the aspect of verbal separation and the aspect of graphic connection. Having understood this, we say: there are readings in it.

The first, which is the well-known reading in it: fatha of the ha' and the ya' together.

The second: kasra of the ha' and fatha of the ya'; this is the reading of Abu 'Amr, Ibn Mubadir, and al-Qutta'i from Ayyub. They made the ha' kasra and not the ya' so that it would be a distinction between it and the ha' of tanbih (alerting), for that is never pronounced with kasra.

The third: fatha of the ha' and kasra of the ya'; this is the reading of Hamzah, al-A'mash, Talhah, and al-Dahhak from 'Asim, and they made the ya' kasra and not the ha' because the ya' is a sister of the kasra, and giving the kasra to its sister is better than giving it to a foreign fatha, for the sake of harmony.

The fourth: imalah of both of them together; this is the reading of al-Kisa'i, al-Mufaddal, Yahya from 'Asim, al-Walid ibn Aslam from Ibn 'Amir, al-Zuhri, and Ibn Jarir. They inclined both for the two aspects mentioned regarding the imalah of the ha' and the imalah of the ya'.

The fifth: the reading of al-Hasan, which is damm of the ha' and fatha of the ya'. It is also reported from him: fatha of the ha' and damm of the ya'. The author of al-Kashshaf narrated from al-Hasan damm of both of them. It was said to him: this narration from al-Hasan is not established, for Ibn Jinni mentioned in his book al-Muhtasab that the reading of al-Hasan is damm of one of them and fatha of the other, not specified. Some said: al-Hasan only proceeded to make one of them damm without specification because he conceived that the 'ayn of the verb in ha' and ya' is an alif converted from waw, like al-dar and al-mal; and that is because these alifs, though unknown since they have no derivation, are treated as analogous to what resembles them in pronunciation.

When an alif falls as the 'ayn, it is necessary to hold that it has been converted from waw, because that is the predominant pattern in the language. So when al-Hasan conceived that the alif of ha' and ya' was converted from waw, he treated it as having the rule of waw and made damm the letter before it, because waw is a sister of damm.

The sixth: ha, ya, with a slight admixture (ishmam) of damm in both of them.

The second issue: Abu Ja'far read (Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad) by separating the letters from one another with the slightest pause, with the clear pronunciation of the nun of 'Ayn; the rest of the readers connect the letters to one another and conceal the nun.

The third issue: the well-known reading is "Sad" with idgham (assimilation), and it is reported from 'Asim and Ya'qub with izhar (clear pronunciation).

The second discussion: The opinions mentioned regarding these opening letters have already been discussed, but what is specific to this position is what has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that His saying, Exalted is He: Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad, is a praise from Allah for Himself. From the Kaf is His description as Kafin (Sufficient); from the Ha is Hadin (Guide); from the 'Ayn is 'Alim (Knowing); and from the Sad is Sadiq (Truthful). Also from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he took the Kaf as al-Kabir (the Great) and al-Karim (the Generous). It is also related from him that he took the Ya' as al-Karim once and as al-Hakim (the Wise) another time. From al-Rabi' ibn Anas regarding the Ya' that it is from Mujir (the Protector). From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, regarding the 'Ayn that it is from 'Aziz (Mighty) and from 'Adl (Just). These sayings are not strong, because we have explained that it is not permissible for Allah, Exalted is He, to deposit in His Book what the language does not indicate, neither literally nor metaphorically; for if we permit that, it opens the door to the saying of those who claim that every outward meaning has an inward meaning, while the language does not indicate what they have mentioned. The indication of the Kaf is no more preferable than its indication of al-Karim, al-Kabir, or another name among the names of the Messenger (ﷺ), the angels, Paradise, or Hell; so restricting it to some of these over others is an arbitrary judgment that the language does not indicate at all.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 2–3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is a mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariyya﴾

On this there are several issues:

First issue: The word "dhikr" (mention) has four readings: in the form of a verbal noun (masdar) or a past tense verb, either lightened (mukhaffafa) or emphasized (mushaddada), or in the imperative form. As for the form of the verbal noun, it must be read with a kasra on "rahmati rabbika" as an annexation (idafa). Then there are three possibilities in it:

One: the dal of "abdahu" and the hamza of "Zakariyya" are read with a fatha, and this is the well-known reading.

Second: both are read with a damma, and the meaning is: that mercy is His servant Zakariyya. This is from Ibn 'Amir.

Third: the first is read with a fatha and the second with a damma, and the meaning is: the mercy of your Lord to His servant, who is Zakariyya.

As for the form of the past tense with shadda, it must be read with a fatha on "rahmatin". As for the past tense with takhfif, there are two possibilities in it:

One of them: a damma on the ba' of "rabbuka", and the meaning is: your Lord mentioned His servant Zakariyya.

Second: a fatha on the ba' of "rabbika" and a damma on "abdihi Zakariyya", this being by placing the object before the subject. These two readings are from al-Kalbi. As for the imperative form, it must be read with a fatha on "rahmatin", and this is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas. Know that, on the assumption that it is taken as the verbal noun or the past tense, the sense would be: this recited portion of the Qur'an is a mention of the mercy of your Lord.

Second issue: It is possible that what is meant by "rahmati rabbika" (namely His servant Zakariyya) is a mercy; then regarding his being a mercy there are two possibilities:

One of them: that he is a mercy upon his community, because he guided them to faith and acts of obedience.

The other: that he is a mercy upon our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and upon the community of Muhammad, because when God Most High explained to Muhammad (ﷺ) His path of sincerity and devotion to God Most High in all matters, that became a word calling him and his community to that same way, so Zakariyya was a mercy. It is also possible that what is meant is that this surah contains a mention of the mercy with which He showed mercy to His servant Zakariyya.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 4–6 (part 1 of 2):

God's words: ﴿When he called out to his Lord in a secret call.﴾ He observed the way of God in concealing his supplication, because raising the voice and concealing it are equal in the sight of God; so concealment was preferable, since it is further from ostentation (riya') and more conducive to sincerity (ikhlas).

Second: he concealed it lest he be blamed for seeking a child in the time of old age.

Third: he kept it secret from his heirs (mawali), whom he feared.

Fourth: his voice was faint because of his weakness and decrepitude, as in the description of the old man: "his voice is feeble and his hearing is tenuous." If it is said that a condition of nida' (calling) is raising the voice, how can it be reconciled that it was both a nida' and secret? The answer is in two respects:

The first: he exerted the utmost effort he could in raising his voice, but the voice was weak due to the extreme weakness caused by old age. So it was a nida' in view of his intention, and secret in view of the reality.

The second: he supplicated during prayer, because God answered him during prayer, as in His words: ﴿Then the angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary: "God gives you good tidings of Yahya"﴾ (Al 'Imran: 39). The fact that the answer came during prayer indicates that the supplication was during prayer; therefore the calling in it must have been secret.

God's words: ﴿He said: "My Lord, my bones have weakened and my head has glistened with grey hair, and I have never been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord. And I fear my heirs after me, and my wife is barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir, who will inherit from me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub, and make him, my Lord, one who is pleasing."﴾

Matters of recitation (al-qira'a) in it:

The first issue: ﴿wahana﴾ was read with all three vowel-harakat.

The second issue: the idgham (assimilation) of the sin into the shin in (min al-ra'si shaiba) is from Abu 'Amr.

The third issue: ﴿wa inni khiftu al-mawali﴾ with a fatha on the ya'; and from al-Zuhri with a sukun on the ya' of al-mawali. 'Uthman

and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Zayd ibn Thabit and Ibn 'Abbas read: khaffat, with a fatha on the kha' and fa', shaddah on the fa', and a kasra on the ta'. This indicates two meanings:

One: that "wara'i" means "after me," the meaning being that they have become few and unable to establish the religion after him; so he asked his Lord to strengthen them with a guardian to be granted to him.

The second: that it means "in front of me," the meaning being that they have passed away before him and gone, and no one remains through whom there is strength and support.

The fourth issue: the well-known reading is ﴿min wara'i﴾ with a kasra on the hamza followed by a sakin ya'; and from Humayd ibn Miqsam likewise but with a fatha on the ya'. Ibn Kathir read (wara'ay) like 'asaya.

The fifth issue: concerning ﴿yaritharni wa yarith﴾ there are several aspects:
One: the well-known reading, with raf' in both as an adjectival clause (sifa).
Second: the reading of Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, al-Zuhri, al-A'mash and Talha, with jazm in both as a response to the supplication (jawab li'l-du'a').
Third: from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, al-Hasan and Qatada: (waliyyan yarithni), with jazm, and warith on the pattern fa'il.
Fourth: from Ibn 'Abbas: (yarithni) warith min Al Ya'qub.
Fifth: from al-Jahdari (wa yarith), a diminutive of warith on the pattern uf'ayl.

Linguistic notes: al-wahn is the weakening of strength. In al-Kashshaf it is said: he likened the whiteness (shayb) to the flame of fire in its brightness, its radiance, and its spreading throughout the hair and its pervading it, and its taking every course, like the blazing of fire; then he expressed it as a metaphor. Then he attributed the kindling (ishtial) to the place of the hair and its root, which is the head, and he brought the grey hair as a specification (tamyiz) and did not add "the head" (to a pronoun), relying on the addressee's knowledge that it is the head of Zakariya; hence this sentence is eloquent. As for du'a' (supplication), it is the request for an act, and its counterpart is response (ijaba), just as the counterpart of a command is obedience. As for the root of the word (waliyy), it indicates the meaning of nearness and proximity; one says: walaytuhu aliyhi walyan, meaning I drew near; and awlaytuhu means I brought him near to me, and what is beyond him became distant; and wali means ... and from it is the verse of Sa'ida [ibn Juayya]:
"'Awadiyy ran beyond your proximity, leaping"
And: "Eat from what is near you (mimma yalika)," and "I sat by what is beside him (mimma yalihi)." From it is al-walyu, which is the rain that follows the al-wasmi; and al-waliyya is the saddle-cloth, because it lies on the back of the beast; and he was guardian (walia) of the orphan and of the slain; and he governed (walia) the land, because whoever takes charge of a matter has drawn near to it. As for God's words: ﴿So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque﴾ it derives from their saying: waliyahu biruknihi, meaning he made him adjacent to it. As for walla 'anni when one turns away, it is from the category of intensifying the middle letter for negation. And their saying: "So-and-so is more entitled (awla) than so-and-so," meaning more deserving; the superlative form from al-wali or al-waliyy is like al-adna and al-aqrab from al-dani and al-qarib, and it also carries the meaning of nearness, because whoever is more deserving of a thing is closer to it. Al-mawla is a noun for the place of the wali, like al-marma and al-mabna are nouns for the place of throwing and building. As for al-'aqir, she is the one who does not bear children; and al-'aqr in the language means wounding, and from it the term 'aqir is taken, because it is a deficiency in the original creation; and "I wounded the horse with the sword" when you struck its legs. As for al-al, they are the particular people of a man to whom his affairs return; then his affairs may return to him through kinship at one time, through companionship at another, like "the household of Pharaoh," and through agreement in religion, like "the household of the Prophet" (ﷺ). Know that Zakariya (peace be upon him) placed three matters before his request:

One: his own weakness.

The second: that God had never at all rejected his supplication.

The third: that the thing sought through supplication is a cause of benefit in religion. Then, after establishing these three matters, he explicitly made the request.

As for the first station, which is his weakness: the effect of weakness either appears inwardly or outwardly, and the weakness that appears inwardly is stronger than that which appears outwardly; for this reason he began by describing the weakness within, which is his words: ﴿my bones have weakened﴾. Its explanation is that the bones are the firmest of the body's organs, and they were made so for two benefits:

The first: so that they serve as a foundation and pillars on which the other organs rely, since all the organs are placed upon the bones, and the bearer must be stronger than the borne.

The second: they are needed in some places to be a shield, by which the other organs are strengthened, like the skull of the head and the bones of the chest; and what is like this must be firm so as to endure the encounter with afflictions, remote from being affected by them. Once this is established, we say: if the bone is the firmest of the organs, then when weakness reaches it, the weakness of everything else with its softness is more fitting; and because the bone, being the bearer of all the other organs, the spread of weakness to the bearer necessitates its spread to the borne; for this reason he singled out the bone for weakness among all the other organs. As for the effect of weakness outwardly, it is the dominance of grey hair over the head. Thus it is established that this utterance indicates the dominance of weakness over the inner and outer, and that increases the supplication in emphasis, since it contains reliance upon God's power and might and disavowal of apparent causes.

The second station: that he was never rejected in supplication at all. The way of making it a means (tawassul) is in two respects:

One: what is reported that a needy man asked one of the great ones and said: "I am the one whom you benefited at such and such a time." He said: "Welcome to one who has sought a means to us through us," and then fulfilled his need.

This is because if he accepted him first, then if he rejected him a second time, the rejection would nullify the earlier favour, and the benefactor does not strive to nullify his own favour.

The second: that opposing habit is difficult upon the soul; so when a person is accustomed to the answering of supplication, if he becomes rejected after that, it would be in the utmost hardship; and the withholding from one from whom benevolence is expected is harder. So Zakariya (peace be upon him) said: "You did not reject me at the beginning, though I had not become accustomed to Your kindness, and I was strong in body and strong in heart; so if You reject me now after You have made me accustomed to acceptance, together with the utmost weakness of mine, that would reach the furthest extent of pain in the heart." Know that the Arabs say: "So-and-so was made happy (sa'ida) by his need" when he attained it, and "was made unhappy (shaqiya) by it" when he failed and did not obtain it. The meaning of "bi-du'a'ika" is "by my supplicating to You," for the verbal action may sometimes be attributed to the agent and sometimes to the object.

The third station: explaining that the sought-after thing is beneficial in religion, which is his words: ﴿I fear my heirs after me﴾. On this there are several discussions:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: "I feared the heirs (mawali) after me," meaning the inheritors after me. From Mujahid: the 'asaba (agnatic relatives). From Abu Salih: the kalala. From al-Asamm: the paternal cousins, who are those closest to him in lineage. From Abu Muslim: mawla is used to mean the helper, cousin, owner, companion; and here it means one who will take over his inheritance in the position of a child. The preferred view is that the intended mawali are those who will succeed him either in governance, or in the wealth he possessed, or in carrying the affair of religion; for it was the custom that whoever was closest to the lawgiver was specifically appointed during his lifetime.

The second: they differed about the nature of his fear of the mawali. Some said: he feared they would corrupt the religion. Others said: rather, he feared that his affair would pass to them after his death in regard to wealth and other matters, while he knew from their condition that they were deficient in knowledge and ability to undertake that office.

There is a third opinion: it is possible that God had informed him that no prophet of the Children of Israel remained who had a father except one; so he feared that this would be from his paternal cousins, since he had no son. So he asked God to grant him a son who would be that prophet. This implies that he was fearful of a matter about which prophets are concerned, even if it does not indicate its details.
Page 156
It is not impossible that Zakariya, alongside prophethood, held political authority in respect of kingship and what is connected with leadership, and so he feared from them after him concerning one or both of these.

As for his words ﴿and I fear﴾, although it is in the past form, it conveys the future as well; as a man says: "I have feared that such and such would happen" and "I was apprehensive that such and such would happen," meaning: I am fearful now, not that the fear has departed from him. Likewise his words ﴿and my wife has been barren﴾, meaning she is barren at present; for a barren woman is not turned into one who bears children customarily. So the report about her in the past form indicates the long duration of this condition. Zakariya's purpose in this statement is to show the improbability of a child being born; so his expression in the past form was stronger. To this the matter returns in his words ﴿and I fear the heirs after me﴾, since he intended by it to report, and about the long duration of the fear; then he dispensed with indicating the present fear by the implication of the situation and what necessitates asking for an heir and manifesting need. Also, the past form may be placed for the future and vice versa; God the Exalted says: ﴿And when God says: "O Jesus son of Mary, did you say to the people: take me and my mother as two gods?"﴾ (Al-Ma'ida: 116). And God knows best.

As for his words ﴿after me﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: Abu 'Ubayda said: it means "before me," in front of me; and others said: it means "after my death." Both are possible. If it is asked: how did he fear them after him, and how did he know they would survive him, let alone that he would fear their evil? We say: this can be known through signs and conjecture, and that is sufficient for the arising of fear; perhaps he knew through some signs that they would continue in their customary corruption and evil.

* * *

There is disagreement over the interpretation of God's words ﴿so grant me from Yourself a guardian﴾. Most hold that he sought a child; others said: rather he sought one who would stand in his place, whether a child or otherwise. The closer view is the first, for three reasons:

The first: God's words in Surah Al 'Imran, relating his statement: ﴿He said: "My Lord, grant me from Yourself good offspring"﴾ (Al 'Imran: 38).

The second: His words in this surah: ﴿so grant me from Yourself a guardian, who will inherit from me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 4–6 (part 2 of 2):

The third (view): the saying of God in Surat al-Anbiya': ﴿And Zakariyya, when he called out to his Lord, "My Lord, do not leave me alone"﴾ (21:89). This indicates that he asked for a child, because he had already said in Surat Maryam that he had heirs (mawali) and that he was not left without heirs. Although it is possible to read this as an heir who could take his place, reading it as a child is more apparent. The proponents of the third view argued: when he was given the good news of a child, he regarded it as something great, out of astonishment, and said, "أنّى يكون لي غلامٌ؟" ("How can I have a boy?"). Had his supplication been for a child, he would not have regarded this as great.

The answer: he, peace be upon him, asked whether what would be granted to him could be granted while he and his wife remained in their present state, or whether it could be granted by transforming them into two young people for whom a child is possible. This is attributed to al-Hasan. Others said: Zakariyya's words in his supplication, ﴿and my wife is barren﴾, mean only that he was asking for a child from her or from another woman, by God making her fit to bear a child. It was as if he, peace be upon him, had said: "I have despaired of having a child from her, so grant me from Yourself an heir (waliyyan) as You wish, either by making her fit so the child is from her, or by granting me one from another woman." When he was given the good news of a boy, he asked, "Will he be granted from her or from another?" He was told that he would be granted from her.

They differed about the meaning of "inheritance" (al-mirath) in several ways:

First: in both places, "inheritance" means the inheritance of wealth. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak.

Second: in both places, it means the inheritance of prophethood. This is the view of Abu Salih.

Third: "He will inherit me in wealth, and will inherit from the family of Ya'qub prophethood." This is the view of al-Suddi, Mujahid and al-Sha'bi, and it is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak.

Fourth: "He will inherit me in knowledge, and will inherit from the family of Ya'qub prophethood." This is reported from Mujahid.

Know that these reports all return to one of five matters: wealth; the office of hubburah (the office of scholarly leadership among the Jews); knowledge; prophethood; and good conduct. The word "inheritance" is used for all of them. As for wealth, it is used in God's saying: ﴿And He caused you to inherit their land, their homes and their wealth﴾ (33:27). As for knowledge, it is used in God's saying: ﴿And We gave Musa the guidance and caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Scripture﴾ (40:53). The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: ("The scholars are the heirs of the prophets. The prophets did not leave a dinar or a dirham as inheritance; they left only knowledge.") God also said: ﴿And We gave Dawud and Sulayman knowledge, and they said, "Praise be to God who has favored us over many of His believing servants." And Sulayman inherited Dawud﴾ (27:15–16). This may refer to inheriting kingship or inheriting prophethood. People also say, "This has bequeathed me (awrathani) sorrow and grief." It has thus been established that the word can bear all these senses.

Those who understood the word as the inheritance of wealth argued from both report and reason. As for report, there is his, peace be upon him, saying: ("May God have mercy on Zakariyya; he had no one to inherit from him"), and its apparent meaning indicates that the intended sense is the inheritance of wealth. As for reason, there are two arguments:

The first: knowledge, good conduct and prophethood are not inherited; rather, they are attained only through acquisition, so it is necessary to read it as referring to wealth.

The second: he said, ﴿and make him, my Lord, pleasing (radiyyan)﴾. Had the intended meaning of inheritance been the inheritance of prophethood, he would have been asking for the prophet, peace be upon him, to be made pleasing, and this is impermissible, because a prophet is only pleasing and protected from sin. As for his, peace be upon him, saying, ("We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity"), this does not prevent it from being specific to him.

Those who understood it as knowledge, or as office and prophethood, argued from what is known of the state of the prophets: that their concern for wealth is not as intense as their concern for religion. It has been said that perhaps he was given from this world what was of great benefit in religion, which is why he was concerned about it. As for the objection, "How can prophethood be inherited?", we say: wealth is only said to be inherited by a son in the sense that he takes his father's place in it and obtains from its disposal the benefit that his father obtained. Ownership of wealth, however, comes from God, not from the one who bequeaths it. Likewise, when it is known that the son will become a prophet after him and will thus take charge of religious affairs after him, it is permissible to say that he inherited him. As for his, peace be upon him, saying, ("We, the company of prophets"), although it is permissible to read it as referring to one person, as in God's saying ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder﴾ (15:9), it is nonetheless metaphorical. Its literal sense is plural, and departing from the literal meaning without a valid reason is not permissible, especially since it has also been reported as: ("We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from"). The better reading is that this refers to everything that contains benefit and goodness in religion. That includes prophethood, knowledge, good conduct, a beneficial office in religion, and righteous wealth, since all these are things for which the motives to preserve them are strong, so that this benefit may be lasting and continuous.

Seventh: most exegetes agree that Ya'qub here is Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon them all, because Zakariyya's wife was the sister of Maryam, and she was from the descendants of Sulayman ibn Dawud, from the descendants of Yahudha ibn Ya'qub. As for Zakariyya, peace be upon him, he was from the descendants of Harun, brother of Musa, peace be upon him. Harun and Musa, peace be upon them, were descendants of Lawi ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq. Prophethood was in the tribe (sibt) of Ya'qub, because he was Israel, ﷺ.

Some exegetes said: the intended Ya'qub here is not the son of Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon him, but Ya'qub ibn Mathan, brother of Imran ibn Mathan, and the family of Ya'qub were the maternal uncles of Yahya ibn Zakariyya. This is the view of al-Kalbi and Muqatil. Al-Kalbi said: the sons of Mathan were the leaders of the Children of Israel and their kings, and Zakariyya was then the head of the rabbis. So he wished that his son would inherit his hubburah, and would inherit from the sons of Mathan their kingship.

Know that they mentioned several meanings of "radiyyan" (pleasing) in the exegesis.

First: the intended sense is "make him pleasing among the prophets", because all of them are pleasing, so the one who is pleasing among them is one who is preferred over all of them and surpasses them in many matters. God answered him in this, and granted him Yahya as a master (sayyid), a chaste one (hasur), and a prophet among the righteous, who did not disobey and did not intend to disobey. This is the utmost to which a person can attain being pleasing.

Second: the intended sense of "pleasing" is that he be pleasing to his community, not rejected as a liar and not confronted with refusal.

Third: the intended sense of "pleasing" is that he not be suspected of anything, that no fault be found in him, and that nothing of disobedience be attributed to him.

Fourth: Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them, said in their supplication: ﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims (submitting) to You﴾ (2:128), and they were at that time Muslims. It seems that the intended sense there is "keep us firm in this," or the intended sense is "make us excellent among Your prophets who submit," and so it is here. Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued from this verse on the matter of the creation of acts: a person is pleasing only by his own action, so when he asked God to make him pleasing, this indicates that the act of the servant is created by God, Exalted. If it is objected that what is meant is that God should show him various kinds of divine kindness (lutf), so that he chooses what makes him pleasing, and this is then attributed to God, Exalted:

The answer is in two parts:

The first: if we read "making him pleasing" as making kindnesses available, such that by his own choice the person becomes pleasing when they are present, that would be a metaphor, and metaphor contradicts the default principle.

The second: that God's making those kindnesses obligatory on Himself, Exalted, is such that it is impermissible for Him to neglect it, and what is obligatory cannot be sought through supplication and humble entreaty.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 4–6 (part 1 of 2):

God's words: ﴿When he called out to his Lord in a secret call.﴾ He observed the way of God in concealing his supplication, because raising the voice and concealing it are equal in the sight of God; so concealment was preferable, since it is further from ostentation (riya') and more conducive to sincerity (ikhlas).

Second: he concealed it lest he be blamed for seeking a child in the time of old age.

Third: he kept it secret from his heirs (mawali), whom he feared.

Fourth: his voice was faint because of his weakness and decrepitude, as in the description of the old man: "his voice is feeble and his hearing is tenuous." If it is said that a condition of nida' (calling) is raising the voice, how can it be reconciled that it was both a nida' and secret? The answer is in two respects:

The first: he exerted the utmost effort he could in raising his voice, but the voice was weak due to the extreme weakness caused by old age. So it was a nida' in view of his intention, and secret in view of the reality.

The second: he supplicated during prayer, because God answered him during prayer, as in His words: ﴿Then the angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary: "God gives you good tidings of Yahya"﴾ (Al 'Imran: 39). The fact that the answer came during prayer indicates that the supplication was during prayer; therefore the calling in it must have been secret.

God's words: ﴿He said: "My Lord, my bones have weakened and my head has glistened with grey hair, and I have never been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord. And I fear my heirs after me, and my wife is barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir, who will inherit from me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub, and make him, my Lord, one who is pleasing."﴾

Matters of recitation (al-qira'a) in it:

The first issue: ﴿wahana﴾ was read with all three vowel-harakat.

The second issue: the idgham (assimilation) of the sin into the shin in (min al-ra'si shaiba) is from Abu 'Amr.

The third issue: ﴿wa inni khiftu al-mawali﴾ with a fatha on the ya'; and from al-Zuhri with a sukun on the ya' of al-mawali. 'Uthman
Page 154
and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Zayd ibn Thabit and Ibn 'Abbas read: khaffat, with a fatha on the kha' and fa', shaddah on the fa', and a kasra on the ta'. This indicates two meanings:

One: that "wara'i" means "after me," the meaning being that they have become few and unable to establish the religion after him; so he asked his Lord to strengthen them with a guardian to be granted to him.

The second: that it means "in front of me," the meaning being that they have passed away before him and gone, and no one remains through whom there is strength and support.

The fourth issue: the well-known reading is ﴿min wara'i﴾ with a kasra on the hamza followed by a sakin ya'; and from Humayd ibn Miqsam likewise but with a fatha on the ya'. Ibn Kathir read (wara'ay) like 'asaya.

The fifth issue: concerning ﴿yaritharni wa yarith﴾ there are several aspects:
One: the well-known reading, with raf' in both as an adjectival clause (sifa).
Second: the reading of Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, al-Zuhri, al-A'mash and Talha, with jazm in both as a response to the supplication (jawab li'l-du'a').
Third: from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, al-Hasan and Qatada: (waliyyan yarithni), with jazm, and warith on the pattern fa'il.
Fourth: from Ibn 'Abbas: (yarithni) warith min Al Ya'qub.
Fifth: from al-Jahdari (wa yarith), a diminutive of warith on the pattern uf'ayl.

Linguistic notes: al-wahn is the weakening of strength. In al-Kashshaf it is said: he likened the whiteness (shayb) to the flame of fire in its brightness, its radiance, and its spreading throughout the hair and its pervading it, and its taking every course, like the blazing of fire; then he expressed it as a metaphor. Then he attributed the kindling (ishtial) to the place of the hair and its root, which is the head, and he brought the grey hair as a specification (tamyiz) and did not add "the head" (to a pronoun), relying on the addressee's knowledge that it is the head of Zakariya; hence this sentence is eloquent. As for du'a' (supplication), it is the request for an act, and its counterpart is response (ijaba), just as the counterpart of a command is obedience. As for the root of the word (waliyy), it indicates the meaning of nearness and proximity; one says: walaytuhu aliyhi walyan, meaning I drew near; and awlaytuhu means I brought him near to me, and what is beyond him became distant; and wali means ... and from it is the verse of Sa'ida [ibn Juayya]:
"'Awadiyy ran beyond your proximity, leaping"
And: "Eat from what is near you (mimma yalika)," and "I sat by what is beside him (mimma yalihi)." From it is al-walyu, which is the rain that follows the al-wasmi; and al-waliyya is the saddle-cloth, because it lies on the back of the beast; and he was guardian (walia) of the orphan and of the slain; and he governed (walia) the land, because whoever takes charge of a matter has drawn near to it. As for God's words: ﴿So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque﴾ it derives from their saying: waliyahu biruknihi, meaning he made him adjacent to it. As for walla 'anni when one turns away, it is from the category of intensifying the middle letter for negation. And their saying: "So-and-so is more entitled (awla) than so-and-so," meaning more deserving; the superlative form from al-wali or al-waliyy is like al-adna and al-aqrab from al-dani and al-qarib, and it also carries the meaning of nearness, because whoever is more deserving of a thing is closer to it. Al-mawla is a noun for the place of the wali, like al-marma and al-mabna are nouns for the place of throwing and building. As for al-'aqir, she is the one who does not bear children; and al-'aqr in the language means wounding, and from it the term 'aqir is taken, because it is a deficiency in the original creation; and "I wounded the horse with the sword" when you struck its legs. As for al-al, they are the particular people of a man to whom his affairs return; then his affairs may return to him through kinship at one time, through companionship at another, like "the household of Pharaoh," and through agreement in religion, like "the household of the Prophet" (ﷺ). Know that Zakariya (peace be upon him) placed three matters before his request:

One: his own weakness.

The second: that God had never at all rejected his supplication.

The third: that the thing sought through supplication is a cause of benefit in religion. Then, after establishing these three matters, he explicitly made the request.
Page 155
As for the first station, which is his weakness: the effect of weakness either appears inwardly or outwardly, and the weakness that appears inwardly is stronger than that which appears outwardly; for this reason he began by describing the weakness within, which is his words: ﴿my bones have weakened﴾. Its explanation is that the bones are the firmest of the body's organs, and they were made so for two benefits:

The first: so that they serve as a foundation and pillars on which the other organs rely, since all the organs are placed upon the bones, and the bearer must be stronger than the borne.

The second: they are needed in some places to be a shield, by which the other organs are strengthened, like the skull of the head and the bones of the chest; and what is like this must be firm so as to endure the encounter with afflictions, remote from being affected by them. Once this is established, we say: if the bone is the firmest of the organs, then when weakness reaches it, the weakness of everything else with its softness is more fitting; and because the bone, being the bearer of all the other organs, the spread of weakness to the bearer necessitates its spread to the borne; for this reason he singled out the bone for weakness among all the other organs. As for the effect of weakness outwardly, it is the dominance of grey hair over the head. Thus it is established that this utterance indicates the dominance of weakness over the inner and outer, and that increases the supplication in emphasis, since it contains reliance upon God's power and might and disavowal of apparent causes.

The second station: that he was never rejected in supplication at all. The way of making it a means (tawassul) is in two respects:

One: what is reported that a needy man asked one of the great ones and said: "I am the one whom you benefited at such and such a time." He said: "Welcome to one who has sought a means to us through us," and then fulfilled his need.

This is because if he accepted him first, then if he rejected him a second time, the rejection would nullify the earlier favour, and the benefactor does not strive to nullify his own favour.

The second: that opposing habit is difficult upon the soul; so when a person is accustomed to the answering of supplication, if he becomes rejected after that, it would be in the utmost hardship; and the withholding from one from whom benevolence is expected is harder. So Zakariya (peace be upon him) said: "You did not reject me at the beginning, though I had not become accustomed to Your kindness, and I was strong in body and strong in heart; so if You reject me now after You have made me accustomed to acceptance, together with the utmost weakness of mine, that would reach the furthest extent of pain in the heart." Know that the Arabs say: "So-and-so was made happy (sa'ida) by his need" when he attained it, and "was made unhappy (shaqiya) by it" when he failed and did not obtain it. The meaning of "bi-du'a'ika" is "by my supplicating to You," for the verbal action may sometimes be attributed to the agent and sometimes to the object.

The third station: explaining that the sought-after thing is beneficial in religion, which is his words: ﴿I fear my heirs after me﴾. On this there are several discussions:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: "I feared the heirs (mawali) after me," meaning the inheritors after me. From Mujahid: the 'asaba (agnatic relatives). From Abu Salih: the kalala. From al-Asamm: the paternal cousins, who are those closest to him in lineage. From Abu Muslim: mawla is used to mean the helper, cousin, owner, companion; and here it means one who will take over his inheritance in the position of a child. The preferred view is that the intended mawali are those who will succeed him either in governance, or in the wealth he possessed, or in carrying the affair of religion; for it was the custom that whoever was closest to the lawgiver was specifically appointed during his lifetime.

The second: they differed about the nature of his fear of the mawali. Some said: he feared they would corrupt the religion. Others said: rather, he feared that his affair would pass to them after his death in regard to wealth and other matters, while he knew from their condition that they were deficient in knowledge and ability to undertake that office.

There is a third opinion: it is possible that God had informed him that no prophet of the Children of Israel remained who had a father except one; so he feared that this would be from his paternal cousins, since he had no son. So he asked God to grant him a son who would be that prophet. This implies that he was fearful of a matter about which prophets are concerned, even if it does not indicate its details.
Page 156
It is not impossible that Zakariya, alongside prophethood, held political authority in respect of kingship and what is connected with leadership, and so he feared from them after him concerning one or both of these.

As for his words ﴿and I fear﴾, although it is in the past form, it conveys the future as well; as a man says: "I have feared that such and such would happen" and "I was apprehensive that such and such would happen," meaning: I am fearful now, not that the fear has departed from him. Likewise his words ﴿and my wife has been barren﴾, meaning she is barren at present; for a barren woman is not turned into one who bears children customarily. So the report about her in the past form indicates the long duration of this condition. Zakariya's purpose in this statement is to show the improbability of a child being born; so his expression in the past form was stronger. To this the matter returns in his words ﴿and I fear the heirs after me﴾, since he intended by it to report, and about the long duration of the fear; then he dispensed with indicating the present fear by the implication of the situation and what necessitates asking for an heir and manifesting need. Also, the past form may be placed for the future and vice versa; God the Exalted says: ﴿And when God says: "O Jesus son of Mary, did you say to the people: take me and my mother as two gods?"﴾ (Al-Ma'ida: 116). And God knows best.

As for his words ﴿after me﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: Abu 'Ubayda said: it means "before me," in front of me; and others said: it means "after my death." Both are possible. If it is asked: how did he fear them after him, and how did he know they would survive him, let alone that he would fear their evil? We say: this can be known through signs and conjecture, and that is sufficient for the arising of fear; perhaps he knew through some signs that they would continue in their customary corruption and evil.

* * *

There is disagreement over the interpretation of God's words ﴿so grant me from Yourself a guardian﴾. Most hold that he sought a child; others said: rather he sought one who would stand in his place, whether a child or otherwise. The closer view is the first, for three reasons:

The first: God's words in Surah Al 'Imran, relating his statement: ﴿He said: "My Lord, grant me from Yourself good offspring"﴾ (Al 'Imran: 38).

The second: His words in this surah: ﴿so grant me from Yourself a guardian, who will inherit from me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾.

The third (view): the saying of God in Surat al-Anbiya': ﴿And Zakariyya, when he called out to his Lord, "My Lord, do not leave me alone"﴾ (21:89). This indicates that he asked for a child, because he had already said in Surat Maryam that he had heirs (mawali) and that he was not left without heirs. Although it is possible to read this as an heir who could take his place, reading it as a child is more apparent. The proponents of the third view argued: when he was given the good news of a child, he regarded it as something great, out of astonishment, and said, "أنّى يكون لي غلامٌ؟" ("How can I have a boy?"). Had his supplication been for a child, he would not have regarded this as great.

The answer: he, peace be upon him, asked whether what would be granted to him could be granted while he and his wife remained in their present state, or whether it could be granted by transforming them into two young people for whom a child is possible. This is attributed to al-Hasan. Others said: Zakariyya's words in his supplication, ﴿and my wife is barren﴾, mean only that he was asking for a child from her or from another woman, by God making her fit to bear a child. It was as if he, peace be upon him, had said: "I have despaired of having a child from her, so grant me from Yourself an heir (waliyyan) as You wish, either by making her fit so the child is from her, or by granting me one from another woman." When he was given the good news of a boy, he asked, "Will he be granted from her or from another?" He was told that he would be granted from her.

They differed about the meaning of "inheritance" (al-mirath) in several ways:

First: in both places, "inheritance" means the inheritance of wealth. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak.

Second: in both places, it means the inheritance of prophethood. This is the view of Abu Salih.

Third: "He will inherit me in wealth, and will inherit from the family of Ya'qub prophethood." This is the view of al-Suddi, Mujahid and al-Sha'bi, and it is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak.

Fourth: "He will inherit me in knowledge, and will inherit from the family of Ya'qub prophethood." This is reported from Mujahid.

Know that these reports all return to one of five matters: wealth; the office of hubburah (the office of scholarly leadership among the Jews); knowledge; prophethood; and good conduct. The word "inheritance" is used for all of them. As for wealth, it is used in God's saying: ﴿And He caused you to inherit their land, their homes and their wealth﴾ (33:27). As for knowledge, it is used in God's saying: ﴿And We gave Musa the guidance and caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Scripture﴾ (40:53). The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: ("The scholars are the heirs of the prophets. The prophets did not leave a dinar or a dirham as inheritance; they left only knowledge.") God also said: ﴿And We gave Dawud and Sulayman knowledge, and they said, "Praise be to God who has favored us over many of His believing servants." And Sulayman inherited Dawud﴾ (27:15–16). This may refer to inheriting kingship or inheriting prophethood. People also say, "This has bequeathed me (awrathani) sorrow and grief." It has thus been established that the word can bear all these senses.

Those who understood the word as the inheritance of wealth argued from both report and reason. As for report, there is his, peace be upon him, saying: ("May God have mercy on Zakariyya; he had no one to inherit from him"), and its apparent meaning indicates that the intended sense is the inheritance of wealth. As for reason, there are two arguments:

The first: knowledge, good conduct and prophethood are not inherited; rather, they are attained only through acquisition, so it is necessary to read it as referring to wealth.

The second: he said, ﴿and make him, my Lord, pleasing (radiyyan)﴾. Had the intended meaning of inheritance been the inheritance of prophethood, he would have been asking for the prophet, peace be upon him, to be made pleasing, and this is impermissible, because a prophet is only pleasing and protected from sin. As for his, peace be upon him, saying, ("We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity"), this does not prevent it from being specific to him.

Those who understood it as knowledge, or as office and prophethood, argued from what is known of the state of the prophets: that their concern for wealth is not as intense as their concern for religion. It has been said that perhaps he was given from this world what was of great benefit in religion, which is why he was concerned about it. As for the objection, "How can prophethood be inherited?", we say: wealth is only said to be inherited by a son in the sense that he takes his father's place in it and obtains from its disposal the benefit that his father obtained. Ownership of wealth, however, comes from God, not from the one who bequeaths it. Likewise, when it is known that the son will become a prophet after him and will thus take charge of religious affairs after him, it is permissible to say that he inherited him. As for his, peace be upon him, saying, ("We, the company of prophets"), although it is permissible to read it as referring to one person, as in God's saying ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder﴾ (15:9), it is nonetheless metaphorical. That includes prophethood, knowledge, good conduct, a beneficial office in religion, and righteous wealth, since all these are things for which the motives to preserve them are strong, so that this benefit may be lasting and continuous.

Seventh: most exegetes agree that Ya'qub here is Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon them all, because Zakariyya's wife was the sister of Maryam, and she was from the descendants of Sulayman ibn Dawud, from the descendants of Yahudha ibn Ya'qub. As for Zakariyya, peace be upon him, he was from the descendants of Harun, brother of Musa, peace be upon him. Harun and Musa, peace be upon them, were descendants of Lawi ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq. Prophethood was in the tribe (sibt) of Ya'qub, because he was Israel, ﷺ.

Some exegetes said: the intended Ya'qub here is not the son of Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon him, but Ya'qub ibn Mathan, brother of Imran ibn Mathan, and the family of Ya'qub were the maternal uncles of Yahya ibn Zakariyya. So he wished that his son would inherit his hubburah, and would inherit from the sons of Mathan their kingship.

The first issue: ﴿wahana﴾ was read with all three vowel-harakat.
