The third issue: ﴿wa inni khiftu al-mawali﴾ with a fatha on the ya'; and from al-Zuhri with a sukun on the ya' of al-mawali. 'Uthman
Page 154
and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Zayd ibn Thabit and Ibn 'Abbas read: khaffat, with a fatha on the kha' and fa', shaddah on the fa', and a kasra on the ta'. This indicates two meanings:

One: that "wara'i" means "after me," the meaning being that they have become few and unable to establish the religion after him; so he asked his Lord to strengthen them with a guardian to be granted to him.

The second: that it means "in front of me," the meaning being that they have passed away before him and gone, and no one remains through whom there is strength and support.

The fourth issue: the well-known reading is ﴿min wara'i﴾ with a kasra on the hamza followed by a sakin ya'; and from Humayd ibn Miqsam likewise but with a fatha on the ya'. Ibn Kathir read (wara'ay) like 'asaya.

The fifth issue: concerning ﴿yaritharni wa yarith﴾ there are several aspects:
One: the well-known reading, with raf' in both as an adjectival clause (sifa).
Second: the reading of Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, al-Zuhri, al-A'mash and Talha, with jazm in both as a response to the supplication (jawab li'l-du'a').
Third: from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, al-Hasan and Qatada: (waliyyan yarithni), with jazm, and warith on the pattern fa'il.
Fourth: from Ibn 'Abbas: (yarithni) warith min Al Ya'qub.
Fifth: from al-Jahdari (wa yarith), a diminutive of warith on the pattern uf'ayl.

Linguistic notes: al-wahn is the weakening of strength. In al-Kashshaf it is said: he likened the whiteness (shayb) to the flame of fire in its brightness, its radiance, and its spreading throughout the hair and its pervading it, and its taking every course, like the blazing of fire; then he expressed it as a metaphor. Then he attributed the kindling (ishtial) to the place of the hair and its root, which is the head, and he brought the grey hair as a specification (tamyiz) and did not add "the head" (to a pronoun), relying on the addressee's knowledge that it is the head of Zakariya; hence this sentence is eloquent. As for du'a' (supplication), it is the request for an act, and its counterpart is response (ijaba), just as the counterpart of a command is obedience. As for the root of the word (waliyy), it indicates the meaning of nearness and proximity; one says: walaytuhu aliyhi walyan, meaning I drew near; and awlaytuhu means I brought him near to me, and what is beyond him became distant; and wali means ... and from it is the verse of Sa'ida [ibn Juayya]:
"'Awadiyy ran beyond your proximity, leaping"
And: "Eat from what is near you (mimma yalika)," and "I sat by what is beside him (mimma yalihi)." From it is al-walyu, which is the rain that follows the al-wasmi; and al-waliyya is the saddle-cloth, because it lies on the back of the beast; and he was guardian (walia) of the orphan and of the slain; and he governed (walia) the land, because whoever takes charge of a matter has drawn near to it. As for God's words: ﴿So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque﴾ it derives from their saying: waliyahu biruknihi, meaning he made him adjacent to it. As for walla 'anni when one turns away, it is from the category of intensifying the middle letter for negation. And their saying: "So-and-so is more entitled (awla) than so-and-so," meaning more deserving; the superlative form from al-wali or al-waliyy is like al-adna and al-aqrab from al-dani and al-qarib, and it also carries the meaning of nearness, because whoever is more deserving of a thing is closer to it. Al-mawla is a noun for the place of the wali, like al-marma and al-mabna are nouns for the place of throwing and building. As for al-'aqir, she is the one who does not bear children; and al-'aqr in the language means wounding, and from it the term 'aqir is taken, because it is a deficiency in the original creation; and "I wounded the horse with the sword" when you struck its legs. As for al-al, they are the particular people of a man to whom his affairs return; then his affairs may return to him through kinship at one time, through companionship at another, like "the household of Pharaoh," and through agreement in religion, like "the household of the Prophet" (ﷺ). Know that Zakariya (peace be upon him) placed three matters before his request:

One: his own weakness.

The second: that God had never at all rejected his supplication.

The third: that the thing sought through supplication is a cause of benefit in religion. Then, after establishing these three matters, he explicitly made the request.
Page 155
As for the first station, which is his weakness: the effect of weakness either appears inwardly or outwardly, and the weakness that appears inwardly is stronger than that which appears outwardly; for this reason he began by describing the weakness within, which is his words: ﴿my bones have weakened﴾. Its explanation is that the bones are the firmest of the body's organs, and they were made so for two benefits:

The first: so that they serve as a foundation and pillars on which the other organs rely, since all the organs are placed upon the bones, and the bearer must be stronger than the borne.

The second: they are needed in some places to be a shield, by which the other organs are strengthened, like the skull of the head and the bones of the chest; and what is like this must be firm so as to endure the encounter with afflictions, remote from being affected by them. Once this is established, we say: if the bone is the firmest of the organs, then when weakness reaches it, the weakness of everything else with its softness is more fitting; and because the bone, being the bearer of all the other organs, the spread of weakness to the bearer necessitates its spread to the borne; for this reason he singled out the bone for weakness among all the other organs. As for the effect of weakness outwardly, it is the dominance of grey hair over the head. Thus it is established that this utterance indicates the dominance of weakness over the inner and outer, and that increases the supplication in emphasis, since it contains reliance upon God's power and might and disavowal of apparent causes.

The second station: that he was never rejected in supplication at all. The way of making it a means (tawassul) is in two respects:

One: what is reported that a needy man asked one of the great ones and said: "I am the one whom you benefited at such and such a time." He said: "Welcome to one who has sought a means to us through us," and then fulfilled his need.

This is because if he accepted him first, then if he rejected him a second time, the rejection would nullify the earlier favour, and the benefactor does not strive to nullify his own favour.

The second: that opposing habit is difficult upon the soul; so when a person is accustomed to the answering of supplication, if he becomes rejected after that, it would be in the utmost hardship; and the withholding from one from whom benevolence is expected is harder. So Zakariya (peace be upon him) said: "You did not reject me at the beginning, though I had not become accustomed to Your kindness, and I was strong in body and strong in heart; so if You reject me now after You have made me accustomed to acceptance, together with the utmost weakness of mine, that would reach the furthest extent of pain in the heart." Know that the Arabs say: "So-and-so was made happy (sa'ida) by his need" when he attained it, and "was made unhappy (shaqiya) by it" when he failed and did not obtain it. The meaning of "bi-du'a'ika" is "by my supplicating to You," for the verbal action may sometimes be attributed to the agent and sometimes to the object.

The third station: explaining that the sought-after thing is beneficial in religion, which is his words: ﴿I fear my heirs after me﴾. On this there are several discussions:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: "I feared the heirs (mawali) after me," meaning the inheritors after me. From Mujahid: the 'asaba (agnatic relatives). From Abu Salih: the kalala. From al-Asamm: the paternal cousins, who are those closest to him in lineage. From Abu Muslim: mawla is used to mean the helper, cousin, owner, companion; and here it means one who will take over his inheritance in the position of a child. The preferred view is that the intended mawali are those who will succeed him either in governance, or in the wealth he possessed, or in carrying the affair of religion; for it was the custom that whoever was closest to the lawgiver was specifically appointed during his lifetime.

The second: they differed about the nature of his fear of the mawali. Some said: he feared they would corrupt the religion. Others said: rather, he feared that his affair would pass to them after his death in regard to wealth and other matters, while he knew from their condition that they were deficient in knowledge and ability to undertake that office.

There is a third opinion: it is possible that God had informed him that no prophet of the Children of Israel remained who had a father except one; so he feared that this would be from his paternal cousins, since he had no son. So he asked God to grant him a son who would be that prophet. This implies that he was fearful of a matter about which prophets are concerned, even if it does not indicate its details.
Page 156
It is not impossible that Zakariya, alongside prophethood, held political authority in respect of kingship and what is connected with leadership, and so he feared from them after him concerning one or both of these.

As for his words ﴿and I fear﴾, although it is in the past form, it conveys the future as well; as a man says: "I have feared that such and such would happen" and "I was apprehensive that such and such would happen," meaning: I am fearful now, not that the fear has departed from him. Likewise his words ﴿and my wife has been barren﴾, meaning she is barren at present; for a barren woman is not turned into one who bears children customarily. So the report about her in the past form indicates the long duration of this condition. Zakariya's purpose in this statement is to show the improbability of a child being born; so his expression in the past form was stronger. To this the matter returns in his words ﴿and I fear the heirs after me﴾, since he intended by it to report, and about the long duration of the fear; then he dispensed with indicating the present fear by the implication of the situation and what necessitates asking for an heir and manifesting need. Also, the past form may be placed for the future and vice versa; God the Exalted says: ﴿And when God says: "O Jesus son of Mary, did you say to the people: take me and my mother as two gods?"﴾ (Al-Ma'ida: 116). And God knows best.

As for his words ﴿after me﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: Abu 'Ubayda said: it means "before me," in front of me; and others said: it means "after my death." Both are possible. If it is asked: how did he fear them after him, and how did he know they would survive him, let alone that he would fear their evil? We say: this can be known through signs and conjecture, and that is sufficient for the arising of fear; perhaps he knew through some signs that they would continue in their customary corruption and evil.

* * *

There is disagreement over the interpretation of God's words ﴿so grant me from Yourself a guardian﴾. Most hold that he sought a child; others said: rather he sought one who would stand in his place, whether a child or otherwise. The closer view is the first, for three reasons:

The first: God's words in Surah Al 'Imran, relating his statement: ﴿He said: "My Lord, grant me from Yourself good offspring"﴾ (Al 'Imran: 38).

The second: His words in this surah: ﴿so grant me from Yourself a guardian, who will inherit from me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 4–6 (part 2 of 2):

The third (view): the saying of God in Surat al-Anbiya': ﴿And Zakariyya, when he called out to his Lord, "My Lord, do not leave me alone"﴾ (21:89). This indicates that he asked for a child, because he had already said in Surat Maryam that he had heirs (mawali) and that he was not left without heirs. Although it is possible to read this as an heir who could take his place, reading it as a child is more apparent. The proponents of the third view argued: when he was given the good news of a child, he regarded it as something great, out of astonishment, and said, "أنّى يكون لي غلامٌ؟" ("How can I have a boy?"). Had his supplication been for a child, he would not have regarded this as great.

The answer: he, peace be upon him, asked whether what would be granted to him could be granted while he and his wife remained in their present state, or whether it could be granted by transforming them into two young people for whom a child is possible. This is attributed to al-Hasan. Others said: Zakariyya's words in his supplication, ﴿and my wife is barren﴾, mean only that he was asking for a child from her or from another woman, by God making her fit to bear a child. It was as if he, peace be upon him, had said: "I have despaired of having a child from her, so grant me from Yourself an heir (waliyyan) as You wish, either by making her fit so the child is from her, or by granting me one from another woman." When he was given the good news of a boy, he asked, "Will he be granted from her or from another?" He was told that he would be granted from her.

They differed about the meaning of "inheritance" (al-mirath) in several ways:

First: in both places, "inheritance" means the inheritance of wealth. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak.

Second: in both places, it means the inheritance of prophethood. This is the view of Abu Salih.

Third: "He will inherit me in wealth, and will inherit from the family of Ya'qub prophethood." This is the view of al-Suddi, Mujahid and al-Sha'bi, and it is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak.

Fourth: "He will inherit me in knowledge, and will inherit from the family of Ya'qub prophethood." This is reported from Mujahid.

Know that these reports all return to one of five matters: wealth; the office of hubburah (the office of scholarly leadership among the Jews); knowledge; prophethood; and good conduct. The word "inheritance" is used for all of them. As for wealth, it is used in God's saying: ﴿And He caused you to inherit their land, their homes and their wealth﴾ (33:27). As for knowledge, it is used in God's saying: ﴿And We gave Musa the guidance and caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Scripture﴾ (40:53). The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: ("The scholars are the heirs of the prophets. The prophets did not leave a dinar or a dirham as inheritance; they left only knowledge.") God also said: ﴿And We gave Dawud and Sulayman knowledge, and they said, "Praise be to God who has favored us over many of His believing servants." And Sulayman inherited Dawud﴾ (27:15–16). This may refer to inheriting kingship or inheriting prophethood. People also say, "This has bequeathed me (awrathani) sorrow and grief." It has thus been established that the word can bear all these senses.

Those who understood the word as the inheritance of wealth argued from both report and reason. As for report, there is his, peace be upon him, saying: ("May God have mercy on Zakariyya; he had no one to inherit from him"), and its apparent meaning indicates that the intended sense is the inheritance of wealth. As for reason, there are two arguments:

The first: knowledge, good conduct and prophethood are not inherited; rather, they are attained only through acquisition, so it is necessary to read it as referring to wealth.

The second: he said, ﴿and make him, my Lord, pleasing (radiyyan)﴾. Had the intended meaning of inheritance been the inheritance of prophethood, he would have been asking for the prophet, peace be upon him, to be made pleasing, and this is impermissible, because a prophet is only pleasing and protected from sin. As for his, peace be upon him, saying, ("We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity"), this does not prevent it from being specific to him.

Those who understood it as knowledge, or as office and prophethood, argued from what is known of the state of the prophets: that their concern for wealth is not as intense as their concern for religion. It has been said that perhaps he was given from this world what was of great benefit in religion, which is why he was concerned about it. As for the objection, "How can prophethood be inherited?", we say: wealth is only said to be inherited by a son in the sense that he takes his father's place in it and obtains from its disposal the benefit that his father obtained. Ownership of wealth, however, comes from God, not from the one who bequeaths it. Likewise, when it is known that the son will become a prophet after him and will thus take charge of religious affairs after him, it is permissible to say that he inherited him. As for his, peace be upon him, saying, ("We, the company of prophets"), although it is permissible to read it as referring to one person, as in God's saying ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder﴾ (15:9), it is nonetheless metaphorical. Its literal sense is plural, and departing from the literal meaning without a valid reason is not permissible, especially since it has also been reported as: ("We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from"). The better reading is that this refers to everything that contains benefit and goodness in religion. That includes prophethood, knowledge, good conduct, a beneficial office in religion, and righteous wealth, since all these are things for which the motives to preserve them are strong, so that this benefit may be lasting and continuous.

Seventh: most exegetes agree that Ya'qub here is Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon them all, because Zakariyya's wife was the sister of Maryam, and she was from the descendants of Sulayman ibn Dawud, from the descendants of Yahudha ibn Ya'qub. As for Zakariyya, peace be upon him, he was from the descendants of Harun, brother of Musa, peace be upon him. Harun and Musa, peace be upon them, were descendants of Lawi ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq. Prophethood was in the tribe (sibt) of Ya'qub, because he was Israel, ﷺ.

Some exegetes said: the intended Ya'qub here is not the son of Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon him, but Ya'qub ibn Mathan, brother of Imran ibn Mathan, and the family of Ya'qub were the maternal uncles of Yahya ibn Zakariyya. This is the view of al-Kalbi and Muqatil. Al-Kalbi said: the sons of Mathan were the leaders of the Children of Israel and their kings, and Zakariyya was then the head of the rabbis. So he wished that his son would inherit his hubburah, and would inherit from the sons of Mathan their kingship.

Know that they mentioned several meanings of "radiyyan" (pleasing) in the exegesis.

First: the intended sense is "make him pleasing among the prophets", because all of them are pleasing, so the one who is pleasing among them is one who is preferred over all of them and surpasses them in many matters. God answered him in this, and granted him Yahya as a master (sayyid), a chaste one (hasur), and a prophet among the righteous, who did not disobey and did not intend to disobey. This is the utmost to which a person can attain being pleasing.

Second: the intended sense of "pleasing" is that he be pleasing to his community, not rejected as a liar and not confronted with refusal.

Third: the intended sense of "pleasing" is that he not be suspected of anything, that no fault be found in him, and that nothing of disobedience be attributed to him.

Fourth: Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them, said in their supplication: ﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims (submitting) to You﴾ (2:128), and they were at that time Muslims. It seems that the intended sense there is "keep us firm in this," or the intended sense is "make us excellent among Your prophets who submit," and so it is here. Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued from this verse on the matter of the creation of acts: a person is pleasing only by his own action, so when he asked God to make him pleasing, this indicates that the act of the servant is created by God, Exalted. If it is objected that what is meant is that God should show him various kinds of divine kindness (lutf), so that he chooses what makes him pleasing, and this is then attributed to God, Exalted:

The answer is in two parts:

The first: if we read "making him pleasing" as making kindnesses available, such that by his own choice the person becomes pleasing when they are present, that would be a metaphor, and metaphor contradicts the default principle.

The second: that God's making those kindnesses obligatory on Himself, Exalted, is such that it is impermissible for Him to neglect it, and what is obligatory cannot be sought through supplication and humble entreaty.

[Page 158]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verse 7:

Concerning this, there are several issues:

The first issue: They differed about who was the one calling out with the words ﴿O Zakariyya﴾. The majority hold that it was Allah, the Exalted, because what precedes this verse indicates that Zakariyya (peace be upon him) was addressing Allah the Exalted and asking Him, namely His saying ﴿My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened and my head has glistened with grey hair﴾ [Maryam: 4], and His saying ﴿And I have never been unsuccessful in my supplication to You, my Lord﴾ [Maryam: 4], and His saying ﴿So grant me⁠﴾ [Maryam: 5]. What follows also indicates that he was addressing Allah the Exalted when he said ﴿My Lord, how can I have a boy?⁠﴾ If what precedes this verse and what follows it is address with Allah the Exalted, then the call must be from Allah the Exalted, or else the composition would be disrupted. Some of them said that this was the call of an angel, and they argued for it with two points:

The first: the saying of the Exalted in Surat Al 'Imran: ﴿So the angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary, "Indeed, Allah gives you good tidings of Yahya⁠﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39].

The second: when Zakariyya (peace be upon him) said, ﴿How can I have a boy when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?⁠﴾ ﴿He said, "Thus [it will be]; your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me.'"⁠﴾ [Maryam: 8–9], and this cannot be the speech of Allah, so it must be the speech of an angel.

As for the answer to the first: it is possible to say that there were two calls: the call of Allah and the call of the angels.

As for the answer to the second: we will explain, God willing, that His saying ﴿He said, "Thus [it will be]; your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me.'"⁠﴾ may be the speech of Allah.

The second issue: If it is asked: if the supplication was with permission, what is the meaning of the glad tidings? And if it was without permission, why did he undertake it?

The answer: this is a matter specific to him, so it is permissible for him to ask without permission. It is also possible that he had been permitted to ask for it but did not know the time, so he was given the glad tidings of it.

The third issue: The exegetes differed concerning His saying ﴿We have not made for him before [any] namesake⁠﴾ [Maryam: 7], in two respects:

One of them, which is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah and Qatadah: that no one had been named with this name before him.

The second: that the intended meaning of "samiy" (namesake) is "equal," as in His saying ﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?⁠﴾ [Maryam: 65]. They differed about this in several ways:

One of them: that he was a master and a chaste one (ḥaṣūr) who did not disobey and did not intend disobedience, as if it were an answer to His saying ﴿and make him, my Lord, pleasing⁠﴾ [Maryam: 6]. It was said to him: "Indeed, We give you good tidings of a boy, We have not made for him before [any] equal in religion," and whoever is like this is in the utmost pleasing. This view is weak, because it entails preferring him over the prophets who were before him, such as Adam, Noah, Abraham and Moses, and that is false by consensus.

The second: that all people are named by their fathers and mothers after they have entered existence, but as for Yahya (peace be upon him), Allah the Exalted is the One who named him before he entered existence, so this was among his distinctive qualities, and there was no one like him or equal to him in this distinction.

The third: that he was born between an aged, decrepit old man and a barren old woman. Know that the first view is preferable, because interpreting "samiy" as "equal" – although it conveys praise and exaltation – is a departure from the literal meaning without necessity, and that is not permissible. As for the saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?⁠﴾, there we departed from the apparent meaning, because He said: ﴿So worship Him and be steadfast in His worship. Do you know of any namesake for Him?⁠﴾ [Maryam: 65], and it is known that merely His being named by that name does not necessitate the obligation of worshipping Him. For this reason we departed from the apparent meaning. Here, however, there is no necessity to depart from the apparent meaning, so it must be applied to it. Moreover, in his being singled out by that name there is a kind of exaltation, for we observe that when a king has a well-known title, his entourage do not bear that title but leave it out of reverence for him. Likewise here.

The fourth issue: Concerning why he (peace be upon him) was named Yahya, al-Tha'labi narrated several views about it:

One of them: from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Allah the Exalted gave life through him to the barrenness of his mother's womb.

The second: from Qatadah, that Allah the Exalted gave life to his heart through faith and obedience, and Allah the Exalted called the obedient one living and the disobedient one dead, by His saying ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life⁠﴾ [al-An'am: 122], and He said ﴿when He calls you to that which gives you life⁠﴾ [al-Anfal: 24].

The third: that he was given life through obedience, to the extent that he did not disobey and did not intend disobedience, following what 'Ikrimah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no one who has not disobeyed or intended [to disobey], except Yahya ibn Zakariyya, for he did not intend it and did not do it."

The fourth: from Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib, that he was martyred, and that martyrs are alive with their Lord, based on His saying ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord⁠﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169].

The fifth: what 'Amr ibn 'Abd Allah al-Maqdisi said: Allah the Exalted revealed to Ibrahim (peace be upon him) that he should say to Sarah, and that was her name, "I shall bring forth from her a servant who will not intend disobedience, whose name is Hayy." So she said: "Give him a letter from your name," and she gave him a letter from her name, so he became Yahya, and her name was Yasarra, so her name became Sarra.

The sixth: that Yahya (peace be upon him) was the first to believe in 'Isa, so his heart became alive through that faith. That is because the mother of Yahya was pregnant with him when Maryam came to visit her, while she was pregnant with 'Isa. The mother of Yahya said to her: "O Maryam, are you pregnant?" She said: "Why do you say that?" She said: "I see that what is in my belly prostrates to what is in your belly."

The seventh: that religion is given life through him, because Zakariyya asked for him for the sake of religion. Know that these views are weak, because names given as epithets do not seek a reason from derivation, and for this reason the people of verification said: "Names of designation stand in place of indications, and they do not convey any attribute to the named whatsoever."

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verse 8:**

[Page 160]

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "My Lord, how can I have a son when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?"﴾

Concerning this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited *ʿitiyyan*, *ṣiliyyan*, *jithiyyan* and *bukiyyan* with a kasra on the ʿayn, the ṣad, the jim and the baʾ. Hafs, on the authority of ʿAsim, recited *wa-bukiyyan* (in the verse ﴿and weeping﴾) with a ḍamma, while the rest recited with a kasra. All the others recited all of them with a ḍamma. Ibn Masʿud recited *ʿataan* and *ṣaliyyan* with a fatha on the ʿayn and the ṣad. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn ʿAbbas recited *ʿisiyyan* with an unpointed sin. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** Regarding the vocabulary, there are three words.

The first is *al-ghulam* (the boy): a male human at the beginning of his sexual desire for intercourse. From it comes *ightalama*, meaning his desire for intercourse became intense. Then the word is used for a student, as in the saying "*ghulam thaʿlab*" (a fox-cub, i.e. a cunning young man).

The second is *al-ʿitiyy* and *al-ʿisiyy*, which are one and the same. One says *ʿataa yaʿtu ʿutuwwan wa-ʿitiyyan*, so he is *ʿaatin*, and *ʿasaa yaʿsu ʿasawwan wa-ʿisiyyan*, so he is *ʿaasin*. The *ʿaasi* is one whom the length of time has changed into a state of misery. A "*layl ʿaatin*" is a long night; it is also said it means an extremely dark night.

The third: he did not say *ʿaqiratan* (with the feminine ending) because a word of the form *faʿil* describing a feminine, when it is not used for the masculine, does not take the *taʾ*, as in *imraʾatun ʿaqir* and *ḥaʾiḍ*. Al-Khalil said: these are masculine attributes that have been applied to a feminine, just as they applied feminine attributes to the masculine when they said *rajulun malhah* (a man who is very attractive), *rabʿah* (a man of medium stature), and *ghulamun nafʿah* (a boy who is useful).

**The third issue:** In this verse there are two questions.

The first: Why did Zakariyya, peace be upon him, express wonder with his words ﴿how can I have a son﴾, when he himself was the one who asked for a boy?

The second question: his statement ﴿how can I have a son﴾ was not mentioned among his community, because he used to keep these matters hidden from his people. This indicates that he mentioned it to himself. And this expression of wonder indicates that he doubted Allah's power over that, and that is disbelief, which is impermissible for the prophets, peace be upon them.

The answer to the first question: As for those who say he did not request a son specifically, the question disappears. As for those who say he did request a son, the answer is that the intent of his statement ﴿how can I have a son﴾ is wonder at the fact that Allah makes them both young and then grants them a child, or leaves them both as old people and grants them a child despite their old age. It is by way of inquiry, not by way of amazement. The evidence for this is the statement of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And Zakariyya, when he called to his Lord: "My Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors." So We answered him and gave him Yahya, and We made his wife fit for him﴾ (Al-Anbiya: 89–90). And this "making fit" is nothing other than that He restored her capacity to bear children. This matter has already been established. Al-Suddi mentioned another answer, saying: when he heard the call bringing the good news, Satan came to him and said, "This voice is not from Allah, exalted is He; rather it is from Satan, mocking you." So when Zakariyya doubted, he said, ﴿how can I have a son﴾. Know that the purpose of al-Suddi in this is that if Zakariyya, peace be upon him, had known that the one giving the good news was Allah, exalted is He, it would not have been permissible for him to say that. Therefore he committed this. Some of the *mutakallimun* (theologians) said this is definitively false, for if the prophets permitted that some of what comes from Allah, exalted is He, might be from Satan, they would permit it for the whole of it, and trust in them regarding revelation would be lost, and for us regarding what they convey to us. It may be answered that this possibility exists at the outset, and it is removed only by a miracle; so perhaps the miracle was not present in this case, and so doubt arose about it but not about other cases. And Allah knows best.

The answer to the second question comes in several aspects:

The first: His statement ﴿Indeed, We give you good news of a boy whose name is Yahya﴾ is not explicit that this boy was his son. Rather it is possible that Zakariyya, peace be upon him, observed courtesy and did not say, "Will I have a son or not?" Rather he mentioned the causes that make the attainment of a child difficult in the ordinary course. So that if the good news was of a child, Allah, exalted is He, would remove the ambiguity and make the speech explicit. When he mentioned that, Allah, exalted is He, stated explicitly that this child would be from him. Therefore the purpose of this speech of Zakariyya was not that he doubted Allah's power over it.

The second: He did not mention that out of doubt, but in a manner of exalting His power. This is like a man who sees his companion has given away something great and valuable, and says, "How could your soul permit the removal of such a thing from your possession!" as an exaltation and an expression of wonder.

The third: It is the nature of one who is given good news of what he desires that a great joy is generated in him at the first moment the news reaches him, so he seeks confirmation of that speech. Either because the intensity of his joy causes him to be distracted from the requirements of reason and thought, and this is like the wife of Abraham, peace be upon him, who, after she was given the good news of Isaac, said: ﴿"Woe is me! Shall I bear a child when I am an old woman and this my husband is an old man? Indeed this is an astonishing thing!"﴾ (Hud: 72). Her wonder was removed by His saying: ﴿"Do you wonder at the decree of Allah?"﴾ (Hud: 73). Or he wants to enjoy hearing that speech once more. Or it is for emphasis in confirming the explanation.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verse 9:

[Page 161]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "So it will be. Your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me, and I had already created you before, when you were nothing.'"﴾

And concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: Regarding His saying ﴿"Your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me'"﴾ there are several aspects (wujuh):

The first of them: the kaf (ك) in kadhalika is in the nominative case (raf'), meaning: "The matter is so," as an affirmation of him (Zechariah's statement), and then he began with "Your Lord says."

The second: it is in the accusative case (nasb). It is said that dhalika is a reference to something vague, whose explanation is "It is easy for Me." This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We decreed to him that matter, that the last remnant of these would be cut off by morning﴾ (al-Hijr: 66).

The third: the intended meaning is: "Do not be surprised, for thus has your Lord said, and there is no contradiction or error in His saying." Then He said after it, "It is easy for Me," as evidenced by "I had already created you before, when you were nothing."

The fourth: we have mentioned that His saying ﴿"How can I have a boy?"﴾ means "Will You give me a boy by making me and my wife young, or by leaving us in old age and yet giving us a child?" And His saying ﴿"So it will be"﴾ means: "We will bestow the child while you and your wife remain in your present state."

The second issue: Al-Hasan recited (wa-huwa 'alayya hayyin). This can only be explained according to the first aspect, i.e.: "The matter is as you said, but your Lord said that, in addition to it, it is easy for Me."

The third issue: applying the word hayyin (easy) to God, may He be exalted, is metaphorical (majaz), because that applies only to one for whom something may be difficult. Rather, the intended meaning is that when He wills something, it comes to be.

The fourth issue: as for the manner of argument from His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And I had already created you before, when you were nothing﴾, we say: when He created him from pure non-existence and absolute nothingness, He was able to create essences, attributes and effects. As for now, creating a child from an old man and an old woman requires only the transformation of attributes, and the One who is able to create essences, attributes and effects together is more worthy of being able to transform attributes. And if He brought him into being from non-existence, then likewise He grants him a child by restoring to him and to his companion the power from which the two waters are produced, whose union creates a child. This is why He said: ﴿So We answered him, and We gave him Yahya, and We made his wife fit for him﴾ (al-Anbiya: 90). This is the manner of the argument.

The fifth issue: The majority hold that His saying ﴿"So it will be. Your Lord says"﴾ implies that the speaker of this is an angel, while acknowledging that His saying ﴿"O Zechariah, indeed We give you good news"﴾ is the speech of God, exalted is He, and His saying ﴿"It is easy for Me"﴾ is the speech of God, exalted is He. This is far-fetched, because if what comes before this statement and what comes after it is the speech of God, exalted is He, then how is it valid to insert these words between these two utterances? Rather, the better view is to say: the speaker of this statement is also God, exalted is He, just as when a great king promises his servant something great, the servant says, "From where will this come to me?" and the king says, "Your sovereign has guaranteed it for you," as if he is alerting by this that his being a sovereign necessitates fulfilling the promise. So it is likewise here.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verse 10:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Said: "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three nights, while sound."﴾

Within this passage there are several issues:

The first issue: Some said that Zechariah's request for a sign was to confirm the glad tidings. This is far-fetched, because by the saying of God, exalted is He, the glad tidings had already been confirmed, so making a sign apparent would not be any stronger in that respect than explicit speech. Others said: the glad tidings of the child came in an unrestricted form, so its time could not be known merely from the glad tidings, and therefore he asked for a sign by which he would know the time of its occurrence. This is the correct view.

Page 162

The second issue: They agreed that this sign was the impediment of speech for him, since mere silence while being able to speak is not a miracle. Then they differed into two views:
One of them: his tongue was bound entirely.

The second: it was impossible for him to speak to the people in the manner of address, although he was able to mention God and to recite the Torah. This second view is, in my opinion, more correct, because the binding of the tongue in an absolute sense may be due to illness, and may be due to the act of God. So Zechariah, peace be upon him, would not know that this binding was a miracle unless he knew that it was not due to illness but purely to the act of God, the Exalted, while the instruments were sound. This cannot be known except by another proof, so that proof would itself require a further proof. But if his tongue was bound from speaking with the people while he was capable of speaking the remembrance of God and reciting the Torah, he would know necessarily that this binding was not due to a cause or sickness, but purely to the act of God, and so it is established that it is a sign and a miracle. What strengthens this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three nights, while sound.﴾ He specified the speech as being with the people, and this indicates by implication that he was able to speak with other than the people.

The third issue: They differed about the meaning of ﴿sawiyyan﴾ (sound, whole). Some said it is an attribute of the three nights. Most of the exegetes said it is an attribute of Zechariah, and the meaning is: your sign is that you will not speak to the people during this period while you are sound, with no illness having befallen you.

**The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 19, Verse 11**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then he came out to his people from the mihrab (the prayer niche), and he signalled to them to glorify [God] morning and evening.﴾

Among the issues here:

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then he came out to his people from the mihrab﴾. It has been said that he had a place where he would be alone for prayer and worship, and then he would go out to his people, and at that point he inspired them (awha ilayhim). It has also been said that it was a place where he and others would pray, except that they would not enter it for prayer without his permission. They gathered, waiting for his coming out to give permission, so he came out to them while unable to speak, and he inspired them.

**The second issue:** The meaning of "he inspired them" (awha ilayhim) cannot be speech, because speech was impossible for him. So the meaning is other than speech, namely that he made it known to them, either by gesture, by a particular sign, or by writing, since all of these convey the intended meaning. They understood that what he had been promised had come to pass, so just as joy came to him, joy came to them as well, and God's honouring of him by answering him became apparent to them. Know that the most fitting interpretation of the verse is gesture, because of the saying of God, exalted is He, in Surat Al 'Imran: ﴿Your sign is that you shall not speak to people for three days except by gesture﴾ [Al 'Imran: 41]. A gesture (ramz) is not a substitute for speech.

**The third issue:** The exegetes (mufassirun) agree that by "glorification" (tasbih) he meant prayer (salah). This is permissible in the language: it is said "subhat al-duha," meaning "the prayer of the forenoon (duha)." It is related from A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, concerning the forenoon prayer: "Indeed I glorify it," meaning: indeed I perform it. Once this is established, we say: it is related from Abu al-'Aliyah that "morning" (bukrah) is the dawn prayer (salat al-fajr) and "evening" (ashiyy) is the afternoon prayer (salat al-'asr). It is also possible that they were only praying with him in his mihrab at these two prayers, and that he would come out to them and give them permission with his tongue. When his tongue became bound, he came out to them as usual and gave them permission without speech. And Allah knows best.

[Page 163]

The words of the Exalted: ﴿O Yahya, take the Book with determination.﴾ ﴿And We gave him judgment while still a boy,﴾ ﴿and tenderness from Us, and purity. He was God-fearing,﴾ ﴿and dutiful to his parents, and he was not domineering or disobedient.﴾ ﴿And peace upon him the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.﴾

Know that the Exalted described Yahya in this verse with nine attributes.

The first attribute: that he was addressed by God the Exalted, in His words: ﴿O Yahya, take the Book with determination.﴾ On this there are several issues.

The first issue: His words ﴿O Yahya, take the Book﴾ indicate that God the Exalted had brought Yahya to the level at which it is permissible to address him in this way, and so the mention of that (the preceding condition) was omitted, because the context points to it.

The second issue: the Book mentioned may be the Torah, which is God's blessing upon the Children of Israel, according to the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We gave the Children of Israel the Book, the judgment and the prophethood﴾ (al-Jathiyah: 16). It may also be a book that God specifically granted to Yahya, as God granted many prophets a book. The first is preferable, because it is better to interpret the speech here in terms of a known referent, and there is no known referent here except the Torah.

The third issue: His words ﴿with determination﴾ do not mean the ability to take hold, because that is known to everyone. Therefore it must be understood in a sense that conveys praise, namely diligence and patience in carrying out the duty of prophethood. Its essential meaning returns to the acquisition of a disposition that makes it easy to undertake what is commanded and to refrain from what is forbidden.

The second attribute: the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We gave him judgment while still a boy.﴾ Know that there are several opinions regarding "judgment" (ḥukm).

The first: it means wisdom (ḥikmah), and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Judge as the judgment of the girl of the tribe when she looked at doves swiftly coming to the watering-place."

It is understanding of the Torah and jurisprudence (fiqh) in religion.

The second, which is the view of Ma'mar, is that it is intellect. It is reported that he said: "We were not created for play."

The third: it is prophethood, for God the Exalted made his intellect firm in his childhood and revealed to him. This is because God the Exalted sent Yahya and Jesus, peace be upon them both, while they were children, unlike Moses and Muhammad, peace be upon them, who had reached maturity. The closer interpretation is that it refers to prophethood, for two reasons.

The first: God the Exalted mentioned in this verse the attributes of his nobility and excellence, and it is known that prophethood is the most noble of human attributes. Mentioning it in the context of praise is therefore more appropriate than mentioning anything else. So his prophethood must be mentioned in this verse, and there is no word suitable to indicate prophethood except this word, so it must be interpreted accordingly.

The second: judgment is that which is fit to be used to judge over others and for others absolutely, and this is not possible except through prophethood. If it is said: "How can the acquisition of intellect, understanding and prophethood in childhood be conceived?" We reply: this questioner either prohibits the breaking of custom or does not prohibit it. If he prohibits it, he has closed the door to prophecies, because the matter of prophecy rests on miracles, and miracles have no meaning except the breaking of customs. If he does not prohibit it, then this objection disappears, for the astonishment at a boy becoming intelligent is no greater than the astonishment at the splitting of the moon and the parting of the sea.

The third attribute: the words of the Exalted: ﴿and tenderness from Us.﴾ Know that "tenderness" (ḥanān) originates from ḥanīn, which is yearning and distress at separation, as one says: "the ḥanīn of the she-camel," which is her sound when she longs for her young. Al-Khalil mentioned this. In a hadith: "He, peace be upon him, used to pray towards a trunk in the mosque; when a pulpit was made for him and he moved to it, that trunk moaned until its moaning was heard." This is the original meaning. Then it was said: "So-and-so showed tenderness (taḥannana) toward so-and-so" when he was kind and merciful toward him. People have differed on describing God as al-Ḥannān (the Tender). Some permitted it and took it to mean the Compassionate and the Merciful. Others forbade it, because of what the root of the word returns to. They said: "No report has been authenticated with this word among the names of God the Exalted." Having understood this, we say: "tenderness" here has two possibilities:

[Page 164]

The first: that it is made an attribute of God.

The second: that it is made an attribute of Yahya.

As for when we make it an attribute of God the Exalted, we say: the implied meaning is "and We gave him judgment as tenderness," that is, mercy from Us. Then there are several possibilities here:

The first: that the tenderness is from God toward Yahya. The meaning is: "We gave him judgment while still a boy," then He said: "and tenderness from Us," meaning: We gave him judgment while still a boy, as tenderness from Us toward him, that is, mercy upon him, "and purity," that is, and purification for him and honouring him.

The second: that the tenderness is from God toward Zachariah, peace be upon him. It is as if the Exalted said: "We only answered Zachariah's supplication by giving him a son, and then We gave him judgment while still a boy, and tenderness from Us toward him," that is, toward Zachariah, "We did that." "And purity," that is, and purification for him from becoming one whose supplication is rejected.

The third: that the tenderness is from God the Exalted toward the community of Yahya, peace be upon him. It is as if the Exalted said: "And We gave him judgment while still a boy," "and tenderness" from Us toward his community, because of the great benefit they gained from his guidance and instruction. As for when we make it an attribute of Yahya, peace be upon him, there are several aspects:

The first: "We gave him judgment and tenderness toward Our servants," that is, showing kindness toward them and good regard for all of them in the rulings he administers over them, just as He described His Prophet, saying: ﴿It was by a mercy from God that you were gentle with them﴾ (Al 'Imran: 159), and He said: ﴿Ardently concerned for you, and to the believers gentle and merciful﴾ (al-Tawbah: 128). Then the Exalted informed that He gave him "purity," meaning that his compassion should not lead him to neglect what is obligatory, because gentleness and softness may at times result in abandoning what is obligatory. Do you not see the words of the Exalted: ﴿And let not pity for them in the religion of God take hold of you﴾ (al-Nur: 2), and He said: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you, and let them find harshness in you﴾ (al-Tawbah: 123), and He said: ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty toward the disbelievers, striving in the way of God, and not fearing the blame of any blamer﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 54).

So the meaning is: We only made for him compassion toward the servants of God together with purity from neglecting the obligations. It is also possible that "We gave him" compassion toward creation and purity from sins, so he did not disobey and did not intend any disobedience. There is another aspect in the verse, which is what is transmitted from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: "and tenderness from Us," meaning: "We gave him judgment while still a boy" in exaltation, since We made him a prophet while he was a boy, and there is no greater exaltation than this. The evidence for this is what is reported: Waraqah ibn Nawfal passed by Bilal while he was being tortured, his back pressed against the scorching sand of al-Batha', and he was saying: "One, One." Waraqah said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, if you kill him, I will certainly take him as a ḥanān," meaning: one to be exalted.

The fourth attribute: His words: ﴿and purity.﴾ On this there are several aspects:

The first: that what is meant is "and We gave him purity," that is, righteous, pure action, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Ibn Juraij.

The second: purity for those who accept from him, so that they may become pure, according to al-Hasan.

The third: "We purified him with good praise," as witnesses purify a person.

The fourth: a charity which God gave on behalf of his parents, according to al-Kalbi.

The fifth: blessing and increase, which is what Jesus, peace be upon him, said: ﴿and made me blessed wherever I am﴾ (Maryam: 31). Know that this indicates that the act of the servant is created by God the Exalted, because He made his purity and his purification from God the Exalted. Interpreting it as divine favours (alṭāf) is far-fetched, because it is a departure from the apparent meaning.

The fifth attribute: His words: ﴿He was God-fearing.﴾ You have known its meaning. In general, it contains the utmost praise, because he is the one who guards against God's prohibition by avoiding it, and guards against His command by not neglecting it. The people most worthy of this description are those who do not disobey God and do not intend disobedience, and Yahya, peace be upon him, was like this. If it is asked: "What is the meaning of ﴿He was God-fearing﴾?" and "This is at the beginning of his obligation," we reply: God the Exalted addressed the Messenger with this and informed about his condition, just as He informed about God's blessings upon him.

The sixth attribute: His words: ﴿and dutiful to his parents.﴾ This is because there is no worship after the glorification of God the Exalted equal to the glorification of the parents. For this reason He said: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and kindness to parents﴾ (al-Isra': 23).

The seventh attribute: His words: ﴿and he was not domineering.﴾ The meaning is describing him with humility and gentleness of disposition, which are among the attributes of the believers, as in His words: ﴿And lower your wing to the believers﴾ (al-Hijr: 88), and He said:

[Page 165]

﴿Had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you﴾ (Al 'Imran: 159). Also, the head of acts of worship is a person's knowledge of himself as lowly and of his Lord as great and perfect. One who knows himself as lowly and knows his Lord as perfect, how could arrogance and tyranny befit him? For this reason, when Iblis became arrogant and rebellious, he was distanced from God's mercy and from religion. It has been said: "the domineering one (jabbār) is he who sees no right owed to anyone over himself," from greatness, and from being so self-satisfied that it would not oblige him to render anyone their due. Sufyan, regarding His words ﴿domineering, disobedient﴾, said: it is the one who gives himself over to anger. The evidence for this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Do you want to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday? You only want to be a tyrant (jabbār) in the land﴾ (al-Qasas: 19). It has also been said: whoever punishes out of his own anger without right is a tyrant, because of the words of the Exalted: ﴿And when you strike, you strike as tyrants (jabbārīn)﴾ (al-Shu'ara': 130).

The eighth attribute: His words: ﴿disobedient.﴾ This is more emphatic than "disobedient" (ʿāṣī), just as "all-knowing" (ʿalīm) is more emphatic than "knowing" (ʿālim).

The ninth attribute: His words: ﴿And peace upon him the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.﴾ On this there are sayings:

The first: Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: "peace upon him" means security from God the day he was born, from Satan reaching him as he reaches all the children of Adam, "and the day he dies," that is, and security for him from the torment of the grave, "and the day he is raised alive," that is, and from the torment of the Resurrection.

The second: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: creatures are most terrified in three situations: the day one is born, when he sees himself out of what he was in; the day one dies, when he sees people he has never seen before; and the day one is raised, when he sees himself in a great gathering. So God honoured Yahya, peace be upon him, and singled him out with peace upon him in these three places.

The third: 'Abd Allah ibn Nafṭawayh said: "peace upon him the day he was born" means the first time he sees this world; "and the day he dies" means the first day in which he sees the first matter of the Hereafter; "and the day he is raised alive" means the first day in which he sees Paradise and Hell, and that is the Day of Resurrection. He said "alive" to indicate that he is among the martyrs, according to the words of the Exalted: ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord, provided for﴾ (Al 'Imran: 169).

Corollaries:

The first: this peace may be from God the Exalted, or from the angels, and in either case the indication of his nobility and excellence does not differ, because the angels do not give greetings except by God the Exalted's command.

The second: Yahya has a distinction in this peace over the other prophets, peace be upon them, such as the words: ﴿Peace upon Noah among the worlds﴾ (al-Saffat: 79), ﴿Peace upon Abraham﴾ (al-Saffat: 109), because He said "the day he was born," and this is not granted to the other prophets, peace be upon them.

The third: it is reported that Jesus, peace be upon him, said to Yahya, peace be upon him: "You are better than me, because God the Exalted gave peace upon you, and I gave peace upon myself." This is not strong, because Jesus's peace upon himself has the same status as God's peace upon Yahya, since Jesus is protected from error and does only what God commanded him.

The fourth: peace upon him the day he was born must be a bounty from God the Exalted, because nothing had preceded from him that would make it a reward for him. As for peace upon him the day he dies and the day he is raised in the gathering, it may be a reward, like praise and honour. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 12–15 (part 2 of 2):

The discussion of the benefits of this story:

The first benefit: teaching the etiquette of supplication (du'a'), and it is in several respects.

The first: His saying, ﴿a secret call﴾. This indicates that the best supplication is that which is of this kind. His exalted saying supports it: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾ (al-A'raf: 55). Also, raising the voice indicates strength and vigor, while lowering the voice indicates weakness and submissiveness. The foundation of supplication is submissiveness, and disavowing one's own power and strength, and relying upon the grace and kindness of God, exalted is He.

The second: It is recommended that one mention at the beginning of the supplication the helplessness and weakness of the self, as in His exalted saying about him: ﴿My bones have weakened and my head has glistened with grey hair﴾. Then one mentions the abundance of God's blessings, [p. 166] as in His saying: ﴿And I have never been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord﴾.

The third: The supplication should be for something connected with religion, not merely for worldly matters, as he said: ﴿And indeed I fear my relatives after me﴾.

The fourth: The supplication should be with the phrase "My Lord" (ya Rabbi), as in this passage.

The second benefit: the manifestation of the ranks of Zakariyya and Yahya, peace be upon them both. As for Zakariyya, there are several matters:

The first: the utmost of his humility within himself and his total devotion to God, exalted is He.

The second: God, exalted is He, answered his supplication.

The third: God, exalted is He, called out to him and gave him glad tidings, or the angels did, or both occurred together.

The fourth: his tongue was restrained from speech but not from glorification (tasbih).

The fifth: it is permissible for the prophets, peace be upon them, to request signs, as in His saying: ﴿My Lord, appoint for me a sign﴾.

The third benefit: God's being capable of creating a child even when both parents are at the extreme of old age, a refutation of the naturalists (ahl al-taba'i').

The fourth benefit: the validity of reasoning in religion, as in His exalted saying: ﴿And I had created you before, when you were nothing﴾.

The fifth benefit: that what is non-existent is not a thing, and the verse is explicit on this. If it is said: the intended meaning is "and you were not a thing mentioned," as in His exalted saying: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ (al-Insan: 1). We reply: the supposition of an ellipsis is contrary to the original meaning. The opponent may say: the verse indicates that the human being was not a thing, and we say so as well, because the human being is a term for composite substances in which particular accidents subsist. The composite substances described with particular accidents are not established in non-existence; what is established is the individual essences of those substances in isolation, not composed, and these are not a human being. Thus it becomes clear that the verse provides no evidence for the point in question.

The sixth benefit: God, exalted is He, mentioned this story in Surat Al 'Imran and mentioned it in this passage, so let us consider its state in both places. We say:

First: In this surah He clarified that he supplicated to his Lord but did not specify the time. In Al 'Imran He specified it with His saying: ﴿Every time Zakariyya entered upon her in the sanctuary, he found with her provision. He said, "O Maryam, from where is this for you?" She said, "It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account." There Zakariyya supplicated to his Lord, he said, "My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring"﴾ (Al 'Imran: 37–38). The meaning is that when Zakariyya, peace be upon him, saw the breaking of custom regarding Maryam, peace be upon her, he desired it for himself and so he supplicated.

Second: God, exalted is He, stated in Al 'Imran that the caller was the angels, by His saying: ﴿So the angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary﴾ (Al 'Imran: 39). In this surah, the more apparent view is that the caller, by His saying: ﴿O Zakariyya, indeed We give you good news﴾, is God, exalted is He. We have already explained that there is no contradiction between the two matters.

Third: He said in Al 'Imran: ﴿How can I have a boy when old age has already reached me and my wife is barren?﴾ (Al 'Imran: 40). So He mentioned first the old age of himself, then the barrenness of the wife. In this surah he said: ﴿How can I have a boy when my wife has been barren and I have reached an extreme old age?﴾ The answer is that the conjunction "wa" (and) does not necessarily imply sequence.

Fourth: He said in Al 'Imran: ﴿And old age has already reached me﴾ (Al 'Imran: 40), and here He said: ﴿And I have reached an extreme old age﴾. The answer is that what has reached you, you have reached.

Fifth: He said in Al 'Imran: ﴿Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gestures﴾ (Al 'Imran: 41), and here He said: ﴿Three nights, sound﴾. The answer: the two verses indicate that the intended meaning is three days with their nights, and God knows best.

The second story: the story of Maryam and the manner of the birth of Isa, peace be upon him. Know that God, exalted is He, placed the story of Yahya before the story of Isa, [p. 167] peace be upon them both, because the creation of a child from two aged, perishing parents is closer to the patterns of customary events than creating a child without a father at all. And the best methods of teaching and making understood is to proceed from the nearer to the nearer, ascending gradually to the more difficult and then the more difficult.

[Page 163]

The words of the Exalted: ﴿O Yahya, take the Book with determination.﴾ ﴿And We gave him judgment while still a boy,﴾ ﴿and tenderness from Us, and purity. He was God-fearing,﴾ ﴿and dutiful to his parents, and he was not domineering or disobedient.﴾ ﴿And peace upon him the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.﴾

Know that the Exalted described Yahya in this verse with nine attributes.

The first attribute: that he was addressed by God the Exalted, in His words: ﴿O Yahya, take the Book with determination.﴾ On this there are several issues.

The first issue: His words ﴿O Yahya, take the Book﴾ indicate that God the Exalted had brought Yahya to the level at which it is permissible to address him in this way, and so the mention of that (the preceding condition) was omitted, because the context points to it.

The second issue: the Book mentioned may be the Torah, which is God's blessing upon the Children of Israel, according to the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We gave the Children of Israel the Book, the judgment and the prophethood﴾ (al-Jathiyah: 16). It may also be a book that God specifically granted to Yahya, as God granted many prophets a book. The first is preferable, because it is better to interpret the speech here in terms of a known referent, and there is no known referent here except the Torah.

The third issue: His words ﴿with determination﴾ do not mean the ability to take hold, because that is known to everyone. Therefore it must be understood in a sense that conveys praise, namely diligence and patience in carrying out the duty of prophethood. Its essential meaning returns to the acquisition of a disposition that makes it easy to undertake what is commanded and to refrain from what is forbidden.

The second attribute: the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We gave him judgment while still a boy.﴾ Know that there are several opinions regarding "judgment" (ḥukm).

The first: it means wisdom (ḥikmah), and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Judge as the judgment of the girl of the tribe when she looked at doves swiftly coming to the watering-place."

It is understanding of the Torah and jurisprudence (fiqh) in religion.

The second, which is the view of Ma'mar, is that it is intellect. It is reported that he said: "We were not created for play."

The third: it is prophethood, for God the Exalted made his intellect firm in his childhood and revealed to him. This is because God the Exalted sent Yahya and Jesus, peace be upon them both, while they were children, unlike Moses and Muhammad, peace be upon them, who had reached maturity. The closer interpretation is that it refers to prophethood, for two reasons.

The first: God the Exalted mentioned in this verse the attributes of his nobility and excellence, and it is known that prophethood is the most noble of human attributes. Mentioning it in the context of praise is therefore more appropriate than mentioning anything else. So his prophethood must be mentioned in this verse, and there is no word suitable to indicate prophethood except this word, so it must be interpreted accordingly.

The second: judgment is that which is fit to be used to judge over others and for others absolutely, and this is not possible except through prophethood. If it is said: "How can the acquisition of intellect, understanding and prophethood in childhood be conceived?" We reply: this questioner either prohibits the breaking of custom or does not prohibit it. If he prohibits it, he has closed the door to prophecies, because the matter of prophecy rests on miracles, and miracles have no meaning except the breaking of customs. If he does not prohibit it, then this objection disappears, for the astonishment at a boy becoming intelligent is no greater than the astonishment at the splitting of the moon and the parting of the sea.

The third attribute: the words of the Exalted: ﴿and tenderness from Us.﴾ Know that "tenderness" (ḥanān) originates from ḥanīn, which is yearning and distress at separation, as one says: "the ḥanīn of the she-camel," which is her sound when she longs for her young. Al-Khalil mentioned this. In a hadith: "He, peace be upon him, used to pray towards a trunk in the mosque; when a pulpit was made for him and he moved to it, that trunk moaned until its moaning was heard." This is the original meaning. Then it was said: "So-and-so showed tenderness (taḥannana) toward so-and-so" when he was kind and merciful toward him. People have differed on describing God as al-Ḥannān (the Tender). Some permitted it and took it to mean the Compassionate and the Merciful. Others forbade it, because of what the root of the word returns to. They said: "No report has been authenticated with this word among the names of God the Exalted." Having understood this, we say: "tenderness" here has two possibilities:

[Page 164]

The first: that it is made an attribute of God.

The second: that it is made an attribute of Yahya.

As for when we make it an attribute of God the Exalted, we say: the implied meaning is "and We gave him judgment as tenderness," that is, mercy from Us. Then there are several possibilities here:

The first: that the tenderness is from God toward Yahya. The meaning is: "We gave him judgment while still a boy," then He said: "and tenderness from Us," meaning: We gave him judgment while still a boy, as tenderness from Us toward him, that is, mercy upon him, "and purity," that is, and purification for him and honouring him.

The second: that the tenderness is from God toward Zachariah, peace be upon him. It is as if the Exalted said: "We only answered Zachariah's supplication by giving him a son, and then We gave him judgment while still a boy, and tenderness from Us toward him," that is, toward Zachariah, "We did that." "And purity," that is, and purification for him from becoming one whose supplication is rejected.

The third: that the tenderness is from God the Exalted toward the community of Yahya, peace be upon him. It is as if the Exalted said: "And We gave him judgment while still a boy," "and tenderness" from Us toward his community, because of the great benefit they gained from his guidance and instruction. As for when we make it an attribute of Yahya, peace be upon him, there are several aspects:

The first: "We gave him judgment and tenderness toward Our servants," that is, showing kindness toward them and good regard for all of them in the rulings he administers over them, just as He described His Prophet, saying: ﴿It was by a mercy from God that you were gentle with them﴾ (Al 'Imran: 159), and He said: ﴿Ardently concerned for you, and to the believers gentle and merciful﴾ (al-Tawbah: 128). Then the Exalted informed that He gave him "purity," meaning that his compassion should not lead him to neglect what is obligatory, because gentleness and softness may at times result in abandoning what is obligatory. Do you not see the words of the Exalted: ﴿And let not pity for them in the religion of God take hold of you﴾ (al-Nur: 2), and He said: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you, and let them find harshness in you﴾ (al-Tawbah: 123), and He said: ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty toward the disbelievers, striving in the way of God, and not fearing the blame of any blamer﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 54).

So the meaning is: We only made for him compassion toward the servants of God together with purity from neglecting the obligations. It is also possible that "We gave him" compassion toward creation and purity from sins, so he did not disobey and did not intend any disobedience. There is another aspect in the verse, which is what is transmitted from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: "and tenderness from Us," meaning: "We gave him judgment while still a boy" in exaltation, since We made him a prophet while he was a boy, and there is no greater exaltation than this. The evidence for this is what is reported: Waraqah ibn Nawfal passed by Bilal while he was being tortured, his back pressed against the scorching sand of al-Batha', and he was saying: "One, One." Waraqah said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, if you kill him, I will certainly take him as a ḥanān," meaning: one to be exalted.

The fourth attribute: His words: ﴿and purity.﴾ On this there are several aspects:

The first: that what is meant is "and We gave him purity," that is, righteous, pure action, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Ibn Juraij.

The second: purity for those who accept from him, so that they may become pure, according to al-Hasan.

The third: "We purified him with good praise," as witnesses purify a person.

The fourth: a charity which God gave on behalf of his parents, according to al-Kalbi.

The fifth: blessing and increase, which is what Jesus, peace be upon him, said: ﴿and made me blessed wherever I am﴾ (Maryam: 31). Know that this indicates that the act of the servant is created by God the Exalted, because He made his purity and his purification from God the Exalted. Interpreting it as divine favours (alṭāf) is far-fetched, because it is a departure from the apparent meaning.

The fifth attribute: His words: ﴿He was God-fearing.﴾ You have known its meaning. In general, it contains the utmost praise, because he is the one who guards against God's prohibition by avoiding it, and guards against His command by not neglecting it. The people most worthy of this description are those who do not disobey God and do not intend disobedience, and Yahya, peace be upon him, was like this. If it is asked: "What is the meaning of ﴿He was God-fearing﴾?" and "This is at the beginning of his obligation," we reply: God the Exalted addressed the Messenger with this and informed about his condition, just as He informed about God's blessings upon him.

The sixth attribute: His words: ﴿and dutiful to his parents.﴾ This is because there is no worship after the glorification of God the Exalted equal to the glorification of the parents. For this reason He said: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and kindness to parents﴾ (al-Isra': 23).

The seventh attribute: His words: ﴿and he was not domineering.﴾ The meaning is describing him with humility and gentleness of disposition, which are among the attributes of the believers, as in His words: ﴿And lower your wing to the believers﴾ (al-Hijr: 88), and He said:

[Page 165]

﴿Had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you﴾ (Al 'Imran: 159). Also, the head of acts of worship is a person's knowledge of himself as lowly and of his Lord as great and perfect. One who knows himself as lowly and knows his Lord as perfect, how could arrogance and tyranny befit him? For this reason, when Iblis became arrogant and rebellious, he was distanced from God's mercy and from religion. It has been said: "the domineering one (jabbār) is he who sees no right owed to anyone over himself," from greatness, and from being so self-satisfied that it would not oblige him to render anyone their due. Sufyan, regarding His words ﴿domineering, disobedient﴾, said: it is the one who gives himself over to anger. The evidence for this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Do you want to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday? You only want to be a tyrant (jabbār) in the land﴾ (al-Qasas: 19). It has also been said: whoever punishes out of his own anger without right is a tyrant, because of the words of the Exalted: ﴿And when you strike, you strike as tyrants (jabbārīn)﴾ (al-Shu'ara': 130).

The eighth attribute: His words: ﴿disobedient.﴾ This is more emphatic than "disobedient" (ʿāṣī), just as "all-knowing" (ʿalīm) is more emphatic than "knowing" (ʿālim).

The ninth attribute: His words: ﴿And peace upon him the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.﴾ On this there are sayings:

The first: Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: "peace upon him" means security from God the day he was born, from Satan reaching him as he reaches all the children of Adam, "and the day he dies," that is, and security for him from the torment of the grave, "and the day he is raised alive," that is, and from the torment of the Resurrection.

The second: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: creatures are most terrified in three situations: the day one is born, when he sees himself out of what he was in; the day one dies, when he sees people he has never seen before; and the day one is raised, when he sees himself in a great gathering. So God honoured Yahya, peace be upon him, and singled him out with peace upon him in these three places.

The third: 'Abd Allah ibn Nafṭawayh said: "peace upon him the day he was born" means the first time he sees this world; "and the day he dies" means the first day in which he sees the first matter of the Hereafter; "and the day he is raised alive" means the first day in which he sees Paradise and Hell, and that is the Day of Resurrection. He said "alive" to indicate that he is among the martyrs, according to the words of the Exalted: ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord, provided for﴾ (Al 'Imran: 169).

Corollaries:

The first: this peace may be from God the Exalted, or from the angels, and in either case the indication of his nobility and excellence does not differ, because the angels do not give greetings except by God the Exalted's command.

The second: Yahya has a distinction in this peace over the other prophets, peace be upon them, such as the words: ﴿Peace upon Noah among the worlds﴾ (al-Saffat: 79), ﴿Peace upon Abraham﴾ (al-Saffat: 109), because He said "the day he was born," and this is not granted to the other prophets, peace be upon them.

The third: it is reported that Jesus, peace be upon him, said to Yahya, peace be upon him: "You are better than me, because God the Exalted gave peace upon you, and I gave peace upon myself." This is not strong, because Jesus's peace upon himself has the same status as God's peace upon Yahya, since Jesus is protected from error and does only what God commanded him.

The fourth: peace upon him the day he was born must be a bounty from God the Exalted, because nothing had preceded from him that would make it a reward for him. As for peace upon him the day he dies and the day he is raised in the gathering, it may be a reward, like praise and honour. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 12–15 (part 2 of 2):

The discussion of the benefits of this story:

The first benefit: teaching the etiquette of supplication (du'a'), and it is in several respects.

The first: His saying, ﴿a secret call﴾. This indicates that the best supplication is that which is of this kind. His exalted saying supports it: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾ (al-A'raf: 55). Also, raising the voice indicates strength and vigor, while lowering the voice indicates weakness and submissiveness. The foundation of supplication is submissiveness, and disavowing one's own power and strength, and relying upon the grace and kindness of God, exalted is He.

The second: It is recommended that one mention at the beginning of the supplication the helplessness and weakness of the self, as in His exalted saying about him: ﴿My bones have weakened and my head has glistened with grey hair﴾. Then one mentions the abundance of God's blessings, [p. 166] as in His saying: ﴿And I have never been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord﴾.

The third: The supplication should be for something connected with religion, not merely for worldly matters, as he said: ﴿And indeed I fear my relatives after me﴾.

The fourth: The supplication should be with the phrase "My Lord" (ya Rabbi), as in this passage.

The second benefit: the manifestation of the ranks of Zakariyya and Yahya, peace be upon them both. As for Zakariyya, there are several matters:

The first: the utmost of his humility within himself and his total devotion to God, exalted is He.

The second: God, exalted is He, answered his supplication.

The third: God, exalted is He, called out to him and gave him glad tidings, or the angels did, or both occurred together.

The fourth: his tongue was restrained from speech but not from glorification (tasbih).

The fifth: it is permissible for the prophets, peace be upon them, to request signs, as in His saying: ﴿My Lord, appoint for me a sign﴾.

The third benefit: God's being capable of creating a child even when both parents are at the extreme of old age, a refutation of the naturalists (ahl al-taba'i').
