Then the Exalted informed that He gave him "purity," meaning that his compassion should not lead him to neglect what is obligatory, because gentleness and softness may at times result in abandoning what is obligatory. Do you not see the words of the Exalted: ﴿And let not pity for them in the religion of God take hold of you﴾ (al-Nur: 2), and He said: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you, and let them find harshness in you﴾ (al-Tawbah: 123), and He said: ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty toward the disbelievers, striving in the way of God, and not fearing the blame of any blamer﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 54).

So the meaning is: We only made for him compassion toward the servants of God together with purity from neglecting the obligations. It is also possible that "We gave him" compassion toward creation and purity from sins, so he did not disobey and did not intend any disobedience. There is another aspect in the verse, which is what is transmitted from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: "and tenderness from Us," meaning: "We gave him judgment while still a boy" in exaltation, since We made him a prophet while he was a boy, and there is no greater exaltation than this. The evidence for this is what is reported: Waraqah ibn Nawfal passed by Bilal while he was being tortured, his back pressed against the scorching sand of al-Batha', and he was saying: "One, One." Waraqah said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, if you kill him, I will certainly take him as a ḥanān," meaning: one to be exalted.

The fourth attribute: His words: ﴿and purity.﴾ On this there are several aspects:

The first: that what is meant is "and We gave him purity," that is, righteous, pure action, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Ibn Juraij.

The second: purity for those who accept from him, so that they may become pure, according to al-Hasan.

The third: "We purified him with good praise," as witnesses purify a person.

The fourth: a charity which God gave on behalf of his parents, according to al-Kalbi.

The fifth: blessing and increase, which is what Jesus, peace be upon him, said: ﴿and made me blessed wherever I am﴾ (Maryam: 31). Know that this indicates that the act of the servant is created by God the Exalted, because He made his purity and his purification from God the Exalted. Interpreting it as divine favours (alṭāf) is far-fetched, because it is a departure from the apparent meaning.

The fifth attribute: His words: ﴿He was God-fearing.﴾ You have known its meaning. In general, it contains the utmost praise, because he is the one who guards against God's prohibition by avoiding it, and guards against His command by not neglecting it. The people most worthy of this description are those who do not disobey God and do not intend disobedience, and Yahya, peace be upon him, was like this. If it is asked: "What is the meaning of ﴿He was God-fearing﴾?" and "This is at the beginning of his obligation," we reply: God the Exalted addressed the Messenger with this and informed about his condition, just as He informed about God's blessings upon him.

The sixth attribute: His words: ﴿and dutiful to his parents.﴾ This is because there is no worship after the glorification of God the Exalted equal to the glorification of the parents. For this reason He said: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and kindness to parents﴾ (al-Isra': 23).

The seventh attribute: His words: ﴿and he was not domineering.﴾ The meaning is describing him with humility and gentleness of disposition, which are among the attributes of the believers, as in His words: ﴿And lower your wing to the believers﴾ (al-Hijr: 88), and He said:

[Page 165]

﴿Had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you﴾ (Al 'Imran: 159). Also, the head of acts of worship is a person's knowledge of himself as lowly and of his Lord as great and perfect. One who knows himself as lowly and knows his Lord as perfect, how could arrogance and tyranny befit him? For this reason, when Iblis became arrogant and rebellious, he was distanced from God's mercy and from religion. It has been said: "the domineering one (jabbār) is he who sees no right owed to anyone over himself," from greatness, and from being so self-satisfied that it would not oblige him to render anyone their due. Sufyan, regarding His words ﴿domineering, disobedient﴾, said: it is the one who gives himself over to anger. The evidence for this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Do you want to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday? You only want to be a tyrant (jabbār) in the land﴾ (al-Qasas: 19). It has also been said: whoever punishes out of his own anger without right is a tyrant, because of the words of the Exalted: ﴿And when you strike, you strike as tyrants (jabbārīn)﴾ (al-Shu'ara': 130).

The eighth attribute: His words: ﴿disobedient.﴾ This is more emphatic than "disobedient" (ʿāṣī), just as "all-knowing" (ʿalīm) is more emphatic than "knowing" (ʿālim).

The ninth attribute: His words: ﴿And peace upon him the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.﴾ On this there are sayings:

The first: Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: "peace upon him" means security from God the day he was born, from Satan reaching him as he reaches all the children of Adam, "and the day he dies," that is, and security for him from the torment of the grave, "and the day he is raised alive," that is, and from the torment of the Resurrection.

The second: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: creatures are most terrified in three situations: the day one is born, when he sees himself out of what he was in; the day one dies, when he sees people he has never seen before; and the day one is raised, when he sees himself in a great gathering. So God honoured Yahya, peace be upon him, and singled him out with peace upon him in these three places.

The third: 'Abd Allah ibn Nafṭawayh said: "peace upon him the day he was born" means the first time he sees this world; "and the day he dies" means the first day in which he sees the first matter of the Hereafter; "and the day he is raised alive" means the first day in which he sees Paradise and Hell, and that is the Day of Resurrection. He said "alive" to indicate that he is among the martyrs, according to the words of the Exalted: ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord, provided for﴾ (Al 'Imran: 169).

The first: this peace may be from God the Exalted, or from the angels, and in either case the indication of his nobility and excellence does not differ, because the angels do not give greetings except by God the Exalted's command.

The second: Yahya has a distinction in this peace over the other prophets, peace be upon them, such as the words: ﴿Peace upon Noah among the worlds﴾ (al-Saffat: 79), ﴿Peace upon Abraham﴾ (al-Saffat: 109), because He said "the day he was born," and this is not granted to the other prophets, peace be upon them.

The third: it is reported that Jesus, peace be upon him, said to Yahya, peace be upon him: "You are better than me, because God the Exalted gave peace upon you, and I gave peace upon myself." This is not strong, because Jesus's peace upon himself has the same status as God's peace upon Yahya, since Jesus is protected from error and does only what God commanded him.

The fourth: peace upon him the day he was born must be a bounty from God the Exalted, because nothing had preceded from him that would make it a reward for him. As for peace upon him the day he dies and the day he is raised in the gathering, it may be a reward, like praise and honour. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 12–15 (part 2 of 2):

The discussion of the benefits of this story:

The first benefit: teaching the etiquette of supplication (du'a'), and it is in several respects.

The first: His saying, ﴿a secret call﴾. This indicates that the best supplication is that which is of this kind. His exalted saying supports it: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾ (al-A'raf: 55). Also, raising the voice indicates strength and vigor, while lowering the voice indicates weakness and submissiveness. The foundation of supplication is submissiveness, and disavowing one's own power and strength, and relying upon the grace and kindness of God, exalted is He.

The second: It is recommended that one mention at the beginning of the supplication the helplessness and weakness of the self, as in His exalted saying about him: ﴿My bones have weakened and my head has glistened with grey hair﴾. Then one mentions the abundance of God's blessings, [p. 166] as in His saying: ﴿And I have never been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord﴾.

The third: The supplication should be for something connected with religion, not merely for worldly matters, as he said: ﴿And indeed I fear my relatives after me﴾.

The fourth: The supplication should be with the phrase "My Lord" (ya Rabbi), as in this passage.

The second benefit: the manifestation of the ranks of Zakariyya and Yahya, peace be upon them both. As for Zakariyya, there are several matters:

The first: the utmost of his humility within himself and his total devotion to God, exalted is He.

The second: God, exalted is He, answered his supplication.

The third: God, exalted is He, called out to him and gave him glad tidings, or the angels did, or both occurred together.

The fourth: his tongue was restrained from speech but not from glorification (tasbih).

The fifth: it is permissible for the prophets, peace be upon them, to request signs, as in His saying: ﴿My Lord, appoint for me a sign﴾.

The third benefit: God's being capable of creating a child even when both parents are at the extreme of old age, a refutation of the naturalists (ahl al-taba'i').

The fourth benefit: the validity of reasoning in religion, as in His exalted saying: ﴿And I had created you before, when you were nothing﴾.

The fifth benefit: that what is non-existent is not a thing, and the verse is explicit on this. If it is said: the intended meaning is "and you were not a thing mentioned," as in His exalted saying: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ (al-Insan: 1). We reply: the supposition of an ellipsis is contrary to the original meaning. The opponent may say: the verse indicates that the human being was not a thing, and we say so as well, because the human being is a term for composite substances in which particular accidents subsist. The composite substances described with particular accidents are not established in non-existence; what is established is the individual essences of those substances in isolation, not composed, and these are not a human being. Thus it becomes clear that the verse provides no evidence for the point in question.

The sixth benefit: God, exalted is He, mentioned this story in Surat Al 'Imran and mentioned it in this passage, so let us consider its state in both places. We say:

First: In this surah He clarified that he supplicated to his Lord but did not specify the time. In Al 'Imran He specified it with His saying: ﴿Every time Zakariyya entered upon her in the sanctuary, he found with her provision. He said, "O Maryam, from where is this for you?" She said, "It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account." There Zakariyya supplicated to his Lord, he said, "My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring"﴾ (Al 'Imran: 37–38). The meaning is that when Zakariyya, peace be upon him, saw the breaking of custom regarding Maryam, peace be upon her, he desired it for himself and so he supplicated.

Second: God, exalted is He, stated in Al 'Imran that the caller was the angels, by His saying: ﴿So the angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary﴾ (Al 'Imran: 39). In this surah, the more apparent view is that the caller, by His saying: ﴿O Zakariyya, indeed We give you good news﴾, is God, exalted is He. We have already explained that there is no contradiction between the two matters.

Third: He said in Al 'Imran: ﴿How can I have a boy when old age has already reached me and my wife is barren?﴾ (Al 'Imran: 40). So He mentioned first the old age of himself, then the barrenness of the wife. In this surah he said: ﴿How can I have a boy when my wife has been barren and I have reached an extreme old age?﴾ The answer is that the conjunction "wa" (and) does not necessarily imply sequence.

Fourth: He said in Al 'Imran: ﴿And old age has already reached me﴾ (Al 'Imran: 40), and here He said: ﴿And I have reached an extreme old age﴾. The answer is that what has reached you, you have reached.

Fifth: He said in Al 'Imran: ﴿Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gestures﴾ (Al 'Imran: 41), and here He said: ﴿Three nights, sound﴾. The answer: the two verses indicate that the intended meaning is three days with their nights, and God knows best.

The second story: the story of Maryam and the manner of the birth of Isa, peace be upon him. Know that God, exalted is He, placed the story of Yahya before the story of Isa, [p. 167] peace be upon them both, because the creation of a child from two aged, perishing parents is closer to the patterns of customary events than creating a child without a father at all. And the best methods of teaching and making understood is to proceed from the nearer to the nearer, ascending gradually to the more difficult and then the more difficult.

[Page 163]

The words of the Exalted: ﴿O Yahya, take the Book with determination.﴾ ﴿And We gave him judgment while still a boy,﴾ ﴿and tenderness from Us, and purity. He was God-fearing,﴾ ﴿and dutiful to his parents, and he was not domineering or disobedient.﴾ ﴿And peace upon him the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.﴾

Know that the Exalted described Yahya in this verse with nine attributes.

The first attribute: that he was addressed by God the Exalted, in His words: ﴿O Yahya, take the Book with determination.﴾ On this there are several issues.

The first issue: His words ﴿O Yahya, take the Book﴾ indicate that God the Exalted had brought Yahya to the level at which it is permissible to address him in this way, and so the mention of that (the preceding condition) was omitted, because the context points to it.

The second issue: the Book mentioned may be the Torah, which is God's blessing upon the Children of Israel, according to the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We gave the Children of Israel the Book, the judgment and the prophethood﴾ (al-Jathiyah: 16). It may also be a book that God specifically granted to Yahya, as God granted many prophets a book. The first is preferable, because it is better to interpret the speech here in terms of a known referent, and there is no known referent here except the Torah.

The third issue: His words ﴿with determination﴾ do not mean the ability to take hold, because that is known to everyone. Therefore it must be understood in a sense that conveys praise, namely diligence and patience in carrying out the duty of prophethood. Its essential meaning returns to the acquisition of a disposition that makes it easy to undertake what is commanded and to refrain from what is forbidden.

The second attribute: the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We gave him judgment while still a boy.﴾ Know that there are several opinions regarding "judgment" (ḥukm).

The first: it means wisdom (ḥikmah), and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Judge as the judgment of the girl of the tribe when she looked at doves swiftly coming to the watering-place."

It is understanding of the Torah and jurisprudence (fiqh) in religion.

The second, which is the view of Ma'mar, is that it is intellect. It is reported that he said: "We were not created for play."

The third: it is prophethood, for God the Exalted made his intellect firm in his childhood and revealed to him. This is because God the Exalted sent Yahya and Jesus, peace be upon them both, while they were children, unlike Moses and Muhammad, peace be upon them, who had reached maturity. The closer interpretation is that it refers to prophethood, for two reasons.

The first: God the Exalted mentioned in this verse the attributes of his nobility and excellence, and it is known that prophethood is the most noble of human attributes. Mentioning it in the context of praise is therefore more appropriate than mentioning anything else. So his prophethood must be mentioned in this verse, and there is no word suitable to indicate prophethood except this word, so it must be interpreted accordingly.

The second: judgment is that which is fit to be used to judge over others and for others absolutely, and this is not possible except through prophethood. If it is said: "How can the acquisition of intellect, understanding and prophethood in childhood be conceived?" We reply: this questioner either prohibits the breaking of custom or does not prohibit it. If he prohibits it, he has closed the door to prophecies, because the matter of prophecy rests on miracles, and miracles have no meaning except the breaking of customs. If he does not prohibit it, then this objection disappears, for the astonishment at a boy becoming intelligent is no greater than the astonishment at the splitting of the moon and the parting of the sea.

Al-Khalil mentioned this. This is the original meaning. Then it was said: "So-and-so showed tenderness (taḥannana) toward so-and-so" when he was kind and merciful toward him. People have differed on describing God as al-Ḥannān (the Tender). Some permitted it and took it to mean the Compassionate and the Merciful. Others forbade it, because of what the root of the word returns to. They said: "No report has been authenticated with this word among the names of God the Exalted." Having understood this, we say: "tenderness" here has two possibilities:

The first: that it is made an attribute of God.

The second: that it is made an attribute of Yahya.

As for when we make it an attribute of God the Exalted, we say: the implied meaning is "and We gave him judgment as tenderness," that is, mercy from Us. Then there are several possibilities here:

The first: that the tenderness is from God toward Yahya. It is as if the Exalted said: "We only answered Zachariah's supplication by giving him a son, and then We gave him judgment while still a boy, and tenderness from Us toward him," that is, toward Zachariah, "We did that." The third: God, exalted is He, called out to him and gave him glad tidings, or the angels did, or both occurred together.

The fourth: his tongue was restrained from speech but not from glorification (tasbih).

The fifth: it is permissible for the prophets, peace be upon them, to request signs, as in His saying: ﴿My Lord, appoint for me a sign﴾.

The third benefit: God's being capable of creating a child even when both parents are at the extreme of old age, a refutation of the naturalists (ahl al-taba'i').

The fourth benefit: the validity of reasoning in religion, as in His exalted saying: ﴿And I had created you before, when you were nothing﴾.

The fifth benefit: that what is non-existent is not a thing, and the verse is explicit on this. If it is said: the intended meaning is "and you were not a thing mentioned," as in His exalted saying: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ (al-Insan: 1). We reply: the supposition of an ellipsis is contrary to the original meaning. The opponent may say: the verse indicates that the human being was not a thing, and we say so as well, because the human being is a term for composite substances in which particular accidents subsist. The composite substances described with particular accidents are not established in non-existence; what is established is the individual essences of those substances in isolation, not composed, and these are not a human being. Thus it becomes clear that the verse provides no evidence for the point in question.

The sixth benefit: God, exalted is He, mentioned this story in Surat Al 'Imran and mentioned it in this passage, so let us consider its state in both places. We say:

First: In this surah He clarified that he supplicated to his Lord but did not specify the time. In Al 'Imran He specified it with His saying: ﴿Every time Zakariyya entered upon her in the sanctuary, he found with her provision. He said, "O Maryam, from where is this for you?" She said, "It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account." There Zakariyya supplicated to his Lord, he said, "My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring"﴾ (Al 'Imran: 37–38). The meaning is that when Zakariyya, peace be upon him, saw the breaking of custom regarding Maryam, peace be upon her, he desired it for himself and so he supplicated.

Second: God, exalted is He, stated in Al 'Imran that the caller was the angels, by His saying: ﴿So the angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary﴾ (Al 'Imran: 39). In this surah, the more apparent view is that the caller, by His saying: ﴿O Zakariyya, indeed We give you good news﴾, is God, exalted is He. We have already explained that there is no contradiction between the two matters.

Third: He said in Al 'Imran: ﴿How can I have a boy when old age has already reached me and my wife is barren?﴾ (Al 'Imran: 40). So He mentioned first the old age of himself, then the barrenness of the wife. In this surah he said: ﴿How can I have a boy when my wife has been barren and I have reached an extreme old age?﴾ The answer is that the conjunction "wa" (and) does not necessarily imply sequence.

Fourth: He said in Al 'Imran: ﴿And old age has already reached me﴾ (Al 'Imran: 40), and here He said: ﴿And I have reached an extreme old age﴾. The answer is that what has reached you, you have reached.

Fifth: He said in Al 'Imran: ﴿Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gestures﴾ (Al 'Imran: 41), and here He said: ﴿Three nights, sound﴾. The answer: the two verses indicate that the intended meaning is three days with their nights, and God knows best.

The second story: the story of Maryam and the manner of the birth of Isa, peace be upon him. Know that God, exalted is He, placed the story of Yahya before the story of Isa, [p. 167] peace be upon them both, because the creation of a child from two aged, perishing parents is closer to the patterns of customary events than creating a child without a father at all. And the best methods of teaching and making understood is to proceed from the nearer to the nearer, ascending gradually to the more difficult and then the more difficult.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 16–17:

Concerning this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: "idh" (when) is a substitute (badal) for "Maryam," a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), because times include what occurs within them. And it is said that the purpose of mentioning Maryam is to mention the time of the occurrence of this wondrous story concerning her.

The second issue: al-nabdh (the root meaning is to throw or cast away), and al-intibadh is its ifti'al form. From it comes: ﴿So they cast it behind their backs﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187]. And "intabadhat" means she withdrew (tanahhat). It is said: "He sat in a nubdhah (a corner) away from the people," and nabdhah, with the nun vowelled with a damma or a fatha, means a side or direction. This is when someone sits close to you such that if you threw something to him it would reach him. "Nabadhtu al-shay'" means I threw the thing. From it comes al-nabidh (date wine), because it is thrown into the vessel. Its original form is manbudh, which was changed to the pattern fa'il. From it the foundling is called manbudh, because he is thrown away. From it comes the prohibition of al-munabadhah in sale, which is that one says: "If I throw this garment or this pebble to you, the sale is binding." Having understood this, we say: the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿When she withdrew from her family to an eastern place﴾ mean she distanced herself and separated herself swiftly to a place lying on the eastern side. Then Allah the Exalted explained that, along with this, she took a screen apart from her family, a concealing veil. The apparent meaning of this is that she did not limit herself to separating herself to a place, but placed between herself and them a barrier of a wall or something else. It is possible that she placed a screen between herself and them, and this second view is more apparent than the first. Then there must be a sound reason for her seclusion, which is not mentioned. The exegetes differed concerning it in several ways:

The first: when she saw menstruation, she withdrew from her usual place of worship in order to wait for purity, so that she could bathe and return. When she became pure, Jibril (peace be upon him) came to her.

The second: she sought solitude so that she would not be distracted from worship.

The third: she sat in an eastern chamber to bathe from menstruation, screened by something that concealed her.

The fourth: she had, in the house of her sister's husband Zakariyya, a separate sanctuary in which she lived. When Zakariyya went out, he would lock her in. So she wished of Allah to find solitude in the mountain, in order to delouse her head. The roof then parted for her, and she went out into the wilderness and sat in an eastern hollow behind the mountain, and then the angel came to her.

The fifth: she became thirsty and went out into the wilderness to fetch water. Know that all these views are possible, and there is nothing in the wording that indicates the preference of any one of them.

The third issue: the eastern place is the one lying to the east of Jerusalem, or to the east of her house. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "I know more than anyone of Allah's creation why the Christians took the east as a qibla, due to His saying: ﴿an eastern place﴾; so they took the birth of 'Isa as a qibla."

The fourth issue: when she sat in that place, Allah sent to her the Spirit (al-Ruh). The exegetes differed concerning this Spirit. Most said: it is Jibril (peace be upon him). Abu Muslim said: it is the spirit which took the form of a human in her womb. The first is closer to the truth, because Jibril (peace be upon him) is called a spirit. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ ﴿upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 193, 194]. He was called a spirit because he is spiritual (ruhani). It is also said he was created from the Spirit, or because religion lives through him, or Allah named him by His Spirit figuratively, out of love for him and closeness, as you say to your beloved, "my spirit." Abu Haywa read "rawhana" with a fatha, because he is the cause of what gives rest (rawh) to the servants, and attaining rest (rawh) with Allah, which is the promise to the righteous in His saying: ﴿As for if he is among those brought near﴾ ﴿then rest and sweet provision and a Garden of Delight﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88, 89], or because he is among those brought near, and they are those promised rest, meaning "our Close One and the one of our rest." When it is established that he is called a spirit, then here it must be that this is what is meant, because He said: ﴿I am only a messenger of your Lord to give you a pure boy﴾ [Maryam: 19], and this is fitting only for Jibril (peace be upon him). They differed about how he appeared to her.

The first: he appeared to her in the form of a beardless young man of handsome face and well-proportioned form.

The second: he appeared to her in the form of a companion of hers, named Yusuf, one of the servants of Bayt al-Maqdis. All of these are possible, and the wording gives no indication of specifying any one. Then he said: He only appeared to her in human form so that she would be at ease with his speech and not repelled by him; for had he appeared to her in the form of angels, she would have recoiled from him and not been able to listen to his speech. There are then difficulties here:

One of them: if it were permissible for an angel to appear in the form of a specific human, then we could not be certain that this person whom I see now is Zayd whom I saw yesterday, since it is possible that an angel or a jinn took his form. Opening this door leads to sophistry. It may be said that this is only permissible in the time of prophethood, but in our time it is not permissible. We reply: this distinction is known only through evidence, so the one ignorant of that evidence must not be certain that this person he sees now is the person he saw yesterday.

The second: it has come in reports that Jibril (peace be upon him) is a very great being. How then did that great being's body become the size of a human body, either by its parts falling away and its structure dispersing, so that Jibril would no longer remain, or by its parts interpenetrating, which entails the interpenetration of parts, and that is impossible?

The third: if we permit Jibril (peace be upon him) to appear in the form of a human, why not permit his appearance in the form of a body smaller than a human, even a fly, a gnat or a mosquito? And it is known that every doctrine that leads to this is false.

The fourth: permitting this leads to the undermining of mass-transmitted report (tawatur). Perhaps the one who fought on the day of Badr was not Muhammad but another person resembling him, and likewise for all.

As for the answer to the first: that permission is binding on all, because whoever acknowledges the world's need for a Creator who chooses has already affirmed that Allah the Exalted is able to create another person like Zayd in his form and features. And if we permit that, then doubt arises as to whether the Zayd we now see is the one we saw yesterday or not. And whoever denies the Creator who chooses and attributes events to the connections of the stars and the configurations of the spheres is bound to permit that a strange connection might occur in the spheres which brings about the existence of a person like Zayd in all matters, and then the said permission returns.

As for the answer to the second: it is not impossible that Jibril (peace be upon him) has primary parts and superior parts, and the primary parts are very few, so he is then able to assume the form of a human. This is if we take him to be corporeal. But if we take him to be spiritual, then what is the improbability in his clothing himself at one time in a great frame and at another time in a small frame?

As for the answer to the third: the basic permission exists in reason, and its corruption is known only through the evidence of revelation. This is the answer to the fourth question. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verse 18:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿She said, "I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing."﴾

There are several interpretations of it:

First: She meant: if it is hoped from you that you will fear God, and that this will be achieved by seeking refuge in Him, then I seek refuge in Him from you. This is in the utmost beauty, because she knew that seeking refuge affects only the God-fearing person. It is like His saying: ﴿And leave what remains of usury, if you are believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 278], meaning: the condition of faith necessitates this, not that God is feared in one state and not in another.

Second: The meaning of "if you are" is: "you are God-fearing" in that you have deemed it permissible to look at me and to be alone with me.

Third: In that time there was a wicked man named Taqi who pursued women, so Maryam, peace be upon her, thought that this visible person was that Taqi. The first is the preferred interpretation.

He said, "I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy" (﴿قالَ إنَّما أنا رَسُولُ رَبِّكِ لِأهَبَ لَكِ غُلامًا زَكِيًّا﴾).

Issues:

**First issue:** When Jibril (Gabriel) saw her fear, he said, "I am only a messenger of your Lord" (﴿إنَّما أنا رَسُولُ رَبِّكِ﴾), so that the fear would leave her. But fear does not leave merely by this statement. There must be some evidence showing that he is Jibril, peace be upon him, and not one of the people. Here it is possible that a miracle appeared by which she recognised Jibril, peace be upon him. It is also possible that she had learned the attributes of the angels from Zakariyya, peace be upon him, so when he said to her, "I am only a messenger of your Lord," he showed her something from inside his body by which she knew he was an angel. That would be the knowledge (of his identity).

Al-Qadi ʿAbd al-Jabbar asked about this in his own tafsir. He said: if she was not a prophetess according to you, and if it is your position that God, exalted is He, sent to His creation only men, then how is this correct? He answered that this happened during the time of Zakariyya, peace be upon him, who was a messenger, and that she knew all of this. But this is weak, because if the miracle was performed for a prophet, then at the very least he, peace be upon him, must have known about it. Zakariyya did not have knowledge of these events, so how is it permissible to make it a miracle for him? Rather, the truth is that this is either a karama (a marvel granted to a righteous person) for Maryam, or an irhas (a sign preceding a prophet's mission) for ʿIsa, peace be upon him.

**Second issue:** Ibn ʿĀmir and Nāfiʿ read ﴿لِيَهَبَ﴾ with a fatha-marked yāʾ after the lām, meaning "that God may give you." The rest read it with an open hamza after it, ﴿لِأهَبَ﴾. As for His saying ﴿لِأهَبَ لَكِ﴾, there are two figurative explanations:

The first: the giving took place through his hand, because he was the one who blew into her collar by God's command. So He made him as if he himself gave to her. Attributing an action to what is its cause is a common usage. God, exalted is He, said about the idols: ﴿إنَّهُنَّ أضْلَلْنَ كَثِيرًا مِنَ النّاسِ﴾ [Ibrahim: 36] ("They have led many of the people astray").

The second: when Jibril, peace be upon him, gave her this good news, that true good news took the place of the gift. If someone says: what is the proof that Jibril, peace be upon him, cannot assemble parts, and create life, reason and speech in them? What is said in response is: Jibril, peace be upon him, is a body, and a body cannot do these things. That he is a body is because he is originated (ḥādith), and every originated thing is either occupying a space (mutaḥayyiz) or subsisting in something that occupies a space. That a body cannot do these things is because, if a body could do that, every body could do it, since bodies are alike. This is weak, because the opponent can say: we do not accept that every originated thing is either occupying a space or subsisting in something that does. Rather, there exist entities that subsist by themselves, neither occupying a space nor subsisting in something that occupies a space. It does not follow from their being so that they are like the essence of God, exalted is He, because sharing in positive attributes does not require similarity, so how much less in negative attributes. Suppose we grant that he is a body; why do you say a body cannot do this? As for your claim that bodies are alike: we mean by it either that they are alike in being located in spaces and moving in directions, or we mean that they are alike in their whole quiddities. The first we accept, but their being in spaces consists of attributes of those essences, and sharing in attributes does not entail sharing in the quiddities of what is described. Suppose we grant that bodies are alike; why could it not be said that God, exalted is He, singled out some of them with this power, to the exclusion of others, so that it is valid from them but not valid from humans?

The answer:

The truth is that what is relied upon in repelling this possibility is only the consensus of the community (ijmāʿ al-ummah, the agreement of the Muslim scholars). And God knows best.

**Third issue:** The word ﴿زَكِيٌّ﴾ (zakī) conveys three matters:

First: that he is pure from sins.

Second: that he grows through being purified, because it is said of one who has no sin that he is zakī, and of a growing crop that it is zakī.

Third: freedom from defects and purity in what he must be, so that he may validly be sent as a prophet. Some of the mutakallimūn (scholastic theologians of kalām) said that it is better to take it in all of these senses. But this is weak, because, as you know from usūl al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence), a single word may not be taken in two meanings, whether it is a literal meaning in both, or a figurative meaning in one and a literal meaning in the other.

**Fourth issue:** He named him zakī although he had none of the things of this world. When you look at your own market, whoever owns nothing is wretched in your eyes. Zakī is only one who owns wealth, but God says he was zakī, because his way of life was poverty, and his richness was wisdom and the Book. As for you, you call zakī only one whose way of life is ignorance and whose path is wealth.

**Issue 1:** Concerning her saying of the angel's good tidings, she was astonished because, by custom, she knew that childbirth happens only from a man. In the view of the people of knowledge, customs are taken into account in ordinary affairs, even though they permit the opposite in terms of power. So her words here are no proof that she did not know that God is able to create a child without a father. How could she not know, since she knew that God created the father of humanity in this manner? Also, she was devoted to worship in seclusion, and whoever is like this must know God's power over such things.

**Issue 2:** Someone may say: her words ﴿and no human has touched me﴾ already include her words ﴿nor have I been unchaste﴾, so why did she repeat them? This question is strengthened by the fact that in Surat Al 'Imran she said: ﴿My Lord, how can I have a son when no human has touched me?﴾ (Al 'Imran: 47), and she did not mention unchastity. The answer has several aspects:

First, she used "touch" as an expression for lawful marriage, since it is a euphemism for it, as in His words: ﴿before you have touched them﴾ (al-Ahzab: 49). Unlawful intercourse is not described this way; one says "he committed fornication with her" or something similar, and it is not fitting to observe euphemisms in such a case.

Second, the repetition is to magnify her status, as in His words: ﴿Guard the prayers and the middle prayer﴾ (al-Baqarah: 238), and His words: ﴿His angels, His messengers, Gabriel and Michael﴾. Likewise here: for a woman who is not known to have a husband, the most severe state of her affairs, when she bears a child, is that she is an adulteress. So the mention of unchastity was singled out after it had already been included in the first statement, because it is the greatest thing in its category.

**Issue 3:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *al-baghiyy* is the immoral woman who seeks men. It is *fa'ul* according to al-Mubarrad, originally *baghuy*, and the *waw* was assimilated into the *ya'*. Ibn Jinni, in his book *al-Tamam*, said it is *fa'il*. If it were *fa'ul*, it would have been said *baghaw*, just as it was said *nahaw 'ani al-munkar* (they forbade the wrong).

[Page 171]

**Issue 4:** Gabriel, peace be upon him, answered her with His words: ﴿He said: "So it will be. Your Lord has said: It is easy for Me."﴾ This is like His words in Al 'Imran: ﴿So it will be; God creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ (Al 'Imran: 47). Nothing is impossible for Him in doing what He wills to create, and He does not need instruments or materials in bringing it into being.

**Issue 5:** The pronoun in ﴿it is easy for Me﴾ and in His words ﴿and that We may make him a sign for the people﴾ may carry two meanings:

The first is that it refers to the creation: that His creating him is easy for Me, and that We make his creation a sign for the people, since he was born without a male, and a mercy from Us, He shows mercy to His servants by manifesting these signs so that the evidence of his truthfulness is more dazzling, and so his word is more readily accepted.

The second is that the pronouns refer to the boy. This is because when she was astonished at how this matter could occur contrary to custom, she was informed that God, exalted is He, would make her son a sign of the occurrence of that strange matter. As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿and as a mercy from Us﴾, it may be coordinated with ﴿and that We may make him a sign for the people﴾, meaning: We did that and [it is] a mercy from Us. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 22–23:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So she conceived him, and withdrew with him to a remote place.﴾ ﴿And the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree. She said: "Would that I had died before this and had become a thing forgotten and utterly lost!"﴾ And in this are several issues:

The first issue: God, exalted is He, mentioned the matter of the breathing (al-nafkh) in several verses. He said: ﴿So We breathed into it of Our Spirit﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12], meaning into Jesus, peace be upon him, just as He said to Adam, peace be upon him: ﴿And I breathed into him of My Spirit﴾ [al-Hijr: 29]. And He said "We breathed into her" because Jesus, peace be upon him, was in her womb. Scholars differed regarding who did the breathing. Some said the breathing was from God, exalted is He, based on His saying: ﴿So We breathed into it of Our Spirit﴾, and its apparent meaning indicates that the one breathing is God, exalted is He, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus before God is as the likeness of Adam; He created him from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. The requirement of a comparison is that similarity occurs except where evidence excludes it, and in the case of Adam the one breathing was God, exalted is He, based on His saying: ﴿And I breathed into him of My Spirit﴾; so likewise here. Others said: the one breathing was Gabriel, peace be upon him, because the apparent meaning of Gabriel's words, ﴿to bestow upon you a pure son﴾ [Maryam: 19], is that he was commanded to be the means of it, so that conception would occur for Maryam, peace be upon her. Thus the breathing must be attributed to him. Then they differed about the manner of that breathing, on two views:

The first: the saying of Wahb that Gabriel breathed into her collar until it reached the womb.

The second: into her skirt, so that it reached the private part.

The third: the saying of al-Suddi: he took hold of her sleeve and breathed into the side of her garment, so the breath entered her chest, and she conceived. Then her cousin, the wife of Zechariah, came to visit her, and when she embraced her she knew that she was pregnant, and Maryam mentioned her own condition. The wife of Zechariah said: "I have found that what is in my womb prostrates to what is in your womb." That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿confirming a word from God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39].

The fourth: the breath was in her mouth and reached her belly, so she conceived at once. When you know this, it becomes clear that there is an ellipsis in the speech, namely: and it was a decreed matter, so He breathed into her and she conceived him.

The second issue: It is said she conceived him when she was thirteen years old, and it is said twenty, and she had menstruated twice before she conceived. The Qur'an contains nothing that indicates any of these circumstances.

The third issue: ﴿withdrew with him﴾ means she secluded herself while he was in her womb, like His saying: ﴿a tree that grows out of Mount Sinai, producing oil﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20], meaning it grows while the oil is in it. Scholars differed on the cause of the withdrawal, in several respects:

One of them: what al-Tha'labi related in "al-'Ara'is" from Wahb, who said: When Maryam conceived Jesus, peace be upon him, a cousin of hers called Yusuf the carpenter was with her, and they were going to the mosque near Mount Zion. Yusuf and Maryam used to serve that mosque, and no one in their time was known to be more diligent or more devout than they. The first to notice Maryam's pregnancy was Yusuf, and he was perplexed about her matter. Whenever he wanted to accuse her, he remembered her righteousness and worship, and that she had never been absent from him for a moment; and whenever he wanted to absolve her, he saw the evident pregnancy. He first spoke, saying: "Something has come into my mind concerning you, and I have been eager to conceal it, but it overcame me, and I saw that speaking of it would relieve my heart." She said: "Speak a good word." He said: "Tell me, Maryam, does seed grow without a seed? Does a tree grow without rain? Can a child come into being without a male?" She said: "Yes. Do you not know that God caused the crop to grow on the day He created it without a seed? And this seed came only from the crop that He grew without seed. Do you not know that God, exalted is He, caused the tree to grow without rain, and by His power made the rain the life of the tree after He had created each of them separately? Or do you say that God is not able to cause the tree to grow until He is aided by water, and that without it He could not grow it?" Yusuf said: "I do not say this, but I say that God is capable of whatever He wills; He says to a thing 'Be,' and it is." Maryam said to him: "Do you not know that God created Adam and his wife without a male or a female?" At that, the suspicion was removed from his heart. He used to act on her behalf in serving the mosque, because weakness had overcome her due to the pregnancy and constriction of the heart. When her time of childbirth drew near, God revealed to her: "Go out from the land of your people, lest they kill your child." Yusuf carried her to the land of Egypt on his donkey. When she reached that country, the pains of childbirth overtook her, and he brought her to the trunk of a palm tree. It was a time of cold, so she embraced it, and she gave birth beside it.

The second: she felt shy before Zechariah, so she went to a distant place where Zechariah would not know of her.

The third: she was known among the Children of Israel for asceticism, because of her mother's vow, and the prophets vied for her upbringing, and Zechariah took charge of her; and because provision used to come to her from God, exalted is He. When she had reached the height of renown, she felt shy before people because of this event, so she went to a distant place where Zechariah would not know of her.

The fourth: she feared for her child if she gave birth among them.

Know that these views are all possible, and the Qur'an contains nothing that indicates any of them.

The fourth issue: They differed about the duration of her pregnancy, on several views:

The first: the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that it was nine months, as with other women, based on the fact that God mentioned her praiseworthy qualities in this context; had her pregnancy been different from women's customary pattern, that would have been more deserving of mention.

The second: that it was eight months, and no child born at eight months has lived except Jesus son of Mary, peace be upon him.

The third, which is the saying of 'Ata', Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak: seven months.

The fourth: that it was six months.

The fifth: three hours: she conceived him in one hour, he was formed in one hour, and she delivered him in one hour.

The sixth, which is also the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father: the duration of the pregnancy was a single hour. This may be inferred from two aspects:

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So she conceived him, and withdrew with him﴾ [Maryam: 22], ﴿And the pains of childbirth drove her﴾ [Maryam: 23], ﴿Then he called to her from beneath her﴾ [Maryam: 24]. The particle "fa" indicates sequence, so these particles show that each of these states occurred immediately after the other without interval, and this requires that the duration of the pregnancy was a single hour. It may be objected: how could her withdrawal to a remote place occur within a single hour? We answer: al-Suddi interpreted it as her going to the farthest point on the side of her sanctuary.

The second: God, exalted is He, said in describing him: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus before God is as the likeness of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. It is thus established that Jesus, as God said to him, "Be," and he was; and the duration of pregnancy cannot be conceived in such a case, but that duration is conceivable only for one who develops from a drop of semen.

The fifth issue: ﴿qasiyyan﴾ means far from her people. One says "makan qasin" and "qasiyy" with the same meaning, like "'asin" and "'asiyy." Then they differed: it was said, the farthest part of the house; it was said, behind the mountain; and it was said she traveled with her cousin Yusuf, and this account has already been mentioned.

The sixth issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: [ajā'a] is a transitive form derived from jā'a, but its usage changed after this derivation to the meaning of compulsion, for you do not say "ji'tu al-makan," but "ajā'anīhi Zayd," just as you say "balaghanīhi" and "ablaghtuhu." The meaning is that the pain of labor drove her to the trunk of the palm tree. It is possible that she went to the palm tree seeking ease of delivery by clinging to it. It is possible that it was for support and leaning on it. It is possible that it was for concealment behind it from anyone whose gossip she feared if he saw her. For this reason God related that she wished for death.

The seventh issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: Ibn Kathir in one narration read "al-makhad" with a kasra, from it is said: "makhadat al-hamilu makhadan wa mikhadan," which is the child's writhing in the womb.

The eighth issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: It was the trunk of a dry palm tree in the desert, having no top, no fruit, and no greenery, and the time was winter. The definiteness (in "al-jidh al-nakhlah") may be either the definiteness of well-known names, like the definiteness of "al-najm" and "al-sa'q," as though there was in that desert a well-known palm trunk among the people, so that when one says "the trunk of the palm tree" it is understood as that one and not any other. Or it may be definiteness of the genus, meaning: to the trunk of this particular tree; as though God guided her to the palm, so that she might feed herself from its dates, which are the most suitable of things for women after childbirth. Also, the palm is the least able to endure cold, and it bears fruit only with pollination, and if its top is cut it does not bear fruit. It is as though He, exalted is He, said: just as the female does not give birth except with a male, so the palm does not bear fruit except with pollination. Then I bring forth the dates without pollination, to show that the appearance of a child without a male is possible.

The ninth issue: Why did she say: ﴿She said: "Would that I had died before this"﴾, although she knew that God had sent Gabriel to her, created her child from the breath of Gabriel, peace be upon him, and promised her that He would make her and her son a sign for all the worlds?

The answer has two aspects:

The first: Wahb said: The distress of strangeness and what she heard from people, from the glad tidings of the angels concerning Jesus, peace be upon him, caused her to forget.

The second: it is the custom of the righteous, when they fall into trial, to say such words. It is related from Abu Bakr that he looked at a bird on a tree and said: "Blessed are you, bird, that you alight on the tree and eat of its fruit! I wish I were a fruit that a bird would peck!" And from 'Umar that he took a straw from the ground and said: "Would that I were this straw, would that I had not been anything!" And 'Ali said on the day of the Camel: "Would that I had died twenty years before this day." And from Bilal: "Would that Bilal had not been born to his mother." Thus it is established that the righteous utter these words when the matter grows severe upon them.

The third: perhaps she said this so that no sin would be committed by one who speaks of her; otherwise she was content with what she had been given good news of.

The tenth issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Nisy" is that which by right is cast away and forgotten, like a menstrual rag and the like, as "dhibh" is the name of what is slaughtered, as in His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ [al-Saffat: 107]. She wished that she had been something trivial, of no account, which by custom would be forgotten. Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash and Hamzah read "nasyan" with a fatha, and the rest read "nisyan" with a kasra. Al-Farra' said: they are two dialects, like "al-watr" and "al-witr," and "al-jasr" and "al-jisr." Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi read "nasi'an" with a hamza, which is milk mixed with water that its people let sour because of its scarcity. Al-A'mash read "minsiyyan" with a kasra by assimilation, like "al-mighir" and "al-minkhir." And God knows best.

Al-Farra' said: they are two dialects, like "al-watr" and "al-witr," and "al-jasr" and "al-jisr." Al-A'mash read "minsiyyan" with a kasra by assimilation, like "al-mighir" and "al-minkhir." And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 24–26:

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then he called to her from beneath her: "Do not grieve; your Lord has placed beneath you a stream.﴾ ﴿And shake towards yourself the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you fresh ripe dates.﴾ ﴿So eat and drink and be comforted. And if you see any human being, say, 'I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any human being.'﴾ In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: "fa-nadaha min tahtiha" (Then he called to her from beneath her). The well-known reading is fa-nadaha, and Zirr and ʿAlqama read fa-khatabaha ("then he addressed her"). Regarding the mim in it there are two readings: fathah on the mim, which is the well-known one, and kasrah on the mim, which is the reading of Nafiʿ, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs. Regarding the caller there are three opinions:

The first: he is ʿIsa (peace be upon him), and this is the view of al-Hasan and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The second: he is Jibril (peace be upon him), and he was like a midwife for the child.

The third: the caller, according to the reading with kasrah, is an angel, and according to the reading with fathah, is ʿIsa (peace be upon him). This is narrated from Ibn ʿUyayna and ʿAsim. The first opinion is closer, for several reasons:

The first: the saying "fa-nadaha min tahtiha" with fathah on the mim is only used when it is already known beforehand that there was someone beneath her, and the one known to be there beneath her is ʿIsa (peace be upon him); so the wording must be taken to refer to him. As for the reading with kasrah on the mim, it does not require that the caller be Jibril (peace be upon him). Thus our statement is established.

The second: that place was a place of seclusion and looking at the nakedness, and that is not fitting for the angels.

The third: the saying "fa-nadaha" is a verb, and its subject must have been previously mentioned. Jibril and ʿIsa (peace be upon them both) were both mentioned before this verse, but the mention of ʿIsa is closer, because of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So she conceived him, and withdrew with him to a remote place﴾ [Maryam: 22], and the pronoun here refers to the Messiah; so it is more appropriate to take it as referring to him.

The fourth, which is the argument of al-Hasan ibn ʿAli (peace be upon him): if ʿIsa had not spoken to her, she would not have known that he could speak, and she would not have pointed to ʿIsa (peace be upon him) [to speak]. As for the one who says the caller is ʿIsa (peace be upon him), the meaning is that God made him speak to her when she gave birth to him, to console her heart and remove the loneliness from her, so that she might witness at the very beginning what Jibril (peace be upon him) had given her good news of concerning the exalted status of that child.

And the one who says the caller is Jibril (peace be upon him) says: he was sent to her to call to her with these words, just as he was sent to her at the beginning, so that this would be a reminder to her of the kinds of good tidings that had preceded.

As for the saying "min tahtiha" (from beneath her): if we take it to refer to the child, there is no question. If we take it to refer to the angel, then there are two possibilities:

The first: that both of them were in a level place, and there was a fixed starting point there, like that palm tree here; so whoever was closer to it was above, and whoever was farther from it was beneath. al-Kalbi explained the saying of the Exalted ﴿when they came upon you from above you and from below you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10] in this way. On this view some said: he called to her from the far end of the valley.

The second: that the place of one of them was higher than the place of the other, so the one who was higher was above the one who was lower. On this view it is narrated from ʿIkrima that when she gave birth she was upon something like a mound.

There is a third possibility, reported from ʿIkrima: that Jibril (peace be upon him) called to her from beneath the palm tree. Then, on all three assumptions, it is possible that Maryam saw him and it is possible that she did not see him, and there is nothing in the wording that indicates either.

The second issue: The exegetes agreed, except al-Hasan and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, that the sarriyy is the river and the stream; it is so named because water flows in it. As for al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd, they took sarriyy to mean ʿIsa. Sarriyy means a noble, exalted person; it is said: "So-and-so is one of the nobles of his people," i.e., one of their chiefs. It is narrated that al-Hasan retracted this view. It is also narrated from Qatada and others that al-Hasan recited this verse while beside him was Humayd ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Himyari: ﴿your Lord has placed beneath you a sarriyy﴾, and said: "If it is indeed a sarriyy, then it is indeed noble." Humayd said to him: "O Abu Saʿid, it is only a stream (jadwal)." Al-Hasan said to him: "For this reason we enjoy your company."

Those who take it to mean the river argue with two points:

The first: that he asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the sarriyy, and he said: "It is the stream."

The second: that the saying "So eat and drink" indicates that it is a river, so that the water is joined to the fresh dates, and she eats and drinks.

Those who take it to mean ʿIsa argue with two points:

The first: that a river would not be beneath her but beside her, and it cannot be answered that what is meant is that He made the river beneath her command, flowing by her command and stopping by her command, as in the saying: ﴿and these rivers flow beneath me﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 51], because this is taking the wording in its metaphorical sense, whereas if we take it to refer to ʿIsa (peace be upon him) there is no need for this metaphor.

The second: that it agrees with the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign, and We gave them refuge on a high ground, a place of stability and flowing water﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50]. The answer to this is what has preceded: that a level place in which there is a fixed starting point is such that whoever is closer to it is above, and whoever is farther from it is beneath.

Two branches:

The first: if we take sarriyy to mean the river, then there are two possibilities: one, that Jibril (peace be upon him) struck with his foot and fresh water appeared; the other, that there was flowing water there already.

The first is closer, because the saying "your Lord has placed beneath you a sarriyy" implies a coming into being at that time, and because God mentioned it to magnify her status, and this is only established according to the view we have stated.

The second: they differed on whether sarriyy is the river in general, which is the view of Abu ʿUbayda and al-Farra', or the small river, as the view of al-Akhfash holds.

The third issue: al-Qaffal said: the jidh (trunk) of the palm tree is the lower part, and what is below the head on which the fruit is. Qutrub said: every piece of wood at the base of a tree is a jidh. As for the "ba'" in the saying "bi-jidh al-nakhla" (by the trunk of the palm tree), it is superfluous (za'ida), and the meaning is "shake towards yourself," i.e., move the trunk of the palm tree. al-Farra' said: the Arabs say hazzahu and hazza bihi, and khudh al-khitam and khudh bil-khitam, and zawwajtuka Fulana and bi-Fulana. al-Akhfash said: it is permissible that the meaning be "shake towards yourself fresh dates by the trunk of the palm tree," i.e., upon its trunk. Having understood this, we say: it has already been established that the time was winter and that the palm tree was dry. They differed as to whether it bore fresh dates in its existing state or had changed, and whether it bore anything other than fresh dates along with them. The apparent sense implies that it had become a palm tree, given the saying "by the trunk of the palm tree," and that it bore only fresh dates.

The fourth issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said: "tusaqit" (it will drop) has nine readings: tassaqat with the ta' assimilated; tatasaqat with both ta's pronounced; tasaqat with the second dropped; yassaqat with the ya' and assimilated ta'; tasaqat; tasqut; yasqut; tusqit; yusqit. The ta' refers to the palm tree and the ya' refers to the trunk.

The fifth issue: "rutaban" is a specification (tamyiz) or an object according to the reading. "Janiyyan" means picked while fresh. It is narrated from Talha ibn Sulayman "jinyyan" with kasrah on the jim for harmony. The meaning is that We gathered for you in the sarriyy and the fresh dates two benefits:

One: eating and drinking.

The second: consolation of the heart, since they are two miracles. If someone asks: for whom were those acts that break habits? We say: the Mu'tazila said they were a miracle for Zakariyya and other prophets, and this is false, because Zakariyya (peace be upon him) had no knowledge of her condition or her place, so how could there be miracles for him? Rather the truth is that they were karamat (marvels) for Maryam, or a preparation (irhas) for ʿIsa (peace be upon him).

The sixth issue: "fa-kulī wa-ishrabī wa-qarrī ʿaynan" (so eat, drink and be comforted). It was read with kasrah on the qaf, the dialect of Najd. We say: it placed eating before drinking because the need of the woman after childbirth for eating fresh dates is greater than her need for drinking water, due to the great amount of blood that had flowed from her. Then He said: "wa-qarrī ʿaynan" (and be comforted). Here there is a question: the harm of fear is greater than the harm of hunger and thirst, and the evidence for this is two things:

One: fear is pain of the soul, while hunger is pain of the body, and the pain of the soul is stronger than the pain of the body.

The second: what is related that a sheep was starved, then fodder was placed before it, and a wolf was tied beside it; so the sheep remained for a long time, despite its severe hunger, not taking the fodder out of fear of the wolf. Then its leg was broken, fodder was placed before it, and it took the fodder despite the pain of the body. This story shows that the pain of fear is greater than the pain of the body.

Given this established, we say: why did God, in the narrative, put the removal of the harm of hunger and thirst before the removal of the harm of fear?

The answer is that this fear was slight, because the good tidings of Jibril (peace be upon him) had already preceded; so she did not need to be reminded again.

The seventh issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said: "tarayinna" was read with a hamza, by Ibn al-Rumi from Abu ʿAmr, and this is from the dialect of those who say labba'tu bil-hajj and halla'tu al-sawiq, because of the affinity between the hamza and the soft letter in substitution. "Sawman" means silence; in the codex of ʿAbd Allah it is "samtan," and it is narrated from Anas ibn Malik the same. It is said "siyaman," except that they did not speak during their fasting; so according to this, the mention of fasting indicated silence. This type of vow was permissible in their law. Would such a vow be permissible in our law? al-Qaffal said: perhaps it is permissible, because abstaining from human speech and devoting thought to the remembrance of God is an act of worship; and perhaps it is not permissible, because of what it contains of constriction and self-torment, like the vow to stand in the sun. It is related that Abu Bakr entered upon a woman who had vowed not to speak, and Abu Bakr said: "Islam has demolished this, so speak." And God knows best.

The eighth issue: God commanded her to vow the fast so that she would not speak with those who accused her, for two reasons:

One: the speech of ʿIsa (peace be upon him) is stronger in removing the accusation than her speech; and in this there is an indication that delegating the matter to the more excellent is preferable.

The second: to avoid arguing with fools; and in it is the point that silence before a fool is obligatory, and among the most humiliating of people is a fool who finds no one to match his foolishness.

The ninth issue: they differed as to whether she said to them: "Innī nadhartu lil-Raḥmāni ṣawman" (Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast). Some said: she did not speak to them with this at all, because she had been commanded to bring this vow when she saw them; so if she had come with this vow and then spoken to them afterward, she would have fallen into contradiction. Rather she refrained and gestured with her head. Others said: she did not vow at that moment, but waited until the people came to her, and then she told them: "Innī nadhartu lil-Raḥmāni ṣawman fa-lan ukallima al-yawma insiyyan" (Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any human being). This expression, although general, was specified by the context in regard to this utterance.
