The fourth, which is the argument of al-Hasan ibn ʿAli (peace be upon him): if ʿIsa had not spoken to her, she would not have known that he could speak, and she would not have pointed to ʿIsa (peace be upon him) [to speak]. As for the one who says the caller is ʿIsa (peace be upon him), the meaning is that God made him speak to her when she gave birth to him, to console her heart and remove the loneliness from her, so that she might witness at the very beginning what Jibril (peace be upon him) had given her good news of concerning the exalted status of that child.

And the one who says the caller is Jibril (peace be upon him) says: he was sent to her to call to her with these words, just as he was sent to her at the beginning, so that this would be a reminder to her of the kinds of good tidings that had preceded.

As for the saying "min tahtiha" (from beneath her): if we take it to refer to the child, there is no question. If we take it to refer to the angel, then there are two possibilities:

The first: that both of them were in a level place, and there was a fixed starting point there, like that palm tree here; so whoever was closer to it was above, and whoever was farther from it was beneath. al-Kalbi explained the saying of the Exalted ﴿when they came upon you from above you and from below you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10] in this way. On this view some said: he called to her from the far end of the valley.

The second: that the place of one of them was higher than the place of the other, so the one who was higher was above the one who was lower. On this view it is narrated from ʿIkrima that when she gave birth she was upon something like a mound.

There is a third possibility, reported from ʿIkrima: that Jibril (peace be upon him) called to her from beneath the palm tree. Then, on all three assumptions, it is possible that Maryam saw him and it is possible that she did not see him, and there is nothing in the wording that indicates either.

The second issue: The exegetes agreed, except al-Hasan and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, that the sarriyy is the river and the stream; it is so named because water flows in it. As for al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd, they took sarriyy to mean ʿIsa. Sarriyy means a noble, exalted person; it is said: "So-and-so is one of the nobles of his people," i.e., one of their chiefs. It is narrated that al-Hasan retracted this view. It is also narrated from Qatada and others that al-Hasan recited this verse while beside him was Humayd ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Himyari: ﴿your Lord has placed beneath you a sarriyy﴾, and said: "If it is indeed a sarriyy, then it is indeed noble." Humayd said to him: "O Abu Saʿid, it is only a stream (jadwal)." Al-Hasan said to him: "For this reason we enjoy your company."

Those who take it to mean the river argue with two points:

The first: that he asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the sarriyy, and he said: "It is the stream."

The second: that the saying "So eat and drink" indicates that it is a river, so that the water is joined to the fresh dates, and she eats and drinks.

Those who take it to mean ʿIsa argue with two points:

The first: that a river would not be beneath her but beside her, and it cannot be answered that what is meant is that He made the river beneath her command, flowing by her command and stopping by her command, as in the saying: ﴿and these rivers flow beneath me﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 51], because this is taking the wording in its metaphorical sense, whereas if we take it to refer to ʿIsa (peace be upon him) there is no need for this metaphor.

The second: that it agrees with the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign, and We gave them refuge on a high ground, a place of stability and flowing water﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50]. The answer to this is what has preceded: that a level place in which there is a fixed starting point is such that whoever is closer to it is above, and whoever is farther from it is beneath.

Two branches:

The first: if we take sarriyy to mean the river, then there are two possibilities: one, that Jibril (peace be upon him) struck with his foot and fresh water appeared; the other, that there was flowing water there already.

The first is closer, because the saying "your Lord has placed beneath you a sarriyy" implies a coming into being at that time, and because God mentioned it to magnify her status, and this is only established according to the view we have stated.

The second: they differed on whether sarriyy is the river in general, which is the view of Abu ʿUbayda and al-Farra', or the small river, as the view of al-Akhfash holds.

The third issue: al-Qaffal said: the jidh (trunk) of the palm tree is the lower part, and what is below the head on which the fruit is. Qutrub said: every piece of wood at the base of a tree is a jidh. As for the "ba'" in the saying "bi-jidh al-nakhla" (by the trunk of the palm tree), it is superfluous (za'ida), and the meaning is "shake towards yourself," i.e., move the trunk of the palm tree. al-Farra' said: the Arabs say hazzahu and hazza bihi, and khudh al-khitam and khudh bil-khitam, and zawwajtuka Fulana and bi-Fulana. al-Akhfash said: it is permissible that the meaning be "shake towards yourself fresh dates by the trunk of the palm tree," i.e., upon its trunk. Having understood this, we say: it has already been established that the time was winter and that the palm tree was dry. They differed as to whether it bore fresh dates in its existing state or had changed, and whether it bore anything other than fresh dates along with them. The apparent sense implies that it had become a palm tree, given the saying "by the trunk of the palm tree," and that it bore only fresh dates.

The fourth issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said: "tusaqit" (it will drop) has nine readings: tassaqat with the ta' assimilated; tatasaqat with both ta's pronounced; tasaqat with the second dropped; yassaqat with the ya' and assimilated ta'; tasaqat; tasqut; yasqut; tusqit; yusqit. The ta' refers to the palm tree and the ya' refers to the trunk.

The fifth issue: "rutaban" is a specification (tamyiz) or an object according to the reading. "Janiyyan" means picked while fresh. It is narrated from Talha ibn Sulayman "jinyyan" with kasrah on the jim for harmony. The meaning is that We gathered for you in the sarriyy and the fresh dates two benefits:

One: eating and drinking.

The second: consolation of the heart, since they are two miracles. If someone asks: for whom were those acts that break habits? We say: the Mu'tazila said they were a miracle for Zakariyya and other prophets, and this is false, because Zakariyya (peace be upon him) had no knowledge of her condition or her place, so how could there be miracles for him? Rather the truth is that they were karamat (marvels) for Maryam, or a preparation (irhas) for ʿIsa (peace be upon him).

The sixth issue: "fa-kulī wa-ishrabī wa-qarrī ʿaynan" (so eat, drink and be comforted). It was read with kasrah on the qaf, the dialect of Najd. We say: it placed eating before drinking because the need of the woman after childbirth for eating fresh dates is greater than her need for drinking water, due to the great amount of blood that had flowed from her. Then He said: "wa-qarrī ʿaynan" (and be comforted). Here there is a question: the harm of fear is greater than the harm of hunger and thirst, and the evidence for this is two things:

One: fear is pain of the soul, while hunger is pain of the body, and the pain of the soul is stronger than the pain of the body.

The second: what is related that a sheep was starved, then fodder was placed before it, and a wolf was tied beside it; so the sheep remained for a long time, despite its severe hunger, not taking the fodder out of fear of the wolf. Then its leg was broken, fodder was placed before it, and it took the fodder despite the pain of the body. This story shows that the pain of fear is greater than the pain of the body.

Given this established, we say: why did God, in the narrative, put the removal of the harm of hunger and thirst before the removal of the harm of fear?

The answer is that this fear was slight, because the good tidings of Jibril (peace be upon him) had already preceded; so she did not need to be reminded again.

The seventh issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said: "tarayinna" was read with a hamza, by Ibn al-Rumi from Abu ʿAmr, and this is from the dialect of those who say labba'tu bil-hajj and halla'tu al-sawiq, because of the affinity between the hamza and the soft letter in substitution. "Sawman" means silence; in the codex of ʿAbd Allah it is "samtan," and it is narrated from Anas ibn Malik the same. It is said "siyaman," except that they did not speak during their fasting; so according to this, the mention of fasting indicated silence. This type of vow was permissible in their law. Would such a vow be permissible in our law? al-Qaffal said: perhaps it is permissible, because abstaining from human speech and devoting thought to the remembrance of God is an act of worship; and perhaps it is not permissible, because of what it contains of constriction and self-torment, like the vow to stand in the sun. It is related that Abu Bakr entered upon a woman who had vowed not to speak, and Abu Bakr said: "Islam has demolished this, so speak." And God knows best.

The eighth issue: God commanded her to vow the fast so that she would not speak with those who accused her, for two reasons:

One: the speech of ʿIsa (peace be upon him) is stronger in removing the accusation than her speech; and in this there is an indication that delegating the matter to the more excellent is preferable.

The second: to avoid arguing with fools; and in it is the point that silence before a fool is obligatory, and among the most humiliating of people is a fool who finds no one to match his foolishness.

The ninth issue: they differed as to whether she said to them: "Innī nadhartu lil-Raḥmāni ṣawman" (Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast). Some said: she did not speak to them with this at all, because she had been commanded to bring this vow when she saw them; so if she had come with this vow and then spoken to them afterward, she would have fallen into contradiction. Rather she refrained and gestured with her head. Others said: she did not vow at that moment, but waited until the people came to her, and then she told them: "Innī nadhartu lil-Raḥmāni ṣawman fa-lan ukallima al-yawma insiyyan" (Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any human being). This expression, although general, was specified by the context in regard to this utterance.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 27–29:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him. They said, "O Mary, you have certainly come up with something unprecedented. O sister of Aaron, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother unchaste."﴾ ﴿So she pointed to him. They said, "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a young child?"﴾ And in this are several issues:

The first issue: The scholars differ regarding how she came to bring the child, and there are several opinions:

The first: What is narrated from Wahb, who said: The pain of childbirth made her forget, and what she had heard from people of the words of the angels concerning the good tidings of Jesus, peace be upon him, had also slipped her mind. When he spoke to her, the confirmation of that came to her, so she carried him and set out with him to her people.

The second: What is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Yusuf brought Mary to a cave and entered it with her for forty days until she was purified from postnatal bleeding. Then she came to her people carrying him, and Jesus spoke to her on the way, saying: "O mother, rejoice, for I am the servant of Allah and His Messiah." Both of these possibilities are conceivable, and there is nothing in the Qur'an that indicates a specific one.

The second issue: Al-Farriy (fariy) means the wondrous, derived from "fary al-jild" (the tearing of the hide). It is related that when they saw her with Jesus, peace be upon him, they said to her: ﴿You have certainly come up with something unprecedented﴾. It is possible that what is meant is a strange thing outside the usual custom, without reproach or blame. It is also possible that their meaning was a great and abhorrent thing, so that this would be said by them in the manner of blame. This second view is more apparent, due to their statement after it: ﴿O sister of Aaron, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother unchaste,﴾ because this statement apparently carries rebuke. As for Aaron, there are four opinions concerning him:

The first: He was a righteous man among the Children of Israel, and every person known for righteousness is attributed to him. The meaning is that you were in piety like Aaron, so how did you become like this? This is the view of Qatadah, Ka'b, Ibn Zayd and al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah. It is mentioned that the funeral of the righteous Aaron was followed by forty thousand people, all of whom were named Aaron, seeking blessing through him and through his name.

The second: That he was the brother of Musa, peace be upon him. And concerning the Prophet ﷺ, it is said that they meant Aaron the Prophet, and she was of his descendants. It is said: ﴿O sister of Aaron﴾ just as one says "O brother of Hamdan," meaning, O one of them.

The third: He was a man openly committing immorality, and she was attributed to him in the sense of comparison, not in the sense of lineage.

The fourth: She had a brother called Aaron, one of the righteous of the Children of Israel, and she was reproached by him. This is the closest view, for two reasons:

The first: The primary meaning of speech is its literal sense, and the apparent meaning of the verse would be taken literally only if she had a brother named Aaron.

The second: She is addressed as his sister, and her parents are described as righteous. In that case the rebuke becomes more severe, because whoever has parents and a brother in such a state, the commission of sin by him is more shameful.

The third issue: The well-known reading is ﴿mā kāna abūki imra'a sawʾin﴾ (your father was not a man of evil), while ʿAmr ibn Raja' al-Tamimi read: "mā kāna abāki imruʾu sawʾin."

The fourth issue: When they exaggerated in rebuking her, she fell silent and pointed to him, that is, to Jesus, peace be upon him, meaning: he is the one who will answer you if you speak to him. It is related from al-Suddi that when she pointed to him they became exceedingly angry and said: "Her mockery of us is worse than her fornication." It is narrated that he was nursing, but when he heard that he stopped nursing, turned his face toward them, leaned on his left side, and pointed with his index finger. It is also said that he spoke to them with this and then did not speak again until he reached the age at which children speak. It is also said that Zechariah, peace be upon him, came to her at the time of the Jews' dispute with her, and said to Jesus, peace be upon him: "Speak your proof, if you have been commanded to do so." Then Jesus, peace be upon him, said at that moment: ﴿Indeed, I am the servant of Allah﴾ [Maryam 19:30]. If it is asked: How did Mary know from Jesus' condition that he would speak? We say: Gabriel, peace be upon him, or Jesus, peace be upon him, called to her from beneath her that she should not grieve, and commanded her, when people saw her, to remain silent. This served as an indication to her that the one who would answer was Jesus, peace be upon him. Or perhaps she knew this through revelation made to Zechariah, or she knew it through revelation made to her, as a form of honor (karamah).

Two discussions remain here:

The first discussion: His words ﴿How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a young child?﴾ — that is, one who is in the cradle; so here "kāna" means "came to be" and "was found," and this is the closest interpretation of this expression, although people have mentioned other meanings.

The second discussion: The scholars differ regarding "al-mahd" (the cradle). It is said that it is her lap, based on the report that she carried him wrapped in a cloth and brought him to her people; when they saw her they said what they said, and she pointed to him while he was in her lap, and she had no prepared dwelling in which a cradle would be set up for her. Or the meaning is: how can we speak to a child whose custom is to sleep in a cradle?

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on surah 19, verse 30 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said: Indeed I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet.﴾ ﴿And He has made me blessed wherever I am, and has enjoined upon me prayer and zakat (obligatory almsgiving) as long as I live.﴾ ﴿And [He has made me] dutiful to my mother, and He has not made me arrogant or wretched.﴾ ﴿And peace is upon me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive.﴾

Know that he described himself with nine attributes.

The first attribute is his saying: ﴿Indeed I am the servant of Allah.﴾ In this there are several benefits.

The first benefit: his speech at that time was a cause for the illusion to which the Christians (al-Naṣārā) turned. Therefore, the first thing he said was only that which removes that illusion, so he said: ﴿Indeed I am the servant of Allah.﴾ Although that speech could be misleading, insofar as it came from him in that state, that illusion disappears and does not remain, insofar as it is an explicit statement of servanthood.

The second benefit: since he affirmed servanthood, if he was truthful in his statement, the purpose is achieved; and if he was lying, the power would not have been a divine power but a satanic power. Under either supposition, his being a god is refuted.

The third benefit: what was most urgently needed at that time was the negation of the accusation of fornication against Maryam, peace be upon her. Then, ʿIsa, peace be upon him, did not state that explicitly, but stated the affirmation of his own servanthood, as if he made the removal of the accusation from Allah, the Exalted, more important than the removal of the accusation from his mother. Therefore, the first thing he said was only that.

[Page 179]

The fourth benefit: speaking about removing this accusation from Allah, the Exalted, implies the removal of the accusation from his mother, because Allah, glorified is He, would not bestow a child of such a lofty rank and great station upon an adulteress. As for speaking about removing the accusation from his mother, it does not imply the removal of the accusation from Allah, the Exalted. Thus, occupying oneself with the former was more important. This is the sum of the benefits contained in this expression.

Know that the doctrine of the Christians is extremely confused. They have agreed that He, glorified is He, is neither a body (jism) nor something that occupies a space (mutahayyiz). Nevertheless, we will mention a conclusive division that refutes their doctrine in all its aspects, so we say: Either they believe that He occupies a space or not. If they believe that He occupies a space, we refute their claim by establishing the proof of the createdness of bodies (ḥudūth al-ajsām), and then everything they built upon it collapses. If they believe that He does not occupy a space, then what some of them say is refuted, namely that the Word (al-kalima) mixed with the humanity (al-nāsūt) like the mixing of water with wine and the blending of fire with charcoal, because that is conceivable only in bodies, and if He is not a body, that is impossible.

Then we say: People have two positions regarding the human being. Some of them say that the human being is this structure (the body), or a body existing within it. Others say that he is a substance (jawhar) free of corporeality and of inherence in bodies. So we say: These Christians either believe that God, or one of His attributes, became united with the body of the Messiah, or with his soul; or they believe that God, or one of His attributes, indwelt the body of the Messiah or his soul; or they say: We do not affirm union or indwelling, but we say that He, the Exalted, granted him the power to create bodies, life, and power, and for this reason he was a god; or they affirm none of these, but say that He took him as a son by way of honor, just as He took Ibrahim as a friend (khalīl) by way of honor. These are the rationally conceivable aspects in this matter, and all of them are false.

As for the first position, union (ittiḥād), it is definitively false. For when two things are united, then during the union they are either both existent, or both non-existent, or one existent and the other non-existent. If both are existent, then they are two and not one, so the union is false. If both are annihilated and a third thing comes into being, then this also is not a union but a claim of the non-existence of those two things and the coming into being of a third thing. If one remains and the other is annihilated, then the non-existent cannot unite with existence, because it is impossible to say: the non-existent itself is the existent. Thus it is clear from this brilliant proof that union is impossible.

As for indwelling (ḥulūl), we have two stages concerning it:

The first: assent (taṣdīq) is preceded by conception (taṣawwur), so it is necessary to investigate the reality (māhiyya) of indwelling, so that we can know whether it is valid for Allah, the Exalted, or not. They have offered three explanations of indwelling:

One of them: the existence of a thing in another, like the existence of rosewater in the rose, of oil in sesame, and of fire in charcoal. Know that this is false, because this is valid only if Allah, the Exalted, were a body, and they agreed with us that He is not a body.

The second: its existence in a thing on the model of the existence of color in a body. We say: what is understood from this dependence is the existence of color in that space as a consequence of the existence of its locus in it. This too is conceivable only regarding bodies, not regarding Allah, the Exalted.

The third: its existence in a thing on the model of the existence of relational attributes (ṣifāt iḍāfiyya) in essences. We say: this too is false, because what is understood from this dependence is need. So if Allah, the Exalted, were in something in this sense, He would be in need, and what is in need is contingent, and what is contingent requires an agent (muʾaththir), and that is impossible. Since it has been established that this indwelling cannot be explained by a summarized meaning that can be affirmed of Allah, the Exalted, its affirmation is impossible.

The second stage: the companions (al-Ashāb, i.e., the Ashʿarī theologians) argued against indwelling absolutely, saying: If He indwelt, He would indwell either necessarily or contingently, and both alternatives are false. Therefore indwelling is false. We have said that He cannot indwell necessarily, because that entails either the createdness of Allah, the Exalted, or the eternity of the locus, and both are false, since we have demonstrated that Allah is eternal and that the body is created. Also, if He indwelt necessarily, He would be in need of the locus, and what is in need of another is contingent in its essence and not necessary in its essence. And we have said that He cannot indwell contingently, because His essence is necessary of existence in itself, and His indwelling in the locus is a contingent matter, and what is described as necessary is other than what is described as contingent. So His indwelling in the locus would be an attribute additional to His essence, and that is impossible for two reasons:

One of them: if His indwelling in the locus were additional to His essence, then the indwelling of that additional thing in its locus would be additional to His essence, or else an infinite regress (tasalsul) would follow, which is impossible.

The second: since His indwelling in that is additional to His essence, when it indwells in a locus, it must be that a created attribute indwells in it. This is impossible, because if He were receptive to contingent events, that receptivity would be among the necessary properties of His essence and would be present eternally, and that is impossible, because the existence of contingent events in eternity is impossible. Therefore the coming about of their receptivity must be impossible.

If it is said: Why is it not possible that He indwells necessarily, since that entails either the createdness of the indwelling entity or the eternity of the locus?

We reply: We do not grant the necessity of either of the two alternatives. Why is it not possible to say that His essence entails indwelling on condition of the existence of the locus? In eternity, the locus did not exist, so the condition of this necessity was not fulfilled, and therefore indwelling was not necessary. And in what is ever-continuing, this condition was fulfilled, so indwelling became necessary.

Even if we grant that it entails either the createdness of the indwelling entity or the eternity of the locus, why is it not possible to say: We have demonstrated the createdness of bodies? We reply: Why is it not possible that its locus is not a body, but rather an intellect (ʿaql), or a soul (nafs), or prime matter (hayūlā), as some of them affirm? And does your proof of the createdness of bodies not apply to the createdness of these things?

As for his second statement: If He indwelt necessarily, He would be in need of the locus. We reply: We do not grant the necessity of either alternative. Rather, there are two other possibilities here:

One of them: although it is impossible for the cause to be separated from its effect, the cause is not in need of the effect. So why is it not possible to say: His essence is independent of that locus, but His essence necessitates the indwelling of itself in that effect? Thus the necessity of its indwelling in that locus is one of the effects of His essence. It has been established that although it is impossible for the cause to be separated from its effect, that does not entail that it needs the effect.

The second: it may be said that in His essence He is independent of the locus and of indwelling, except that the locus necessitates, by its own essence, the attribute of indwelling. So what is in need of the locus is an attribute of His, namely His indwelling in that locus, but not His essence. And the need of one of His relational attributes for another does not entail the need of His essence for another. This is because all the relational attributes that belong to Him, such as being first and last, being concomitant, being an agent, being known, and being mentioned, can only be realized upon the occurrence of spatial occupation. And how could it not be so, since relations require two terms for their realization?

Even if we grant that, why is it not possible for Him to indwell contingently? His statement: it entails that His indwelling in it is additional to Him. And it entails infinite regress?

We reply: Since His indwelling in the locus is possible, His indwelling in the locus is additional to Him. As for the indwelling of that indwelling in the locus being necessary, it does not follow that the indwelling of the indwelling is additional to Him, so infinite regress does not follow.

His statement, secondly: It entails that He becomes a locus of contingent events. We reply: Why is that not possible? His statement: It entails that He is receptive to contingent events in eternity?

We reply: There is no doubt that His capacity to bring things into existence is established for Him, either by His essence or by something that terminates in His essence. In any case, it entails that it is valid for Him to be an agent in eternity. So everything you have mentioned regarding agency, we mention regarding receptivity.

The answer: We establish this proof in another way, so that these objections fall away. We say: His essence is either sufficient for the necessitation of this indwelling or not sufficient for it. If the first is the case, then it is impossible for that necessitation to depend on the fulfillment of a condition, and so we return to what we said: it entails either the eternity of the locus or the createdness of the indwelling entity. If the second is the case, then His being the necessitator of that indwelling is an additional attribute to His essence, created in it. Then, on all assumptions, it follows that the indwelling in the locus is created, and the coming about of something in it. But it is impossible for Him to be receptive to contingent events, because otherwise He would be receptive to them in eternity, which is impossible as we have explained. As for the counter-argument from power (qudra), it does not apply, because He, by His essence, is capable of bringing things into existence in eternity, so He is capable of bringing things into existence in what is ever-continuing. Here too, if His essence were receptive to contingent events, it would be receptive to them in eternity, and then the aforementioned impossibility follows. This is the complete account of these proofs.

We have other aspects for refuting the Christian doctrine:

One of them: they agreed with us that His essence, glorified and exalted is He, did not indwell the humanity (nāsūt) of ʿIsa, peace be upon him. Rather, they said: the Word (al-kalima) indwelt in him, and by the Word they mean knowledge (ʿilm).

So we say: When knowledge indwelt in ʿIsa, then at that moment, either it is said that it remained in the essence of Allah, the Exalted, or it did not remain in it. If the first, it entails the existence of one attribute in two loci, and that is inconceivable. Moreover, if it were valid to say that the knowledge existing in the essence of ʿIsa, peace be upon him, is the very same knowledge existing in the essence of Allah, the Exalted, then why would that not be valid for each one, so that the knowledge existing in each one would be the knowledge existing in the essence of Allah, the Exalted? If the second, it must be said that Allah, the Exalted, did not remain knowing after the indwelling of His knowledge in ʿIsa, peace be upon him, and no rational person would say that.

**[Page 182]**

Second: a debate that took place between me and one of the Christians. I said to him: "Do you accept that the absence of evidence does not indicate the absence of what it evidences, or not? If you deny it, it follows for you that God, exalted is He, is not eternal, because the evidence for His existence is the world. If it follows from the absence of evidence that the thing evidenced is absent, then it follows from the absence of the world in eternity that the Creator is absent in eternity. And if you accept that the absence of evidence does not necessarily entail the absence of what it evidences..."

Then we say: If you permit the union (*ittihad*) of the Word of God, exalted is He, with Jesus, or its indwelling (*hulul*) in him, then how do you know that the Word of God did not enter Zayd and 'Amr? Rather, how do you know that it did not indwell this cat and this dog?

He said to me: "This question does not befit you, because we only affirm that union or indwelling on the basis of what appeared at the hand of Jesus, peace be upon him, of raising the dead and healing the blind and the leper. When we find nothing of that appearing at the hand of anyone else, how can we affirm union or indwelling?"

I said to him: "From this statement I have realized that you did not grasp the beginning of the argument, because you conceded to me that the absence of evidence does not indicate the absence of what it evidences. So if this indwelling is not impossible in general, then at most what exists is that there is a sign indicating its occurrence in the case of Jesus, peace be upon him, and that sign has not been found in the case of Zayd and 'Amr. But the absence of evidence does not indicate the absence of what it evidences. Therefore, the absence of the appearance of these extraordinary acts at the hand of Zayd and 'Amr, or on the cat and the dog, does not entail the absence of that indwelling. Thus it is established that, however much you permit the claim of union and indwelling, it necessarily follows that you must permit the occurrence of that union and that indwelling in the case of every individual, indeed in the case of every animal and plant. And there is no doubt that a doctrine which drives its adherent to such a feeble claim must be definitively false."

Then I said to him: "And how did the raising of the dead and the healing of the blind and the leper indicate what you have said? Is it not the case that the transformation of the staff into a serpent is more remote than the transformation of the dead into a living being? If that appeared at the hand of Moses, peace be upon him, and did not indicate his divinity, then it is all the more fitting that this does not indicate the divinity of Jesus."

**[Page 182 continued]**

Third: We say that the indications of Jesus' states point to servitude more strongly than they point to lordship, because he was diligent in worship, and worship is fitting only for servants. He was in the utmost detachment from this world and in withdrawal from its people, to the point that the Christians themselves said that the Jews killed him. Whoever is in such weakness, how can lordship befit him?

Fourth: The Messiah is either eternal or originated, and to claim his eternity is false, because we know by necessity that he was born, was a child, then became a young man, ate and drank, and what befalls all human beings befell him. And if he was originated, then he was created, and there is no meaning to servitude except that. If it is said: "The meaning of his divinity is that the attribute of divinity inhered in him," we reply: Grant that it was so. Yet the inhering entity is the attribute of God, while the Messiah is the locus, and the locus is originated and created. So the Messiah is nothing but a originated servant. How, then, can he be described as divine?

Fifth: A son must necessarily be of the same kind as the father. If God had a son, he would necessarily be of His kind. Then the two would share in some respects. If the two are not distinguished from each other by anything, then each of them is the other. And if distinction occurs, then that by which they are distinguished is other than that by which they share. Thus composition would occur in the essence of God, and every composite is possible; so the Necessary Being would be possible. This is an impossible contradiction. All of this applies on the assumption of union and indwelling.

As for the third possibility: that it is said the meaning of his being God is that He, glory be to Him, singled out Himself or His body with the power to create bodies and to exercise control over this world. This too is false, because the Christians report of him weakness and incapacity, and that the Jews killed him. Had he been able to create bodies, they would not have been able to kill him. Rather, he would have been killing them and creating for himself an army to defend him.

As for the fourth possibility: that He took him as a son for Himself as a mark of honor. This has been held by a group of Christians called the Armiyusiyya, and there is not much error in it except in the wording. This is the summary of what concerns the Christians, and by it is established the truth of what God, exalted is He, related of him, that he said: "I am the servant of God."

* * *

The second attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has given me the Book﴾. On this there are several issues.

First issue: People differed concerning it. The majority hold that he uttered this statement while still an infant. Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi (d. 319 AH) said that he only said this when he was like an adolescent who understands, though he had not reached the age of legal responsibility. As for the first group, they have two opinions:

One: that he was a prophet at that young age.

Two: it is related from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: the meaning of "He has given me the Book" is that He decreed and determined that He would later send him as a prophet. When he had spoken those words, he fell silent and returned to the state of infancy. When he reached thirty years of age, God sent him as a prophet.

Those who insisted on the invalidity of the first view argued with several points:

One: A prophet is only complete, whereas an infant is imperfect in form, such that a challenge from an infant would be repulsive. Indeed, in repelling people it would be even worse than if he were a woman.

Two: If he had been a prophet in that infancy, his perfection of intellect would have preceded his claim to prophethood, since a prophet must be of complete intellect. But his perfection of intellect at that time was beyond the normal course, so the miracle would precede the challenge, and that is not permissible.

Three: If he had been a prophet at that time, it would have been obligatory for him to occupy himself with explaining the rulings and defining the laws. Had that occurred, it would have become widely known and transmitted. Since that did not happen, we know that he was not a prophet at that time.

The first group replied to the first argument: the child's imperfection is not inherent in him; rather, the matter returns to the smallness of his body and the deficiency of his understanding. When God removes these things, repulsion does not occur; rather, there is desire to listen to his words, and in this state he is more complete and perfect.

As for the second argument: why could it not be said that the perfection of his intellect, though it occurred before his claim, is itself a miracle for Zakariyya, peace be upon him? Or it may be said that it is a sign preparing for his prophethood (*irhas*), or a miraculous gift (*karama*) for Maryam, peace be upon her. Among us, signs preparing for prophethood and miraculous gifts for the righteous are permissible.

As for the third argument: why could it not be said that merely sending him to them without explaining any of the laws and rulings is permissible, and that after he reached maturity he then began to explain those rulings? Thus it is established by this that there is no impossibility in his being a prophet at that time.

His saying ﴿He has given me the Book﴾ indicates that he was a prophet at that time, so it must be taken according to its apparent meaning, unlike what Ikrimah said. As for the statement of Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi, it is remote, because the need for the speech of Jesus, peace be upon him, arose only when the accusation fell upon Maryam, peace be upon her.

Second issue: They differed concerning that Book. Some said it is the Torah, because the definite article in "the Book" refers to what is known, and the Book known to them is the Torah. Abu Muslim said: the intended meaning is the Gospel, because the definite article here is for the category, that is: "He has given me from this kind." Others said: the intended meaning is both the Torah and the Gospel, because the definite article denotes comprehensiveness.

Third issue: They differed as to when He gave him the Book and when He made him a prophet, because His saying ﴿He has given me the Book and made me a prophet﴾ indicates that this had already taken place, either immediately preceding that speech or some time before it. The apparent meaning is that before he spoke to them, God had given him the Book, made him a prophet, and commanded him to pray and to give alms, to call to God and to His religion, and to the Law specific to him. It was said that this revelation came to him while he was in his mother's womb. It was said that when he separated from his mother, God gave him the Book and prophethood, and that he spoke with his mother and informed her of his condition, and told her that he would speak to them in a way that indicates the innocence of her situation. For this reason she pointed to him with speech.

**The third attribute:** His saying: ﴿And He has made me a prophet﴾. Some have said: he informed that he was a prophet (nabi), but he was not a messenger (rasul), because at that time he had not brought the sharia (sacred law). The meaning of his being a prophet is that he was of elevated rank. This view is weak, because the prophet in the terminology of the sharia is the one whom God has singled out with prophethood and messengership, especially when mention of the law is joined to it, which is His saying: ﴿and has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah﴾.

**The fourth attribute:** His saying: ﴿And He has made me blessed wherever I am﴾. One may ask: how did He make him blessed when people before him were upon the correct religion, and when he came some of them became Jews and some Christians, saying in trinitarian terms, and only a few remained upon the truth?

The answer: they have mentioned several aspects regarding the meaning of "blessed" (mubarak):

First: barakah in the language means permanence, and its root is from the kneeling of a camel (buruk al-ba'ir). So the meaning is: He made me firm upon the religion of God, steadfast in it.

Second: he was blessed because he taught people their religion and called them to the path of truth. If they went astray, it was from their own side, not from his. Al-Hasan reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The mother of Isa, peace be upon him, took Isa to the kuttab (school) and said to the teacher: I entrust him to you on condition that you do not beat him. The teacher said to him: Write. He said: What should I write? He said: Write abjad. Isa, peace be upon him, raised his head and said: Do you know what abjad is? The teacher raised the whip to strike him. He said: O teacher, do not strike me; if you do not know, then ask me, for I will teach you: the alif is from the blessings (alaa) of God, the ba' is from the splendour (bahaa') of God, the jim is from the beauty (jamal) of God, and the dal is from the discharge (ada') of the truth to God."

Third: barakah means increase and elevation. It is as if he said: He made me, in all circumstances, victorious, successful, and triumphant, because as long as I remain in this world, I will be upright over others with proof; and when the appointed time comes, God the Exalted will honour me by raising me to heaven.

Fourth: he is blessed for the people in that through my supplication there comes about the reviving of the dead and the healing of the blind and the leper. It is related from Qatadah that a woman saw him while he was reviving the dead and healing the blind and the leper, and she said: "Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breast you were nursed at!" Isa, peace be upon him, replied to her: "Blessed is whoever recites the Book of God, follows what is in it, and is not a tyrant (jabbar) or a wretch."

As for His saying: ﴿wherever I am﴾, it indicates that his condition did not change, unlike what has been said, that he returned to the state of childhood and the removal of accountability.

* * *

**The fifth attribute:** His saying: ﴿and has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah as long as I remain alive﴾. If it is asked: how was he commanded with prayer and zakah while he was a small child, and the pen is lifted from him, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The pen is lifted from three: from the child until he reaches maturity," and so on? The answer to this is from two aspects:

[Page 184]

First: His saying: ﴿and has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah﴾ does not indicate that God enjoined him to perform them immediately, but after reaching maturity. So perhaps the meaning is that God enjoined him with them and with their performance at the time specified for him, which is the time of maturity.

Second: Perhaps God the Exalted, when Isa was separated from his mother, made him mature, intelligent, and complete in limbs and physical form. Its confirmation is His saying: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Isa to God is like the likeness of Adam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. Just as God created Adam complete and perfect at once, so too is the case with Isa, peace be upon him. This second view is closer to the apparent meaning because of His saying: ﴿as long as I remain alive﴾, which indicates that this obligation was directed at him throughout the whole period of his life. But one may say: if the matter were so, the people, when they saw him, would have seen him as a person complete in limbs and perfect in form, and speech coming from such a person would not be strange, so they should not have been amazed. So perhaps the better view is that God made him, despite his small body, strong in constitution and complete in intellect, such that he could perform prayer and zakah. The verse indicates that his accountability did not change, whether he was on earth, or when he was raised to heaven, or when he will descend once more.

**The sixth attribute:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and dutiful to my mother﴾, i.e., He made me dutiful to my mother. This indicates our statement that the act of the servant is created by God the Exalted, because the verse indicates that his being dutiful came about by God's making. Creating it and inclining him toward the divine favours (alutaf) is a departure from the apparent meaning. Then His saying: ﴿and dutiful to my mother﴾ is an indication of exonerating his mother from fornication, for if she had been an adulteress, the infallible Messenger would not have been commanded to honour her.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: He made his very self dutiful because of his extreme piety toward her. Its accusative (nasb) is by a verb in the sense of "enjoined upon me," since "enjoined upon me with prayer" and "obligated me to it" are one and the same.

**The seventh attribute:** His saying: ﴿and has not made me a tyrant, wretched﴾. This also indicates our statement, because when he explained that He made him dutiful and did not make him a tyrant, this would be appropriate only if God had made others tyrants and undutiful to their mothers. For if God did that to everyone, there would be no special distinction for Isa, peace be upon him, in this. It is known that he, peace be upon him, mentioned this in the context of distinction. His saying: ﴿and has not made me a tyrant﴾ means: He did not make me arrogant; rather, I am submissive, because I am humble toward her. If I were a tyrant, I would be disobedient and wretched.

It is reported that Isa, peace be upon him, said: "My heart is soft, and I am humble within myself." It is also reported from some scholars: "You will not find the one who is undutiful to his parents except a tyrant and wretched," and he recited: ﴿and dutiful to my mother, and has not made me a tyrant, wretched﴾. "And you will not find one who mistreats his slaves except a proud boaster," and he recited: ﴿Indeed, God does not love one who is a proud boaster, boastful﴾ [An-Nisa': 36].

**The third attribute:** His saying: ﴿And He has made me a prophet﴾. Some have said: he informed that he was a prophet (nabi), but he was not a messenger (rasul), because at that time he had not brought the sharia (sacred law). The meaning of his being a prophet is that he was of elevated rank. **The fifth attribute:** His saying: ﴿and has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah as long as I remain alive﴾. If it is asked: how was he commanded with prayer and zakah while he was a small child, and the pen is lifted from him, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The pen is lifted from three: from the child until he reaches maturity," and so on? The answer to this is from two aspects:

[Page 184]

First: His saying: ﴿and has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah﴾ does not indicate that God enjoined him to perform them immediately, but after reaching maturity. So perhaps the meaning is that God enjoined him with them and with their performance at the time specified for him, which is the time of maturity.

Second: Perhaps God the Exalted, when Isa was separated from his mother, made him mature, intelligent, and complete in limbs and physical form. Its confirmation is His saying: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Isa to God is like the likeness of Adam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. Just as God created Adam complete and perfect at once, so too is the case with Isa, peace be upon him. This second view is closer to the apparent meaning because of His saying: ﴿as long as I remain alive﴾, which indicates that this obligation was directed at him throughout the whole period of his life. But one may say: if the matter were so, the people, when they saw him, would have seen him as a person complete in limbs and perfect in form, and speech coming from such a person would not be strange, so they should not have been amazed. So perhaps the better view is that God made him, despite his small body, strong in constitution and complete in intellect, such that he could perform prayer and zakah. The verse indicates that his accountability did not change, whether he was on earth, or when he was raised to heaven, or when he will descend once more.

**The sixth attribute:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and dutiful to my mother﴾, i.e., He made me dutiful to my mother. This indicates our statement that the act of the servant is created by God the Exalted, because the verse indicates that his being dutiful came about by God's making. Creating it and inclining him toward the divine favours (alutaf) is a departure from the apparent meaning. Then His saying: ﴿and dutiful to my mother﴾ is an indication of exonerating his mother from fornication, for if she had been an adulteress, the infallible Messenger would not have been commanded to honour her.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: He made his very self dutiful because of his extreme piety toward her. Its accusative (nasb) is by a verb in the sense of "enjoined upon me," since "enjoined upon me with prayer" and "obligated me to it" are one and the same.

**The seventh attribute:** His saying: ﴿and has not made me a tyrant, wretched﴾. This also indicates our statement, because when he explained that He made him dutiful and did not make him a tyrant, this would be appropriate only if God had made others tyrants and undutiful to their mothers. For if God did that to everyone, there would be no special distinction for Isa, peace be upon him, in this. It is known that he, peace be upon him, mentioned this in the context of distinction. His saying: ﴿and has not made me a tyrant﴾ means: He did not make me arrogant; rather, I am submissive, because I am humble toward her. If I were a tyrant, I would be disobedient and wretched.

It is reported that Isa, peace be upon him, said: "My heart is soft, and I am humble within myself." It is also reported from some scholars: "You will not find the one who is undutiful to his parents except a tyrant and wretched," and he recited: ﴿and dutiful to my mother, and has not made me a tyrant, wretched﴾. "And you will not find one who mistreats his slaves except a proud boaster," and he recited: ﴿Indeed, God does not love one who is a proud boaster, boastful﴾ [An-Nisa': 36].

**The eighth attribute:** it is His saying: ﴿And peace is upon me the day I was born, and the day I die, and the day I am raised alive﴾. Concerning it there are several issues.

**First issue:** Some have said that the definite article in *al-salam* (the *lam al-ta'rif*, the definite article) refers back to what was mentioned in the story of Yahya, peace be upon him, in His saying: ﴿And peace is upon him﴾ (Maryam: 15). That is, the peace directed at him in the three situations is also directed at me. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "The correct view is that this definite article is a compensation (*ta'wid*) with a curse upon those who accused Maryam of fornication. Its verification is that the article is for comprehensiveness (*istighraq*). So when he says: ﴿And peace is upon me﴾, it is as if he said: all peace is upon me and upon my followers, so nothing remains for the enemies except the curse. A parallel to this is the saying of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And peace is upon those who follow guidance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47], meaning that the punishment is upon those who denied and turned away. The situation was one of obstinacy and stubborn opposition, and this kind of indirect implication suits it."

**Second issue:** Some have narrated from Isa, peace be upon him, that he said to Yahya: "You are better than me. Allah sent peace upon you, and I sent peace upon myself." Al-Hasan answered: "His sending peace upon himself is by Allah's sending peace upon him."

[p. 185]

**Third issue:** The judge (*al-Qadi*) said: "Peace (*al-salam*) is an expression for that by which security is achieved, and from it comes *al-salamah* (safety) in blessings and the removal of calamities. So it is as if he asked his Lord and requested from Him what Allah, exalted is He, informed that He had done for Yahya. Prophets must be those whose supplications are answered. The most urgent states in which a human being needs safety are these three situations: the day of birth, the day of death, and the day of resurrection. So he requested, for all the states in which he needs safety and the gathering of happiness from Allah, exalted is He, that he be protected from calamities and fears in every state."

"Know that the Jews and Christians deny that Isa, peace be upon him, spoke in infancy. They argued against it: this is one of the extraordinary events whose transmission is strongly motivated, so if it had occurred it would have been transmitted by mass transmission (*tawatur*). And if that had happened, the Christians would have known it, especially since they are among the most diligent of people in investigating his circumstances and the most exaggerating about him, to the point that they claimed he was god. There is no doubt that speaking in infancy is among the great virtues and complete excellences. Since the Christians did not know of it, despite their intense love and thorough investigation of his circumstances, we know that it did not occur. Moreover, the Jews openly showed their enmity toward him when he openly claimed prophethood. Had he spoken in infancy and claimed the mission, their enmity toward him would have been greater and their intention to kill him would have been more serious. Since none of that happened, we know that he did not speak."

"As for the Muslims, they argued by reason that he did speak: had his speech not indicated to them the innocence of his mother from fornication, they would not have abandoned enforcing the prescribed punishment for fornication against her. Their abandoning of that is evidence that he, peace be upon him, spoke in the cradle. They answered the first objection by saying that perhaps those present at his speech were few, so it did not become widely known. As for the second, perhaps the Jews were not present there and did not hear his speech, so they did not busy themselves with the intention of killing him."

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 34–35:**

The words of God Most High: ﴿That is Jesus, son of Mary, the word of truth about which they dispute.﴾ ﴿It is not for God to take a son; glory be to Him. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ In this are several issues:

**The first issue:** ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿qawla al-ḥaqqi﴾ with a fatḥah (naṣb). Ibn Masʿūd reads (qāla al-ḥaqqa) and (qāla Allāhu). Al-Ḥasan reads (qūla al-ḥaqqi) with a ḍammah on the qāf, and likewise in al-Anʿām: (qawluhu al-ḥaqqu). The words qawl (qawl), qāl (qāl) and qūl (qūl) have one meaning, like al-rahb, al-rahab and al-ruhb (fear). As for its being marfūʿ (nominative), it is either a predicate following another predicate or the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtadaʾ). As for its being manṣūb (accusative), it is either in the sense of praise (madḥ), if it is explained as the Word of God, or it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing the content of the sentence, like your saying: "He is the truth with God, not falsehood." And God knows best.

**The second issue:** There is no doubt that the intended meaning of His words ﴿That is Jesus, son of Mary﴾ is a reference to what preceded, namely His words ﴿I am the servant of God; He has given me the Scripture﴾. That is: the one described with these attributes is Jesus, son of Mary. And in His words ﴿Jesus, son of Mary﴾ there is an indication that he was the child of this woman and her son, not that he was the son of God. As for ﴿the word of truth﴾, there are several interpretations:

First: that the very person of Jesus, peace be upon him, is the word of truth. This is because al-Ḥaqq (the Truth) is one of God's names, so there is no difference between saying "Jesus is the Word of God" and saying "Jesus is the word of the Truth."

Second: that the intended meaning is: "That is Jesus, son of Mary, the true word," but you have added the described noun to its description, so it is like His words ﴿Indeed this is the true certainty﴾ (al-Wāqiʿah 95). The benefit of your saying "the true word" is to emphasize what you mentioned first, namely that Jesus, peace be upon him, is the son of Mary.

Third: that ﴿the word of truth﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, as if it were said: "That is Jesus, son of Mary, and our description of him is the word of truth." So He, Exalted is He, first described him, then mentioned that this described one is Jesus, son of Mary, then mentioned that this whole description is the word of truth, in the sense that it is established and cannot be overturned, as the doubt that occurs among them has been overturned. And it has the meaning of "Indeed this is the true certainty."

As for their disputing about Jesus, peace be upon him, it refers to the positions we have related from the Jews and Christians, which were mentioned earlier in Surat Āl ʿImrān. It is related that when Jesus, peace be upon him, was raised up, four of their greatest men and scholars were present. The first was asked: "What do you say about Jesus?" He said: "He is God, God is God, and his mother is God." Some people followed him in this, and they are the Israelites. The fourth was asked: "What do you say?" He said: "He is the servant of God and His messenger, and he is the believing Muslim." And he said: "Do you not know that Jesus used to eat and sleep, and that God, Exalted is He, is not subject to that?" Thus he refuted them.

As for His words ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾, it may bear two meanings:

The first: that the existence of a son for Him is impossible. So our statement ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾ is like His saying "It is not for God to say to anyone, 'He is my son,'" because this statement is false, and falsehood does not befit the wisdom and perfection of God, Exalted is He. Thus His words ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾ are like our saying "It is not for God to do wrong," meaning that this does not befit His wisdom and the perfection of His divinity. Al-Jubbāʾī used this verse, on the basis of this interpretation, to argue that it is not for God to do everything, because He, Exalted is He, has declared that He does not have this (i.e., such an act of origination). That is, He does not have this choice. Our companions (the Ashʿarīs) answered him that lying is impossible for God, Exalted is He, and therefore He said ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾.

* * *

As for His words ﴿Glory be to Him. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** When He, Exalted is He, said ﴿Glory be to Him﴾ and then immediately said ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾, this served as a proof of His transcendence above having a son. The explanation is that whatever is made a son of God is either eternal and without beginning, or it is originated. If it is eternal, that is impossible, because if it were necessary in its own essence, then there would be more than one necessarily existent being, and this is absurd. If it is possible in its essence, then it would be dependent for its existence upon the necessarily existent in its essence, which is self-sufficient in its essence, so the possible would be in need in its essence, and thus it would be a servant of Him, because there is no meaning of servanthood except that. As for the one made a son being originated, its existence would be after its non-existence, by the creation and bringing-into-being of that Eternal One. This is what is meant by His words ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾. So it would be a servant of Him, not a son of Him. Thus it is established that it is impossible for God to have a son.

**The second issue:** Our companions used His words ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ as evidence for the eternity (qidam) of the speech of God, Exalted is He. They said: because the verse indicates that when He, Exalted is He, wishes to bring something into existence, He says to it "Be," and it is. So if His saying "Be" were originated, its origination would require another saying, and this would lead to an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible. Thus it is established that the speech of God is eternal, not originated. The Muʿtazilah used the verse as evidence for the origination of the speech of God, Exalted is He, in several ways:

First: He introduced the particle ʾidhā (when) into it, and this particle indicates the future. So the saying must occur only in the future.

Second: the letter fāʾ indicates sequence (taʿqīb), and the fāʾ in His words ﴿then it only says to him﴾ indicates that this saying is subsequent to that decree. And what is subsequent to something else is originated.

Third: the fāʾ in His words ﴿and it is﴾ indicates that the thing comes into existence immediately after that saying without any interval. So the speech of God precedes the origination of the originated thing with a precedence without interval. And what precedes the originated thing with a precedence without interval is itself originated. So the speech of God is originated.

Know that the arguments of both groups are weak. As for the argument of our companions, it requires that His saying "Be" be eternal, and that is false by consensus. As for the argument of the Muʿtazilah, it requires that the speech of God, Exalted is He, be what is composed of letters and sounds, and that is originated, and there is no dispute about that. What is claimed is the eternity of something else.

**The third issue:** Some people took the verse according to its apparent meaning and claimed that when He, Exalted is He, originates something, He says to it "Be." This is weak, because He either says to it "Be" before its origination or at the time of its origination. If it is the first, then that would be address to the non-existent, and that is futile. If it is the second, then at the time of its origination it has already come into existence through power and will, so what effect does His saying "Be" have on it? Some people claimed that what is meant by His saying "Be" is the creating and forming (takhlīq and takwīn), because power over a thing is different from the bringing-into-being of a thing. Indeed God, Glory be to Him, is capable in eternity without being the one who brings into being in eternity. Also, He is now capable of worlds other than this world without being the one who brings them into being. The capability (qādiriyyah) is other than the being the one who brings into being (mukawwiniyyah), and the bringing-into-being (takwīn) is not the very thing brought into being (mukawwan). For we say: the thing brought into being has come into existence only because God, Exalted is He, brought it into being and caused it to exist. So if the bringing-into-being were the very thing brought into being, then our statement "the thing brought into being has come into existence through God's bringing it into being" would be equivalent to our statement "the thing brought into being has come into existence through itself," and that is impossible. Thus it is established that the bringing-into-being is other than the thing brought into being. So His saying "Be" is an indication of the attribute called bringing-into-being. Others said that His saying "Be" is an expression for the effectiveness of the power and will of God, Exalted is He, over possible things. Their occurrence by that power and will, without resistance or repulsion, is like the obedient servant, subjugated and submissive to the commands of his master. So God, Exalted is He, expressed that meaning by this expression, by way of metaphor (istiʿārah).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 36–37:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.﴾ ﴿Then the factions differed among themselves, so woe to those who disbelieved, from the scene of a tremendous day.﴾ ﴿How well they will hear and see on the day they come to Us! But the wrongdoers today are in clear error.﴾ ﴿And warn them of the day of regret, when the matter will be decided, while they are heedless and do not believe.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We shall inherit the earth and whoever is upon it, and to Us they will be returned.﴾

Know that His words, ﴿And indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him﴾, contain several issues.

The first issue: The Medinans and Abu 'Amr read ﴿أنَّ﴾ (*anna*) with a fatha, meaning "and because He is my Lord and your Lord, worship Him." The Kufans and Abu 'Ubayda read it with a kasra (*inna*) as a new sentence (*ibtida'*, beginning). In the codex of Ubayy, the reading is ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ﴾ with a kasra and without a waw, meaning "because of that, worship Him."

The second issue: It is not correct for Allah Himself to say ﴿And indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him﴾. Therefore, the speaker must be someone other than Allah the Exalted, and there are two opinions on this:

The first: The implied meaning is: "So say, O Muhammad, indeed Allah is my Lord and your Lord," after the manifest proofs have been shown that 'Isa is the servant of Allah.

The second: Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: The waw in ﴿وإنَّ اللَّهَ﴾ is a conjunction joining the words of 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿He said, "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture"﴾ [Maryam: 30]. It is as if he said: "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah, and indeed He is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him." Wahb ibn Munabbih said: When he informed them of his mission, his birth and his description, he made a covenant with them that Allah is my Lord and your Lord, meaning that we are all servants of Allah the Exalted.

Page 188

The third issue: His words ﴿And indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord﴾ indicate that the one who governs people and arranges their affairs is Allah the Exalted, contrary to the view of the astrologers, who hold that the governors of people and the arrangers of their affairs regarding happiness and misery are the stars. It also indicates that the God is one, because the word *Allah* is a proper name for Him, glorified be He. When He says ﴿Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord﴾, it means that there is no lord of the creatures other than Allah the Exalted, and this indicates monotheism (*tawhid*). As for His words ﴿so worship Him﴾, it is established in *usul al-fiqh* (the principles of jurisprudence) that the placing of a ruling upon a fitting attribute indicates causation (*'illiyya*, the relation of cause and effect). Here, the command to worship is placed upon the mention of the attribute of lordship (*rububiyya*). This indicates that worshipping Him, glorified be He, is obligatory for us only because He is our Lord. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 38–40:**

As for His saying, ﴿Hear them and see them the day they come to Us﴾, there are several issues.

**The first issue:** They said: *al-ta'ajjub* (wonder) is the regarding of something as great while being ignorant of the cause of its greatness. Then the term *ta'ajjub* may be used for mere regarding of something as great, without the cause being hidden, or when the greatness has no cause of its occurrence. Al-Farra' said: Sufyan said: "I recited before Shurayh: ﴿Nay, you wonder, and they mock﴾ [al-Saffat: 12], and he said: 'Indeed God is not amazed at anything; only one who does not know is amazed.' I mentioned that to Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and he said: 'Shurayh is a poet, pleased with his own knowledge, and Abdullah [Ibn Mas'ud] knew better than him about this.' He recited it: ﴿Nay, I have wondered, and they mock.﴾" The meaning is that there proceeded from God, exalted is He, an act which, if a similar act proceeded from creatures, would indicate the occurrence of wonder in their hearts. By this interpretation, *al-makr* (plotting) and *al-istihza'* (mockery) are attributed to God, exalted is He. Having understood this, we say: *ta'ajjub* has two forms:

The first: *ma af'alahu* (how [something] is!).

The second: *af'il bihi* (look at him!), as in His saying, ﴿Hear them and see them the day they come to Us﴾. The grammarians have offered interpretations of it:

The first: They said: *akrim bi-Zayd* (how generous is Zayd!) originally comes from *akrama Zaydun*, meaning "Zayd became possessed of generosity," just as *aghadda al-ba'ir* means "the camel became possessed of a tumor" (*ghuddah*). However, it has come in the form of an imperative while its meaning is a declarative statement, just as declarative forms have come with imperative meaning, such as His saying: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves [for three periods]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228], ﴿And mothers shall nurse their children﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233], and ﴿Say: Whoever is in error, the Most Merciful will extend for him an extension﴾ [Maryam: 75], meaning: the Most Merciful extends for him an extension. Similarly, the saying *rahimahu Allah* (may God have mercy on him) is declarative, though its meaning is supplication, and the *ba'* is superfluous.

The second: It may be said that it is a command to everyone to make Zayd generous, i.e., to describe him with generosity, and the *ba'* is superfluous, like His saying: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195]. I have heard from some men of letters an interpretation of this.

The third: That your saying *akrim bi-Zayd* indicates that Zayd has reached such a degree of generosity that, as it were, he has himself become generosity. So even if you wish to make another generous, it is he who attaches you to your aim and achieves your purpose for you, just as one who says *uktub bi-l-qalam* (write with the pen) means that the pen is what attaches you to your aim and achieves your purpose.

**The second issue:** His saying ﴿Hear them and see them the day they come to Us﴾ has three aspects:

The first, which is the well-known and strongest view, is that its meaning is "How much they hear and how much they see!" But wonder in relation to God, exalted is He, is impossible, as has been stated before. Rather, what is meant is that their hearing and seeing on that day are deserving of being marvelled at, after they had been deaf and blind in the world.

It has also been said: its meaning is a threat, regarding what they will hear and see that will distress their sight and split their hearts.

The second: Al-Qadi said: It is possible that what is meant is: "Make these people hear and see [the state of] those people who come to Us, so that they may take warning and be deterred."

The third: Al-Jubba'i said: It is permissible to say: "Make people hear about these [people] and see them," so that they may know their situation and the evil of their end, and thus refrain from doing the same as they did.

As for His saying ﴿But the wrongdoers today are in clear error﴾, there are two views:

The first: ﴿But the wrongdoers today are in clear error﴾, and in the Hereafter they will recognize the truth.

The second: ﴿But the wrongdoers today are in clear error﴾, and they in the Hereafter are in error regarding Paradise, unlike the believers.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And warn them﴾, there is no doubt that it is a command to Muhammad ﷺ to warn those of his time. It is appropriate to take this as an indication that His saying ﴿so the factions differed﴾ means the differing of all of them in the time of the Messenger ﷺ. As for warning, it is intimidation regarding punishment, so that they may beware of abandoning the worship of God, exalted is He. As for the Day of Regret, there is no doubt that it is the Day of Resurrection, since the regret of the people of the Fire is greatest then. It has been said that they will also feel regret in Paradise if they were not among the foremost who attained the high ranks. The first view is the correct one, because regret is grief, and that is not fitting for the people of reward.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When the matter is decided﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: ﴿When the matter is decided﴾ by the presentation of proofs and the explanation of the matter of reward and punishment.

The second: ﴿When the matter is decided﴾ on the Day of Regret, with the annihilation of this world and the cessation of obligation. The first is closer, because of His saying ﴿while they are heedless and do not believe﴾. It is as if He, exalted is He, made clear that the proofs and clear signs had appeared while they were in heedlessness and did not believe.

The third: It has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ was asked about His saying "the matter is decided," and he said: "When death is brought in the form of a white-speckled ram, and it is slaughtered while the two groups look on. The people of Paradise will increase in joy upon joy, and the people of the Fire in grief upon grief."

Know that death is an accident (*'arad*), so it cannot become a living body. Rather, what is meant is that there will be no death at all after that. As for His saying, ﴿while they are in heedlessness﴾, that means heedless of that day and of the manner of their regret, ﴿and they do not believe﴾, that is, in that day. Then He said after it: ﴿Indeed, We will inherit the earth and whoever is upon it﴾, meaning these matters will lead to there being no one who controls harm or benefit except God, exalted is He. ﴿And to Us they will be returned﴾, meaning to the place of Our judgment and decree, because He, exalted is He, is far above place, so that return would be to Him. This is a great warning and an eloquent admonition to the disobedient.
