**The Third Story: The Story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And mention in the Book Ibrahim. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet.﴾ ﴿When he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship that which does not hear and does not see and does not avail you at all?"﴾ ﴿"O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to a straight path."﴾ ﴿"O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has been, to the Most Merciful, disobedient."﴾ ﴿"O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you would be a companion to Satan."﴾

Know that the purpose of this surah is to explain tawhid (the oneness of God), prophethood, and resurrection. Those who deny tawhid are those who affirm a deity other than God, exalted is He, and they are of two groups. Among them are those who affirm a deity other than God that is living, rational and understanding, and they are the Christians. Among them are those who affirm a deity other than God that is inanimate, not living, not rational, and not understanding, and they are the worshippers of idols. Although the two groups share in error, the error of the second group is greater. So when God, exalted is He, had explained the error of the first group, He spoke of the error of the second group, who are the worshippers of idols, and said: ﴿And mention in the Book﴾. The waw in His saying ﴿And mention﴾ is a conjunction with His saying ﴿A mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariyya﴾, as if, when the story of Isa and Zakariyya (peace be upon them both) had ended, He said: "You have mentioned the condition of Zakariyya, so mention the condition of Ibrahim." He was commanded to mention him because neither he, nor his people, nor the people of his town were occupied with knowledge and the study of books. So when he reports this story exactly as it was, without addition or subtraction, that would be a report of the unseen and an overpowering miracle indicating his prophethood. And he began the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) for several reasons:

The first: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was the father of the Arabs, and they acknowledged his high station and the purity of his religion, as God said: ﴿The religion of your father Ibrahim﴾ (al-Hajj: 78), and God said: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Ibrahim except one who makes a fool of himself?﴾ (al-Baqarah: 130). It is as if God said to the Arabs: "If you are imitators of your forefathers, as your saying is: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps﴾, then it is known that the most noble and greatest in rank of your forefathers is Ibrahim (peace be upon him), so imitate him in abandoning the worship of idols. And if you are among those who reason by evidence, then look into these proofs that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) presented, so that you may know the corruption of worshipping idols. In sum, follow Ibrahim, either by imitation or by reasoning."

The second: Many of the disbelievers in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) used to say: "How can we abandon the religion of our fathers and forefathers?" So God mentioned the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and explained that he abandoned the religion of his father, refuted his statement with evidence, and preferred following evidence over following his father, so that the disbelievers would know that preferring the side of the father over the side of evidence is a rejection of the most noble and greatest father, who is Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

The third: Many of the disbelievers used to hold fast to imitation and deny reasoning, as God said: ﴿They said, "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion"﴾ (az-Zukhruf: 23), and ﴿They said, "We found our fathers worshipping them"﴾ (al-Anbiya: 53). So God related about Ibrahim (peace be upon him) his adherence to the method of reasoning, as a warning to these people about the invalidity of this method. Then God said, describing Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet.﴾ Regarding the word siddiq there are two views:

One: that it is an intensive form signifying that he was truthful, meaning one whose habit is truthfulness, because this pattern indicates that; it is said "a man who is khimmir" and "sikkir" for one devoted to these actions.

The second: that it is one who frequently affirms the truth until he becomes known for it. The first is preferable, because one who affirms something is not described as a siddiq unless he is truthful in that affirmation; thus the matter returns to the first meaning. If it is said: Did not God say: ﴿And those who believed in God and His messengers—those are the siddiqun and the martyrs﴾ (al-Hadid: 19)?

We say: Those who believe in God and His messengers are truthful in that affirmation. Know that a prophet must be truthful in everything he reports, because God affirmed him, and whoever God affirms is truthful; otherwise lying would be attributed to the speech of God, exalted is He. From this it follows that the Messenger is truthful in everything he says. Moreover, the messengers are witnesses of God over the people, as God said: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness and We bring you, [O Muhammad], as a witness against these?﴾ (an-Nisa: 41). And a witness's testimony is accepted only when he is not a liar.

If it is said: What is your view regarding Ibrahim (peace be upon him) in his saying: ﴿Rather, it was done by the largest of them﴾ (al-Anbiya: 63) and ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾? We say: We have explained, in interpreting these verses, by clear proofs, that none of that is a lie. Since it has been established that every prophet must be a siddiq, and not every siddiq must be a prophet, it becomes clear that the rank of the siddiq is close to the rank of the prophet; therefore he moved from mentioning his being a siddiq to mentioning his being a prophet.

As for the prophet, its meaning is that he is elevated in rank with God and with the people, and what higher elevation is there than the elevation of one whom God made an intermediary between Himself and His servants?

His saying ﴿was a siddiq﴾: it has been said that it means "became", and it has been said that its meaning is "he was found to be a siddiq and a prophet", i.e., he was, from the beginning of his existence to its end, described by truthfulness and preservation.

The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: This sentence came as a parenthetical insertion between the substituted noun and its substitute, I mean "Ibrahim" and "when he said". Its parallel is your saying: "I saw Zayd, and what a man your brother is." It is permissible for "idh" to be connected to "kana" or to "siddiqan nabiyyan", meaning: he was combining the attributes of the siddiqun and the prophets when he addressed his father with those addresses. As for his saying ﴿O father﴾ (yā abatī), the taa' is a substitute for the ya' of possession, and one does not say "yā abatī" so as not to combine the substitute and what it substitutes; it may be said "yā abatā", since the alif is a substitute for the ya'. Know that God related that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) spoke with his father in four types of speech:

* * *

The first type: his saying: ﴿Why do you worship that which does not hear and does not see and does not avail you at all?﴾ He described the idols with three attributes, each of which is damaging to divinity. The explanation of this is from several aspects:

The first: worship is the ultimate of glorification, so it is deserved only by one who possesses ultimate bounty, and that is the deity from whom the roots and branches of blessings come, as we established in explaining His saying: ﴿And indeed, God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him﴾ (Ali Imran: 51), and His saying: ﴿How do you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ (al-Baqarah: 28), and the verse. Just as it is known necessarily that it is not permissible to occupy oneself with thanking something that does not bestow blessings, so it must not be permissible to occupy oneself with worshipping it.

The second: if it does not hear, does not see, and does not distinguish between one who obeys it and one who disobeys it, then what benefit is there in worshipping it? This alerts you that the deity must be knowing of all known things, so that the worshipper is safe from the occurrence of error on the part of the one worshipped.

The third: supplication is the essence of worship. If the idol does not hear the supplication of the supplicant, then what benefit is there in worshipping it? And if it does not see the one who draws near to it, then what benefit is there in that drawing near?

The fourth: the one who hears, sees, and benefits or harms is better than one who is devoid of all that, and a human is described by these attributes, so he is better and more perfect than the idol. How, then, is it fitting for the more excellent to worship the baser?

The fifth: if it neither benefits nor harms, then no benefit is hoped from it and no harm is feared from it, so what benefit is there in worshipping it?

The sixth: if it cannot protect itself from being broken and destroyed, as God related about Ibrahim (peace be upon him) that he smashed them and made them into fragments, then what hope can others have in them?

Know that he censured the idol from three aspects:

One: it does not hear.

Two: it does not see.

Three: it does not avail you at all. It is as if he said to him: "Rather, divinity belongs only to my Lord, for He hears and answers the supplication of the supplicant, and sees, as He said: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ (Ta-Ha: 46), and He fulfills needs: ﴿Is He who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him?﴾ (an-Naml: 62)."

Know that His saying here ﴿Why do you worship﴾ is to be understood as referring to worship itself. As for His saying at the third stage: ﴿Do not worship Satan﴾, it is not said that this means worship; rather what is meant is obedience, because they did not worship Satan. Therefore it must be understood as obedience. Moreover, we say: when we abandon the apparent meaning here due to evidence, it does not follow that the apparent meaning must be abandoned in the first stage without evidence.

If it is said: Either it is said that the father of Ibrahim believed of those idols that they were gods, in the sense that they were powerful, choosing, creating beings for people and animals; or it is said that he did not believe that, but rather believed that they were images of the stars, and the stars are the gods that govern this world, so the glorification of the images of the stars follows from glorifying the stars; or he believed that these idols were images of human persons who are honored by God, so glorifying them requires that those persons be intercessors for them with God; or he believed that those idols were talismans constructed according to particular conjunctions of the stars, of a kind rarely attained, and that they are thereby empowered; or other excuses reported from idol worshippers. If the father of Ibrahim was of the first category, he was in utter madness, because knowing that this carved wood, at this very hour, did not create the heavens and the earth is among the most evident necessary knowledge, so one who doubts it lacks the most evident necessary knowledge, and so he was insane; and an insane person cannot be addressed with argument or debated. If he was of the second category, then these proofs do not refute any of that, because that doctrine is refuted only by establishing proof that the stars are not living and not capable of creating bodies and creating life; and it is known that the proof mentioned here does not establish that objective. So we know that this proof is useless under every assumption. We say: There is no dispute that it is not hidden from a rational person that carved wood is not fit to create the world, and rather their doctrine is on the second basis. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) presented this proof against them because they believed that worshipping them yields benefit, either by way of the special property arising from the talismans, or by way of the stars benefiting and harming. So Ibrahim (peace be upon him) showed that there is no benefit in obeying them and no harm in turning away from them, and therefore it must be that their worship is not good.

The answer to the first point: what is meant by guidance is the explanation of the proof, its clarification and its elucidation.

At this point the questioner returned and said: I do not deny that there must be guidance (dalalah) to the proof, but I say that coming to know that guidance is obtained only from one who has a complete soul, far from deficiency and error, and that is the soul of the infallible Prophet or the infallible Imam. So if you concede that there must be a Prophet for this purpose, you have conceded that the aim is achieved. The respondent answered and said: I did not concede that there must be guidance from a Prophet in coming to know the proofs, but I say: this path is easier, and Abraham (peace be upon him) called him to the easiest of the easy. *  *  *

The third type: His saying, ﴿O my father, do not worship Satan; indeed Satan has been disobedient to the Most Merciful.﴾ That is: do not obey him, because he disobeys God; thus he repelled him from accepting from him by this attribute, because it is the greatest of repulsive qualities. Know that Abraham (peace be upon him), out of his thoroughness in sincerity, did not mention from Satan's offenses anything but his being disobedient to God, and he did not mention his enmity toward Adam (peace be upon him), as if reflecting on the magnitude of that disobedience troubled his thought and covered his mind. Also, disobedience to God, exalted is He, issues only from one of weak judgment, and whoever is like that is worthy that his opinion not be heeded and that his words be given no weight.

If it is said: this statement depends on establishing several matters:
First: establishing the Creator.
Second: establishing Satan.
Third: establishing that Satan is disobedient to God.
Fourth: that since he is disobedient, obeying him in anything is not permissible.
Fifth: that the belief which that man held was derived from obedience to Satan. And it is part of the nature of the argument presented to an opponent that it be composed of premises that are known and accepted. Perhaps Abraham's father disputed all these premises. How? For what is related of him is that he did not affirm any god other than Nimrod, so how would he accept the existence of the God, the Most Merciful? And if he did not accept His existence, how could he accept that Satan was disobedient to the Most Merciful? Furthermore, even granting that, how would the opponent accept by mere this statement that his doctrine is derived from Satan? Rather, perhaps he would turn that back on his opponent? We say: the proof relied upon in refuting the doctrine of Azar is the one he mentioned first, in his saying: ﴿Why do you worship what neither hears nor sees and cannot avail you anything?﴾ As for this statement, it operates as a warning and a caution that moves him to consider that proof. On this assumption the objection falls away.

*  *  *

The fourth type: His saying, ﴿O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so that you become a companion (waliyy) of Satan.﴾ Al-Farra' said: the meaning of "I fear" is "I know." Most scholars hold that it is to be taken in its apparent sense. The first opinion is valid only if Abraham (peace be upon him) knew that his father would die in that disbelief, and that has not been established. Therefore it must be taken in its apparent sense, for he could believe and become one of the people of reward, or he could persist and die in disbelief and become one of the people of punishment. Whoever is in this state is one who fears, not one who is certain. Know that one who supposes that harm will reach another is not called fearful unless it is such that the arrival of that harm to him would necessarily cause the pain of his heart, as one says: "I am afraid for my son."

As for His saying ﴿so that you become a companion (waliyy) of Satan﴾, the commentators have mentioned several meanings for waliyy:
First: that if he deserves God's punishment, he will be with Satan in the Fire. Association (wilayah) is a cause of companionship, and applying the name of the cause to the effect is a metaphor. Even if it cannot be understood as true wilayah, because of His saying: ﴿The intimate friends that day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67], and His saying: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disavow others and curse one another﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25], and what He relates of Satan, that he will say to them: ﴿I disavow what you associated with me before﴾ [Ibrahim: 22].

Know that this difficulty arises only if the punishment meant is the punishment of the Hereafter. But if what is meant is the punishment of this world, the difficulty falls away.

Second: that the punishment is understood as abandonment (khidhlan), meaning: I fear that God's abandonment will touch you, so that you become a supporter of Satan, and God will disown you, as He said: ﴿Whoever takes Satan as a waliyy instead of God has indeed suffered a manifest loss﴾ [al-Nisa': 119].

Third: waliyy means one who follows Satan and comes after him, as the rain that comes after (another) is called waliyy. If it is said: His saying ﴿I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so that you become a waliyy of Satan﴾ implies that the state of being Satan's companion is worse and greater than the punishment itself, what is the reason for that?

The answer: God's good pleasure (ridwan) is greater than the reward, as He said: ﴿And the pleasure of God is greater; that is the great triumph﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72]. So it is necessary that the companionship of Satan, which stands in opposition to God's good pleasure, be greater and worse than the punishment itself.

Know that Abraham (peace be upon him) arranged this speech in the utmost excellence, for he first drew attention to what indicates the prohibition of worshipping idols, then commanded him to follow him in reflection and inference and in abandoning blind imitation; then he drew attention to the fact that obeying Satan is not permissible according to reason; then he concluded the speech with a warning that restrains from undertaking what is not fitting. First: fulfilling the right of fatherhood, as He said: ﴿and to parents, kindness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]. Guidance to religion is among the greatest kinds of kindness, and when there is added to it the observance of courtesy and gentleness, that becomes light upon light.

Second: the one who guides to the truth must be gentle and kind, presenting speech not by way of harshness, for presenting it harshly becomes a cause of the listener's turning away, and so that is in reality an effort at misguidance.

Third: what Abu Hurayrah narrated, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God revealed to Abraham (peace be upon him): You are My intimate friend (khalil), so make your character good, even with the disbelievers; you will enter the entrances of the righteous. And God knows best.

The second type: His saying, ﴿O my father, there has come to me of knowledge what has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to an even path.﴾ Its meaning is clear. The people of ta'lim (the Ta'limiyya, who insist on an infallible teacher) and the people of taqlid (blind adherence to authority) both hoped to hold on to it. As for the people of ta'lim, they said: He commanded him to follow in religion, and he did not command him to hold to a proof that cannot be obtained except through following. As for the people of taqlid, they too held on to it from this angle. Some people objected that he commanded him to follow so that guidance might be attained; therefore guidance is not attained except by following him, and there is no following unless he is guided. Our statement is that it is necessary to follow him, so circularity (dawr) occurs, and that is invalid.

The answer to the first point: what is meant by guidance is the explanation of the proof, its clarification and its elucidation.

At this point the questioner returned and said: I do not deny that there must be guidance (dalalah) to the proof, but I say that coming to know that guidance is obtained only from one who has a complete soul, far from deficiency and error, and that is the soul of the infallible Prophet or the infallible Imam. So if you concede that there must be a Prophet for this purpose, you have conceded that the aim is achieved. The respondent answered and said: I did not concede that there must be guidance from a Prophet in coming to know the proofs, but I say: this path is easier, and Abraham (peace be upon him) called him to the easiest of the easy. *  *  *

Also, disobedience to God, exalted is He, issues only from one of weak judgment, and whoever is like that is worthy that his opinion not be heeded and that his words be given no weight.

If it is said: this statement depends on establishing several matters:

Second: establishing Satan.
Third: establishing that Satan is disobedient to God.

Fifth: that the belief which that man held was derived from obedience to Satan. And it is part of the nature of the argument presented to an opponent that it be composed of premises that are known and accepted. Perhaps Abraham's father disputed all these premises. How? **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 19, verses 46–48:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said, "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham? If you do not desist, I will surely stone you. So leave me for a long time."﴾ ﴿He said, "Peace be upon you. I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Indeed, He has ever been gracious to me."﴾ ﴿"And I will withdraw from you and what you invoke besides Allah, and I will call upon my Lord. Perhaps I will not be in vain in calling upon my Lord."﴾

Know that when Abraham, peace be upon him, invited his father to monotheism, mentioned the proof of the corruption of worshipping idols, followed that proof with eloquent admonition, and presented all of this combined with gentleness and kindness, his father responded with an answer that contradicted all of it. He met his argument with mere imitation (taqlid). He did not give in response to his argument anything except his words: ﴿Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?﴾ So he insisted on claiming their divinity out of ignorance and blind imitation. He met his admonition with foolishness, threatening him with beating and abuse. He met his gentleness in his words ﴿O my father﴾ with harshness, for he did not say to him "O my son," but said: ﴿O Abraham.﴾ Allah the Exalted related this to Muhammad (ﷺ) only to lighten his heart from the harm that reached him from the polytheists, so that he would know that ignorant people have been on this blameworthy course since time began.

As for his words ﴿Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?﴾: if it is meant as a question (istifham), then it is abandonment (khidhlan), because he already knew from him what had been repeated of his admonition and his calling attention to the proof, and this implies that he was utterly averse to that. So what is the benefit of this statement? And if it is meant as an expression of wonder (ta'ajjub), then what is there to wonder at in turning away from an argument that has no benefit in it? The entire wonder lies in the act of worshipping them, for the proof that Abraham, peace be upon him, presented not only nullifies the permissibility of worshipping them, but also points to the wonder that a rational person could be content with worshipping them. So his father answered that apparent wonder, which was based on proof, with a corrupt wonder not based on any proof or doubt. There is no doubt that this wonder is deserving of being wondered at.

As for his words ﴿If you do not desist, I will surely stone you. So leave me for a long time﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Regarding "stoning" (al-rajm) here, there are two opinions.

The first: it is stoning by the tongue, which is insult and censure. From this is His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [al-Nur: 4], meaning with insult. From it also comes "al-rajim" (the accursed), meaning one who is pelted with curse. Mujahid said: "Rajm in the whole Qur'an means insult."

The second: it is stoning by hand. On this interpretation, they mention several aspects:

One of them: "I will stone you" by revealing your affair to the people so that they stone you and kill you.

The second: "I will stone you with stones so that you distance yourself from me."

The third, from al-Mu'arrij: "I will kill you" in the dialect of Quraysh.

The fourth, Abu Muslim said: "I will stone you" means by stones, but it may be said in the sense of expulsion and distancing by extension. What indicates that he intended expulsion is His saying: ﴿and leave me for a long time﴾. Know that the origin of rajm is throwing stones, so it is more appropriate to interpret it that way. If it is said: Does His saying ﴿and leave me for a long time﴾ not indicate that the intended meaning is stoning by insult? We say: No. That is because he threatened him with stoning if he remained close to him, and ordered him to distance himself in flight from that, so it is in the sense of His saying ﴿and leave me for a long time﴾.

**The second issue:** Regarding His saying ﴿and leave me for a long time﴾ (wa-ihjurni maliyyan), there are two opinions.

One of them: the intended meaning is "abandon me with words."

The second: it means separation in place and land, and this is the emigration (hijrah) of the Messenger and the believers. That is, distance yourself from me so that I do not see you. This second opinion is closer to the apparent meaning.

**The third issue:** Regarding His saying ﴿maliyyan﴾ (for a long time), there are two opinions.

The first: "maliyyan" means for a long period of time, derived from their saying: "a long duration of time passed over so-and-so" (ataa 'ala fulanin mala'atun mina al-dahr), meaning a long time.

The second: "maliyyan" means by departing from me and abandoning me before I wound you with beating so that you are unable to move. It is said: "So-and-so is maliyyun with such-and-such" when he is capable of it and equal to it.

**The fourth issue:** He conjoined "wa-ihjurni" (and leave me) to a conjoined element that is omitted, which is indicated by "la-arjumannaka" (I will surely stone you). That is: "Beware of me and leave me, lest I stone you." Then, when Abraham, peace be upon him, heard that from his father, he answered on two matters:

One of them: he promised him distance from him. This is because when his father ordered him to distance himself, he showed compliance with that command. His words ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ are a farewell and a parting, like His saying: ﴿To us are our deeds and to you are your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek the ignorant﴾ and ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾ [al-Qasas: 55; al-Furqan: 63]. This is evidence for the permissibility of parting from one being advised when obstinacy appears from him, and that it is good to repay evil with good. It may also be that he prayed for him for safety, seeking to win him over. Do you not see that he promised him forgiveness? Then, when he bade his father farewell with the words ﴿Peace be upon you﴾, he added to that what indicated that although he was distant from him, his compassion for him remained as it was. This is his words: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you.﴾

This verse was used as an argument by those who criticized the infallibility (ismah) of the prophets. The argument's formulation is: Abraham, peace be upon him, did what was impermissible, because he sought forgiveness for his father while he was a disbeliever, and seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever is not permissible. Thus, by the combination of these premises, it is established that Abraham, peace be upon him, did what was impermissible. We say that he sought forgiveness for his father because of Allah the Exalted's words, relating from Abraham: ﴿Peace be upon you. I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾, and His saying: ﴿Forgive my father, for he was among the astray﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 86]. As for his father being a disbeliever, that is by the explicit text of the Qur'an and by consensus (ijma'). As for seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever being impermissible, that is for two reasons:

The first: the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who have believed to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113].

The second: His saying in Surah al-Mumtahanah: ﴿There has already been for you an excellent pattern in Abraham﴾ up to His saying ﴿except for the saying of Abraham to his father, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you"﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4]. He commanded the people to follow him in everything except this act, so it must be that this was a sin on his part.

The answer: There is no dispute except regarding your statement that seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever is impermissible, for the discussion on it has several aspects:

One of them: The certainty that Allah the Exalted punishes the disbeliever is known only through revelation (sam'). Perhaps Abraham, peace be upon him, did not find in his law (shar') anything indicating certainty of the punishment of the disbeliever, and therefore he sought forgiveness for his father.

The second: Seeking forgiveness (istighfar) may mean seeking favor (istimahah), as in His saying: ﴿Say to those who believe that they should forgive those who do not expect the days of Allah﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 14]. The meaning is: "I will ask my Lord not to requite you for your disbelief, as long as I am alive, with the hastened punishment of this world."

The third: He, peace be upon him, sought forgiveness for his father only because he hoped from him faith. When he despaired of that, he abandoned seeking forgiveness. Perhaps in his law seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever from whom faith is hoped was permissible. The evidence that this possibility occurred is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who have believed to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Hellfire﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113]. He made clear that the prohibition of seeking forgiveness occurs only after they come to know that they are among the companions of the Hellfire.

Then He said after that: ﴿And the request of forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to Abraham that he was an enemy to Allah, he disassociated himself from him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]. So the verse indicates that he had promised him forgiveness if he believed, and when he did not believe, he did not seek forgiveness for him but disassociated himself from him. If it is said: If the matter is so, why did we get prohibited from following him in His saying ﴿There has already been for you an excellent pattern in Abraham﴾ up to His saying ﴿except for the saying of Abraham to his father, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you"﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4]? We say: The verse indicates that it is not permissible for us to follow him in that. But the prohibition of following him in that does not indicate that it was a sin.

Indeed, many matters are among the special characteristics of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is not permissible for us to follow him in them, even though they were permissible for him, peace be upon him.

Fourth: Perhaps this seeking of forgiveness was of the category of leaving the better course (tark al-awla), and the good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near (to Allah). As for His saying ﴿Indeed, He has ever been gracious to me﴾, meaning kind and gentle. It is said: "Fulan ahfa in the request with fulan" when he was gentle with him and exaggerated in kindness. From this is His saying: ﴿If He should ask you for them and press you, you would be stingy﴾ [Muhammad: 37], meaning even if the request was gentle. The meaning is that He, glorified is He, because of His kindness to me and His favor upon me, has accustomed me to being answered; so when I seek forgiveness for you, the desired outcome is achieved. It is as if He made me, by that, certain that if he repents, forgiveness will be attained for him.

**The second answer among the two answers:** His saying ﴿And I will withdraw from you and what you invoke besides Allah﴾. To withdraw from something is to distance oneself from it. The meaning is: I part from you in place, and I part from you in your way as well, and I distance myself from you, and I occupy myself with worshipping my Lord, who benefits and harms, who created me and bestowed favors upon me. For you, by worshipping idols, are following the path of destruction, so it is obligatory upon me to avoid you. The meaning of His saying ﴿Perhaps I will not be in vain in calling upon my Lord﴾ is: I hope that I will not be like that. He mentioned this as a form of humility, like His saying: ﴿And the one from whom I hope that He will forgive my sin on the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 82]. As for His saying ﴿shaqiyyan﴾ (in vain), despite the humility toward Allah in it, it contains an allusion to the wretchedness of them in calling upon their gods, according to what he had established earlier in His saying: ﴿Why do you worship what neither hears nor sees, and does not benefit you at all?﴾

He did not give in response to his argument anything except his words: ﴿Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?﴾ So he insisted on claiming their divinity out of ignorance and blind imitation. He met his admonition with foolishness, threatening him with beating and abuse. He met his gentleness in his words ﴿O my father﴾ with harshness, for he did not say to him "O my son," but said: ﴿O Abraham.﴾ Allah the Exalted related this to Muhammad (ﷺ) only to lighten his heart from the harm that reached him from the polytheists, so that he would know that ignorant people have been on this blameworthy course since time began.

As for his words ﴿Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?﴾: if it is meant as a question (istifham), then it is abandonment (khidhlan), because he already knew from him what had been repeated of his admonition and his calling attention to the proof, and this implies that he was utterly averse to that. So what is the benefit of this statement? And if it is meant as an expression of wonder (ta'ajjub), then what is there to wonder at in turning away from an argument that has no benefit in it? The entire wonder lies in the act of worshipping them, for the proof that Abraham, peace be upon him, presented not only nullifies the permissibility of worshipping them, but also points to the wonder that a rational person could be content with worshipping them. So his father answered that apparent wonder, which was based on proof, with a corrupt wonder not based on any proof or doubt. There is no doubt that this wonder is deserving of being wondered at.

As for his words ﴿If you do not desist, I will surely stone you. So leave me for a long time﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Regarding "stoning" (al-rajm) here, there are two opinions.

The first: it is stoning by the tongue, which is insult and censure. From this is His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [al-Nur: 4], meaning with insult. From it also comes "al-rajim" (the accursed), meaning one who is pelted with curse. Mujahid said: "Rajm in the whole Qur'an means insult."

The second: it is stoning by hand. On this interpretation, they mention several aspects:

One of them: "I will stone you" by revealing your affair to the people so that they stone you and kill you.

The second: "I will stone you with stones so that you distance yourself from me."

The third, from al-Mu'arrij: "I will kill you" in the dialect of Quraysh.

The fourth, Abu Muslim said: "I will stone you" means by stones, but it may be said in the sense of expulsion and distancing by extension. What indicates that he intended expulsion is His saying: ﴿and leave me for a long time﴾. Know that the origin of rajm is throwing stones, so it is more appropriate to interpret it that way. If it is said: Does His saying ﴿and leave me for a long time﴾ not indicate that the intended meaning is stoning by insult? We say: No. That is because he threatened him with stoning if he remained close to him, and ordered him to distance himself in flight from that, so it is in the sense of His saying ﴿and leave me for a long time﴾.

**The second issue:** Regarding His saying ﴿and leave me for a long time﴾ (wa-ihjurni maliyyan), there are two opinions.

One of them: the intended meaning is "abandon me with words."

The second: it means separation in place and land, and this is the emigration (hijrah) of the Messenger and the believers. That is, distance yourself from me so that I do not see you. This second opinion is closer to the apparent meaning.

**The third issue:** Regarding His saying ﴿maliyyan﴾ (for a long time), there are two opinions.

The first: "maliyyan" means for a long period of time, derived from their saying: "a long duration of time passed over so-and-so" (ataa 'ala fulanin mala'atun mina al-dahr), meaning a long time.

The second: "maliyyan" means by departing from me and abandoning me before I wound you with beating so that you are unable to move. It is said: "So-and-so is maliyyun with such-and-such" when he is capable of it and equal to it.

**The fourth issue:** He conjoined "wa-ihjurni" (and leave me) to a conjoined element that is omitted, which is indicated by "la-arjumannaka" (I will surely stone you). That is: "Beware of me and leave me, lest I stone you." Then, when Abraham, peace be upon him, heard that from his father, he answered on two matters:

One of them: he promised him distance from him. This is because when his father ordered him to distance himself, he showed compliance with that command. His words ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ are a farewell and a parting, like His saying: ﴿To us are our deeds and to you are your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek the ignorant﴾ and ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾ [al-Qasas: 55; al-Furqan: 63]. This is evidence for the permissibility of parting from one being advised when obstinacy appears from him, and that it is good to repay evil with good. It may also be that he prayed for him for safety, seeking to win him over. Do you not see that he promised him forgiveness? Then, when he bade his father farewell with the words ﴿Peace be upon you﴾, he added to that what indicated that although he was distant from him, his compassion for him remained as it was. This is his words: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you.﴾

This verse was used as an argument by those who criticized the infallibility (ismah) of the prophets. The argument's formulation is: Abraham, peace be upon him, did what was impermissible, because he sought forgiveness for his father while he was a disbeliever, and seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever is not permissible. Thus, by the combination of these premises, it is established that Abraham, peace be upon him, did what was impermissible. We say that he sought forgiveness for his father because of Allah the Exalted's words, relating from Abraham: ﴿Peace be upon you. I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾, and His saying: ﴿Forgive my father, for he was among the astray﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 86]. As for his father being a disbeliever, that is by the explicit text of the Qur'an and by consensus (ijma'). As for seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever being impermissible, that is for two reasons:

The first: the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who have believed to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113].

The second: His saying in Surah al-Mumtahanah: ﴿There has already been for you an excellent pattern in Abraham﴾ up to His saying ﴿except for the saying of Abraham to his father, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you"﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4]. He commanded the people to follow him in everything except this act, so it must be that this was a sin on his part.

The answer: There is no dispute except regarding your statement that seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever is impermissible, for the discussion on it has several aspects:

One of them: The certainty that Allah the Exalted punishes the disbeliever is known only through revelation (sam'). Perhaps Abraham, peace be upon him, did not find in his law (shar') anything indicating certainty of the punishment of the disbeliever, and therefore he sought forgiveness for his father.

The second: Seeking forgiveness (istighfar) may mean seeking favor (istimahah), as in His saying: ﴿Say to those who believe that they should forgive those who do not expect the days of Allah﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 14]. The meaning is: "I will ask my Lord not to requite you for your disbelief, as long as I am alive, with the hastened punishment of this world."

The third: He, peace be upon him, sought forgiveness for his father only because he hoped from him faith. When he despaired of that, he abandoned seeking forgiveness. Perhaps in his law seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever from whom faith is hoped was permissible. The evidence that this possibility occurred is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who have believed to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Hellfire﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113]. He made clear that the prohibition of seeking forgiveness occurs only after they come to know that they are among the companions of the Hellfire.

Then He said after that: ﴿And the request of forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to Abraham that he was an enemy to Allah, he disassociated himself from him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]. So the verse indicates that he had promised him forgiveness if he believed, and when he did not believe, he did not seek forgiveness for him but disassociated himself from him. If it is said: If the matter is so, why did we get prohibited from following him in His saying ﴿There has already been for you an excellent pattern in Abraham﴾ up to His saying ﴿except for the saying of Abraham to his father, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you"﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4]? We say: The verse indicates that it is not permissible for us to follow him in that. But the prohibition of following him in that does not indicate that it was a sin.

Indeed, many matters are among the special characteristics of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is not permissible for us to follow him in them, even though they were permissible for him, peace be upon him.

Fourth: Perhaps this seeking of forgiveness was of the category of leaving the better course (tark al-awla), and the good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near (to Allah). As for His saying ﴿Indeed, He has ever been gracious to me﴾, meaning kind and gentle. It is said: "Fulan ahfa in the request with fulan" when he was gentle with him and exaggerated in kindness. From this is His saying: ﴿If He should ask you for them and press you, you would be stingy﴾ [Muhammad: 37], meaning even if the request was gentle. The meaning is that He, glorified is He, because of His kindness to me and His favor upon me, has accustomed me to being answered; so when I seek forgiveness for you, the desired outcome is achieved. It is as if He made me, by that, certain that if he repents, forgiveness will be attained for him.

**The second answer among the two answers:** His saying ﴿And I will withdraw from you and what you invoke besides Allah﴾. To withdraw from something is to distance oneself from it. The meaning is: I part from you in place, and I part from you in your way as well, and I distance myself from you, and I occupy myself with worshipping my Lord, who benefits and harms, who created me and bestowed favors upon me. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 49–50:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when he had withdrawn from them and what they worshipped other than Allah, We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and We made each of them a prophet.﴾ ﴿And We gave them of Our mercy and made for them a true tongue of high repute.﴾

[Page 197]

Know that no one has lost by [giving up things for] Allah. When Abraham, peace be upon him, withdrew from them in their religion and in their land, and chose emigration to his Lord, to wherever He commanded him, that did not harm him in his religion or his worldly life. Rather, it benefited him: He compensated him with prophet-children. There is no station, in religion or in worldly life, higher for a human being than that Allah makes him a messenger to His creation and obliges the creation to obey him and submit to him, together with the great rank he attains in the Hereafter. Thus Allah's making them prophets was among the greatest blessings in this world and the Hereafter.

Then the Exalted explained that, despite this, He gave them of His mercy, meaning He gave them of prophethood what He gave, and this includes wealth, status, followers, pure lineage and good offspring. Then He said: ﴿and made for them a true tongue of high repute.﴾ The "true tongue" is good praise, and He expressed by "tongue" that which is found through the tongue, just as He expressed by "hand" that which is given by the hand, which is a gift. Allah answered his supplication in His words: ﴿and make for me a true tongue among later generations﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 84], so He made him an exemplar, until the followers of all religions claimed him. He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿the religion of your father Abraham﴾, and: ﴿Then We revealed to you, [Muhammad], to follow the religion (millah) of Abraham, a hanif (upright monotheist)﴾ [al-Nahl: 123].

Some have said: The Friend (khalil) withdrew from the creation, as he said: ﴿And I will withdraw from you and what you invoke other than Allah﴾. Therefore, without doubt, Allah blessed his offspring, so He said: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and We made each of them a prophet.﴾

Second: He disavowed his father for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, as He said: ﴿So when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him. Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]. Without doubt, Allah named him a father to the Muslims, so He said: ﴿the religion of your father Abraham﴾ [al-Hajj: 78].

Third: He laid his son down on his forehead to slaughter him, as He said: ﴿And when they had both submitted and he put him down upon his forehead﴾ [al-Saffat: 103]. Without doubt, Allah ransomed him, as He said: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ [al-Saffat: 107].

Fourth: He submitted himself, and said: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 131]. So Allah made the fire cool and safe for him, as He said: ﴿We said, "O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham."﴾ [al-Anbiya: 69].

Fifth: He was compassionate toward this nation, as he said: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129]. Without doubt, Allah made him a partner in the five daily prayers, as in the words: "As You prayed and sent blessings upon Abraham and the family of Abraham."

Sixth: Concerning Sarah, in His words: ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled [his commitments]﴾ [al-Najm: 37]. Without doubt, He made the place where his feet stood blessed: ﴿And take, [O believers], from the station of Abraham a place of prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125].

Seventh: He opposed all creation for the sake of Allah, as He said: ﴿for indeed they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77]. Without doubt, Allah took him as a close friend (khalil), as He said: ﴿And Allah took Abraham as a close friend﴾ [al-Nisa: 125], so that the soundness of our statement is known: that no one has lost by [giving up things for] Allah.

Third: He laid his son down on his forehead to slaughter him, as He said: ﴿And when they had both submitted and he put him down upon his forehead﴾ [al-Saffat: 103]. Without doubt, Allah ransomed him, as He said: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ [al-Saffat: 107].

Fourth: He submitted himself, and said: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 131]. So Allah made the fire cool and safe for him, as He said: ﴿We said, "O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham."﴾ [al-Anbiya: 69].

Fifth: He was compassionate toward this nation, as he said: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129]. Without doubt, Allah made him a partner in the five daily prayers, as in the words: "As You prayed and sent blessings upon Abraham and the family of Abraham."

Sixth: Concerning Sarah, in His words: ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled [his commitments]﴾ [al-Najm: 37]. Without doubt, He made the place where his feet stood blessed: ﴿And take, [O believers], from the station of Abraham a place of prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125].

Seventh: He opposed all creation for the sake of Allah, as He said: ﴿for indeed they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77]. Without doubt, Allah took him as a close friend (khalil), as He said: ﴿And Allah took Abraham as a close friend﴾ [al-Nisa: 125], so that the soundness of our statement is known: that no one has lost by [giving up things for] Allah.

(The Fourth Story: the story of Musa, peace be upon him)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Mention in the Book Musa. Indeed he was chosen (mukhlaṣan), and he was a messenger and a prophet.﴾ ﴿And We called him from the right side of the mount, and We brought him near as a confidant.﴾ ﴿And We granted him, out of Our mercy, his brother Harun as a prophet.﴾

Know that Allah, exalted is He, described Musa, peace be upon him, with several attributes.

The first: that he was *mukhlaṣan*. If it is read with a *fatḥah* on the *lām* (*mukhlaṣan*, "chosen"), it derives from *al-iṣṭifā'* (choosing) and *al-ijtibā'* (selecting), as though Allah chose him and singled him out. If it is read with a *kasrah* on the *lām* (*mukhliṣan*, "sincere"), its meaning is that he was sincere to Allah in monotheism in worship. *Ikhlāṣ* (sincerity) is the intention in worship that the one worshipped be worshipped alone by it. When the Qur'an is transmitted in two readings, each of them is established and certain, so Allah made both of these matters attributes of Musa, peace be upon him.

The second: his being a messenger and a prophet. There is no doubt that these are two different attributes. However, the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theological school) claimed that they are mutually entailing, so that every messenger is a prophet and every prophet is a messenger. Some people denied this. We have explained the discussion of this in the Surah of al-Hajj, in His saying: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet﴾ [Al-Hajj: 52].

The third: His saying: ﴿And We called him from the right side of the mount﴾. *Min* here means "from the direction of," i.e., from the side of the right. *Al-Ayman* is an attribute of either *al-Ṭūr* (the mount) or *al-Jānib* (the side).

The fourth: His saying: ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾. Since He mentioned that he was a messenger, He said: ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant.﴾ Regarding His saying ﴿We brought him near﴾ there are two views:

One: the intended meaning is nearness of place. This is reported from Abu al-'Aliyah: He brought him close until he heard the scratching of the pen when the Torah was being written on the tablets.

The second: nearness of rank, i.e., He elevated his status and honored him by conversing with him. Al-Qadi (the judge, al-Baydawi) said: This is closer to the meaning, because the use of "nearness" with respect to Allah has by convention come to mean only rank. In this sense, the term *taqarrub* (drawing near) is used for worship, and it is said of the angels, peace be upon them, that they are *muqarrabun* (those brought near). As for ﴿najiyyan﴾, it has been said that it means He saved him from his enemies, and it has been said that it derives from *munājāh* (private conversation) in address, and this is the preferred view.

The fifth: His saying: ﴿And We granted him, out of Our mercy, his brother Harun as a prophet.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Harun, peace be upon him, was older than Musa, peace be upon them both. Allah granted him prophethood, not his person and brotherhood alone. This was an answer to his supplication in His saying: ﴿And appoint for me a minister from my family, Harun, my brother, strengthen my back through him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 29–31]. Allah answered him with His saying: ﴿You have been given your request, O Musa﴾ [Ta-Ha: 36], and His saying: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother﴾ [Al-Qasas: 35].

**The Fifth Story: The Story of Isma'il (peace be upon him)**

God Most High says: ﴿And mention in the Book Isma'il. Indeed, he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet.﴾ ﴿He used to enjoin his family to prayer and zakat, and he was pleasing to his Lord.﴾

Know that this Isma'il is Isma'il son of Ibrahim, peace be upon them both. Know also that God Most High described Isma'il (peace be upon him) with several qualities.

The first is His saying: ﴿Indeed, he was true to his promise.﴾ This "promise" may refer to what was between him and God Most High, or to what was between him and the people.

As for the first meaning, it is that he did not oppose anything he was commanded to do in obedience to his Lord. This is because when God Most High sends an angel to the prophets and commands them to convey the sharʿ (the sacred law), there must be a promise from them that requires them to carry this out, and it indicates their performance of all the other acts of worship that pertain to them.

As for the second meaning, it is that when he (peace be upon him) promised people something, he fulfilled his promise. God Most High described him with this noble trait. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he promised a companion of his that he would wait for him in a certain place, and he waited for him for a year. Also, he promised himself to be patient in the face of slaughter, and he fulfilled it when he said: ﴿You will find me, if God wills, among the patient﴾ [al-Saffat: 102]. It is also related that a man said to Isa (peace be upon him): "Wait for me until I come to you." Isa (peace be upon him) said: "Yes." The man left and forgot the appointment, then came for a need to that place, and Isa (peace be upon him) was still there waiting for the appointment. And it is narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "He made an appointment with a man, and that man forgot, and he waited for him from the forenoon until near sunset."

Al-Sha'bi was asked about a man who makes an appointment, until what time should he wait for him. He said: "If he made the appointment during the day, then the whole day; and if he made it at night, then the whole night." Ibrahim ibn Zayd was asked about this and said: "If you make an appointment with him at the time of a prayer, then wait for him until the time of another prayer."

The second quality is His saying: ﴿And he was a messenger and a prophet﴾, and its explanation has already passed.

The third quality is His saying: ﴿And he used to enjoin his family to prayer and zakat.﴾ The closest interpretation of "family" is that it refers to those to whom he was obliged to convey the sharʿ. Thus, it includes his entire community, since what is incumbent upon a man regarding his family specifically was incumbent upon him regarding all of them. This is if the command is understood as referring to the obligatory prayer and zakat. But if it is understood as recommended (nadb) in both, then the meaning is that, just as he would perform tahajjud (night prayer), he would command his family, that is, those in his household at that time, to do the same. His concern for them in religion took precedence over his concern for them in worldly matters, unlike most people. It was also said that he would begin with his family in enjoining righteousness and worship so that he might make them an example for others, as God Most High said: ﴿And warn your closest kinsmen﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 214], ﴿And enjoin your family to prayer and be steadfast in it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 132], ﴿Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]. Also, they have more right to be given charity, so it is fitting that they be given priority in religious benevolence.

As for zakat, it is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it means obedience to God Most High and sincerity. It seems that he interpreted it as that by which the doer grows (yazku) in the sight of his Lord. The apparent meaning, when zakat is mentioned alongside prayer, is that it refers to obligatory charities, and that he knew from his close family that they were bound to pay zakat, so he would command them to do so, or command them to give charity voluntarily to the poor.

The fourth quality is His saying: ﴿And he was pleasing to his Lord﴾, and this is in the highest degree of praise, because the one pleasing to God is the one who attains the highest ranks in all his acts of obedience.

(The Sixth Story: the story of Idris, peace be upon him)

The Exalted said: ﴿And mention in the Book Idris. Indeed he was a man of truth and a prophet.﴾ ﴿And We raised him to a high station.﴾

Know that Idris, peace be upon him, is the grandfather of Nuh's father, and he is Nuh ibn Lamak ibn Mutawshalakh ibn Akhnukh. It is said that he was named Idris because of his frequent study (of scripture), and his name was Akhnukh. Allah the Exalted described him with several attributes:

The first: he was a ṣiddīq (a man of perfect truthfulness).

The second: he was a prophet, and the discussion of these two has already passed.

The third: the Exalted's saying, ﴿And We raised him to a high station.﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: it refers to elevation in rank, like the Exalted's saying to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And We raised high your remembrance﴾ [al-Sharh: 4]. Allah the Exalted honored him with prophethood, revealed to him thirty scrolls, and he was the first to write with the pen and to look into the science of the stars and calculation, and the first to sew garments and wear them, whereas people had worn hides.

The second: that what is meant is elevation in place, to a lofty position. This is the more preferred view, because elevation linked with the word "place" (makan) signifies elevation in location, not in degree. Then they differed. Some of them said that Allah raised him to the heavens and to Paradise while he was alive and did not die. Others said: rather, he was raised to the heavens and his soul was taken. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, asked Kaʿb about the Exalted's saying: ﴿And We raised him to a high station﴾. He said: a friend of his from among the angels came to him, and he asked him to speak to the Angel of Death so that he would delay the taking of his soul. So that angel carried him between his wings and ascended with him to the heavens. When he was in the fourth heaven, behold, the Angel of Death was saying: "I have been sent, and I was told: take the soul of Idris in the fourth heaven." And I was saying: "How is that, when he is on the earth?" Idris turned and the Angel of Death saw him, and he took his soul there.

Know that Allah the Exalted praised him by raising him to the heavens, because it is the custom that none is raised there except one who is of great rank and standing. For this reason He said regarding the angels: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain His worship﴾ [al-Anbiya: 19]. Here ends the stories.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verse 58:

God Almighty said: ﴿Those are they upon whom Allah bestowed favor, of the prophets, of the offspring of Adam, and of those whom We carried with Noah, and of the offspring of Abraham and Israel, and of those whom We guided and chose. When the signs of the Most Merciful were recited to them, they fell down prostrating and weeping.﴾

Know that He, Exalted is He, praised each one of the prophets mentioned earlier with the praise specific to him, then gathered them at the end and said: ﴿Those are they upon whom Allah bestowed favor﴾, that is, with prophethood and other things whose description has already preceded. "Those" (ulaika) refers to those mentioned in the surah from Zechariah to Idris. He then gathered them in being of the offspring of Adam. Then He singled out some of them as being of the offspring of those who were carried with Noah. The one who is specifically of the offspring of Adam but not of those carried with Noah is Idris, peace be upon him, for he preceded Noah, as is established in the reports. Those who are of the offspring of those carried with Noah are Abraham, peace be upon him, since he was a descendant of Sam son of Noah, and Ishmael, Isaac and Jacob are of the offspring of Abraham. Then He singled out some of them as being of the sons of Israel, that is, Jacob: they are Moses, Aaron, Zechariah, John and Jesus through the mother's side. Allah, glorified and exalted, arranged the conditions of the prophets, peace be upon them, whom He mentioned, in this order, drawing attention thereby to the fact that just as they were preferred through their deeds, they have additional distinction through being born of these prophets. Then He made clear that they are among those whom We guided and chose, drawing attention thereby to the fact that they were singled out for these ranks by the guidance of Allah Exalted for them, and because He chose them for messengerhood. Then He said: ﴿When the signs of the Most Merciful were recited to them, they fell down prostrating and weeping.﴾ "Were recited to them" means to these prophets. Thus Allah Exalted made clear that, together with the blessings of Allah upon them, they reached the level at which, upon the recitation of the signs of Allah, they fall down prostrating and weeping, in humility, submission, caution and fear. By "the signs of Allah" is meant what Allah Exalted singled them out with, of the revealed Books sent down to them.

Abu Muslim said: "What is meant by the signs in which is mentioned the punishment sent down upon the disbelievers." This is far-fetched, because all the other signs in which Paradise and Hell are mentioned, and so on, are more fitting for them to prostrate and weep at. Therefore it is necessary to apply it to every sign that is recited which contains promise and threat, encouragement and warning, for when the one who reflects contemplates all of that, it is correct that he prostrates and weeps at it.

They differed concerning prostration. Some of them said: it is the prayer. Others said: what is meant is the prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa, the prostration performed upon reciting certain verses), according to the manner in which we have been commanded to worship. It was also said: what is meant is humility and submission. The apparent meaning requires a specific prostration at the time of recitation. Then it is possible that what is meant is the prostration of recitation of the Qur'an, and it is possible that they, at times of fear, had been commanded to prostrate, so they would do that not because of the mention of prostration in the verse.

Al-Zajjaj said concerning بُكِيًّا (bukiyyan, "weeping"): it is the plural of bakin, like shahid and shuhud, and qa'id and qu'ud. Then he said: a person in the state of falling down is not yet prostrating, so what is meant is that they fell down intending to prostrate. As for the one who said that بُكِيًّا is a verbal noun (masdar), he erred, because سُجَّدًا (sujjadan, "prostrating") is the plural of sajid, and بُكِيًّا is coordinated with it.

And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Recite the Qur'an and weep; and if you do not weep, then feign weeping."

And from Salih al-Murri, who said: "I recited the Qur'an to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a dream, and he said to me: 'O Salih, this is recitation, so where is the weeping?'"

And from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "When you recite the prostration of Surat Subhan (al-Isra), do not hasten to prostrate until you weep. If the eye of any one of you does not weep, then let his heart weep."

And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The Qur'an was sent down with sorrow, so recite it with sorrow."

And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "No eye is moistened with tears because of it except that Allah forbids its body to the Fire."

And from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "No one who weeps out of fear of Allah will enter the Fire."

The scholars said: in the prostration of recitation one supplicates with what is fitting for it. So if one recites the verse of the prostration in Surat Tanzil (al-Sajdah, "The Prostration"), one says: "O Allah, make me among those who prostrate to Your Face and glorify You with Your praise, and I seek refuge in You from being among those who are arrogant towards Your command." If one recites the prostration of Surat Subhan, one says: "O Allah, make me among those who weep towards You and are humbled before You." If one recites this prostration, one says: "O Allah, make me among Your servants upon whom You have bestowed favor, who are guided, who prostrate to You, and who weep upon the recitation of the signs of Your Book."

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 59–60:**

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected the prayer and followed their desires, so they will meet with perdition﴾ ﴿except those who repent and believe and do righteous deeds; those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged at all﴾.

Know that when the Exalted described these prophets with praiseworthy attributes, encouraging us to follow their way, He mentioned after them those who are the opposite of them, so He said: ﴿Then there succeeded them a generation﴾. The apparent meaning of the speech is that what is meant by "after these prophets" is a succession of their offspring. It is said: "khalafahu" when one follows up on him (a'qabahu). Then it was said that for the posterity of good it is "khalaf" with a fatha on the lam, and for the posterity of evil it is "khalf" with a sukun, just as they said: "wa'd" (promise) for what guarantees good and "wa'id" (threat) for what guarantees evil. In a hadith: "«In Allah is a successor (khalaf) from every one who perishes»". And in a verse of Labid:

*They have departed, those by whose sides one used to live, and I remain in a khalf like the hide of a mangy camel.*

Then He described them with neglecting the prayer and following desires. Neglecting the prayer corresponds to His saying: ﴿they fell down in prostration﴾, and following desires corresponds to His saying: ﴿and weeping﴾; because their weeping indicates their fear, while the following of these people of their desires indicates the absence of fear in them. The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿neglected the prayer﴾ is that they abandoned it. But abandoning it may be by not performing it at all, and it may be by not performing it in its time, although the first is more apparent. As for following desires, Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him both) said: they are the Jews, who abandoned the obligatory prayer, drank wine, and considered marriage to a sister from the father's side permissible. Some scholars argued from His saying: ﴿except those who repent and believe﴾ that one who abandons the prayer is an unbeliever. Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued from it that faith is other than deeds, because He said: ﴿and believe and do righteous deeds﴾, so He conjoined deeds to faith, and the conjoined is other than that to which it is conjoined. Al-Ka'bi answered this: that He distinguished between repentance and faith, and repentance is from faith, so likewise righteous deeds are from faith even though they are distinguished. This answer is weak, because conjoining faith to repentance requires that there be a difference between them, since repentance is a resolve to abandon and faith is affirmation of Allah the Exalted, and these two are different; so likewise in this case. Then the Exalted explained that whoever has this attribute will ﴿meet with ghayy﴾, and they mentioned several meanings for ghayy:

First: that every evil among the Arabs is ghayy, and every good is rushad (right guidance). The poet said:

*Whoever meets with good, people will praise his affair, and whoever goes astray will not lack a blamer for his ghayy.*

Second: al-Zajjaj said: "﴿yalqawna ghayyan﴾" means they will meet with the recompense of ghayy, as in His saying: ﴿yalqa athaman﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], i.e., the requital of sins.

Third: ghayy as deviation from the path of Paradise.

Fourth: ghayy is a valley in Hell from which its valleys seek refuge.

The first two meanings are closer. If there is a place in Hell called by this name, it is permissible, and it does not exclude that what we have mentioned is intended, because it is the meaning understood in the language. Then the Glorified explained that this threat is for one who does not repent. As for one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds, for them is Paradise, and they will not be touched by any wrong. Here there are two questions:

The first: The exception indicates that repentance, faith, and righteous deeds are all necessary, and the matter is not so; because one who repents from his disbelief but the time of prayer has not come, or a woman who is menstruating, for her prayer is not obligatory; likewise zakat is not obligatory, and fasting as well. So if he dies in that time, he is among the people of salvation, although no deed has proceeded from him. Thus it is not permissible for the reward to depend on righteous deeds. The answer: this case is rare, and what is meant is the general case.

The second question: His saying: ﴿and they will not be wronged at all﴾. This is valid only if reward is owed in return for deeds, because if everything were by bounty, the occurrence of wrong would be impossible. But by your doctrine there is no entitlement for the servant through his deed except by promise. The answer: since it resembles it, it is given the ruling of it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 19, verses 61–63:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Gardens of Eden, which the Most Merciful has promised to His servants in the unseen. Indeed, His promise is ever fulfilled.﴾ ﴿They will not hear therein any vain talk, but only "Peace." And for them is their provision therein, morning and evening.﴾ ﴿That is the Garden which We shall give as an inheritance to those of Our servants who were devout.﴾

Know that when the Exalted mentioned, regarding the one who repents, that he enters Paradise, He described Paradise with several attributes.

The first is His saying: ﴿Gardens of ʿAdn (Eden), which the Most Merciful has promised to His servants in the unseen.﴾ *Al-ʿAdn* means settlement, and He described it as lasting, unlike the gardens of this world, which do not last. For this reason its scenery does not change, unlike the gardens of this world, whose condition varies in the greenness of the leaves, the appearance of blossoms, and the fruit. The Exalted also clarified that it is "the promise of the Most Merciful to His servants." As for His saying ﴿in the unseen﴾, there are two interpretations:

One: He promised them the Garden while it is absent from them and not present, or they are absent from it and do not see it.

The second: The intended meaning is that the Most Merciful promised it to those who would be servants *bil-ghayb* (in the unseen), that is, those who worship Him in private, unlike the hypocrites, who worship Him outwardly but not in private. This is the view of Abu Muslim. The first interpretation is stronger, because the Exalted has shown that the promise is from Him, and even if it concerns something unseen, it is as though it were witnessed and present. For this reason He said after it: ﴿Indeed, His promise is ever fulfilled (*ma'tiyyan*).﴾ As for His word *ma'tiyyan*, it has been said that it is a passive form with the meaning of an active one. The better view is that the promise is the Garden and they come to it. Al-Zajjaj said: Whatever reaches you, you have reached it, and whatever comes to you, you have come to it. The purpose of His saying ﴿Indeed, His promise was ever fulfilled﴾ is to show that the promise is from Him, and even if it concerns something unseen, it is as though it were witnessed and present, and the aim is to establish this in the hearts.

The second is His saying: ﴿They will not hear therein any vain talk, but only "Peace."﴾ *Al-laghw* in speech is what is meant to be discarded and cast aside, namely reprehensible speech. A parallel is His saying: ﴿You will not hear therein any vain talk﴾ (Al-Ghashiyah 88:11). In this there is clear indication of the obligation to avoid vain talk, since God has declared the abode in which there is no obligation free of it. How beautiful is His saying: ﴿When they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ (Al-Furqan 25:72), and ﴿When they hear vain talk, they turn away from it and say, "For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek the ignorant."﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:55). As for His saying ﴿but only "Peace,"﴾ there are two discussions:

The first discussion: There is a difficulty here, namely that peace is not of the same kind as vain talk, so how can peace be made an exception from vain talk? The answer to this has several aspects:

One: The meaning of *salam* is a supplication for safety, and the people of Paradise have no need for this supplication, so its apparent form would be of the kind of vain talk and idle chatter, were it not for the benefit of honour that it contains.

Two: That it be taken as an exception that is disconnected (*munqati'*) from the main category.

Three: That this be of the kind of the poet's saying:

*Page 203*

*"There is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched from the clashing of the battalions."*

The second discussion: That this peace may be the greeting of some of them to others, or the greeting of the angels, or the greeting of God the Exalted, as He said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate. "Peace be upon you, for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the final home."﴾ (Al-Ra'd 13:23–24), and His saying: ﴿"Peace," a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾ (Ya-Sin 36:58).

The fourth is the Exalted's saying: ﴿And for them is their provision therein, morning and evening.﴾ Regarding this there are two questions:

The first question: The purpose of these verses is to describe Paradise with magnificent conditions, and the arrival of provision to them in the morning and evening is not among the magnificent matters. The answer has two parts:

The first: al-Hasan said: God intended to encourage every people with what they loved in this world. For this reason He mentioned bracelets of gold and silver, and the wearing of silk, which were the customs of non-Arabs (*ʿajam*), and the couches (*ara'ik*), which are canopies set up over beds, and which were customary among the nobles of the Arabs in Yemen. Nothing was more beloved to the Arabs than lunch and dinner, so He promised them that.

The second: The intended meaning is the continuity of provision, as when you say, "I am with so-and-so in the morning and in the evening, and in the morning and evening," meaning continuity, not the two specific times.

The second question: The Exalted said: ﴿They will not see therein sun or extreme cold.﴾ (Al-Insan 76:13). And He, peace be upon him, said: "There is no morning with your Lord, nor evening." And *al-bukrah* and *al-ʿashiyy* exist only where there is morning and evening. The answer: The intended meaning is that they eat at the measure of the morning and the evening, although there is no morning or evening in Paradise, since there is no night in it. It may be understood as what has been said, that He made for the measure of the day a sign by which they know the measures of the morning and the evening. It may also be that the intended meaning is that their provision is for them whenever they wish, as is the custom with the morning and the evening.

The fifth is His saying: ﴿That is the Garden which We shall give as an inheritance to those of Our servants who were devout.﴾ Regarding this there are several discussions:

The first: His saying ﴿That is the Garden﴾. This demonstrative is valid because the Garden is unseen.

The second: They mentioned several views regarding *nurith* (We give as inheritance):

One: *Nurith* is a metaphor, meaning We preserve the Garden for him just as we preserve the property of the deceased for the heir.

Two: The intended meaning is that We transfer those dwellings from one who, had he obeyed, would have had them, to Our servants who feared their Lord. This transfer is called an inheritance. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Three: The devout meet their Lord on the Day of Resurrection after their deeds have ended, while their fruits remain, and these fruits are the Garden. So when He admits them to the Garden, He has given them an inheritance from their piety, just as an heir takes the property of the deceased.

Four: The meaning of *man kana taqiyyan* (whoever was devout) is one who holds fast to guarding against his disobediences and makes it his habit, and who guards against neglecting the obligations. Al-Qadi said: In this there is an indication that the Garden is reserved for those who were devout, and that a wrongdoer who commits major sins is not described by that. The answer: The verse indicates that the devout one enters it, and there is no indication in it that one who is not devout does not enter it. Furthermore, the one who commits a major sin is devout with regard to disbelief (*kufr*), and whoever is truly described as devout with regard to disbelief is truly described as devout, because the concept of "devout" is part of our statement "devout with regard to disbelief." Since the one who commits a major sin is truly described as devout, it is necessary that he be included under it. Therefore, the verse indicating that the one who commits a major sin enters the Garden is more fitting than the verse indicating that he does not enter it.
