The second is His saying: ﴿They will not hear therein any vain talk, but only "Peace."﴾ *Al-laghw* in speech is what is meant to be discarded and cast aside, namely reprehensible speech. A parallel is His saying: ﴿You will not hear therein any vain talk﴾ (Al-Ghashiyah 88:11). In this there is clear indication of the obligation to avoid vain talk, since God has declared the abode in which there is no obligation free of it. How beautiful is His saying: ﴿When they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ (Al-Furqan 25:72), and ﴿When they hear vain talk, they turn away from it and say, "For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek the ignorant."﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:55). As for His saying ﴿but only "Peace,"﴾ there are two discussions:

The first discussion: There is a difficulty here, namely that peace is not of the same kind as vain talk, so how can peace be made an exception from vain talk? The answer to this has several aspects:

One: The meaning of *salam* is a supplication for safety, and the people of Paradise have no need for this supplication, so its apparent form would be of the kind of vain talk and idle chatter, were it not for the benefit of honour that it contains.

Two: That it be taken as an exception that is disconnected (*munqati'*) from the main category.

Three: That this be of the kind of the poet's saying:

*Page 203*

*"There is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched from the clashing of the battalions."*

The second discussion: That this peace may be the greeting of some of them to others, or the greeting of the angels, or the greeting of God the Exalted, as He said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate. "Peace be upon you, for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the final home."﴾ (Al-Ra'd 13:23–24), and His saying: ﴿"Peace," a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾ (Ya-Sin 36:58).

The fourth is the Exalted's saying: ﴿And for them is their provision therein, morning and evening.﴾ Regarding this there are two questions:

The first question: The purpose of these verses is to describe Paradise with magnificent conditions, and the arrival of provision to them in the morning and evening is not among the magnificent matters. The answer has two parts:

The first: al-Hasan said: God intended to encourage every people with what they loved in this world. For this reason He mentioned bracelets of gold and silver, and the wearing of silk, which were the customs of non-Arabs (*ʿajam*), and the couches (*ara'ik*), which are canopies set up over beds, and which were customary among the nobles of the Arabs in Yemen. Nothing was more beloved to the Arabs than lunch and dinner, so He promised them that.

The second: The intended meaning is the continuity of provision, as when you say, "I am with so-and-so in the morning and in the evening, and in the morning and evening," meaning continuity, not the two specific times.

The second question: The Exalted said: ﴿They will not see therein sun or extreme cold.﴾ (Al-Insan 76:13). And He, peace be upon him, said: "There is no morning with your Lord, nor evening." And *al-bukrah* and *al-ʿashiyy* exist only where there is morning and evening. The answer: The intended meaning is that they eat at the measure of the morning and the evening, although there is no morning or evening in Paradise, since there is no night in it. It may be understood as what has been said, that He made for the measure of the day a sign by which they know the measures of the morning and the evening. It may also be that the intended meaning is that their provision is for them whenever they wish, as is the custom with the morning and the evening.

The fifth is His saying: ﴿That is the Garden which We shall give as an inheritance to those of Our servants who were devout.﴾ Regarding this there are several discussions:

The first: His saying ﴿That is the Garden﴾. This demonstrative is valid because the Garden is unseen.

The second: They mentioned several views regarding *nurith* (We give as inheritance):

One: *Nurith* is a metaphor, meaning We preserve the Garden for him just as we preserve the property of the deceased for the heir.

Two: The intended meaning is that We transfer those dwellings from one who, had he obeyed, would have had them, to Our servants who feared their Lord. This transfer is called an inheritance. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Three: The devout meet their Lord on the Day of Resurrection after their deeds have ended, while their fruits remain, and these fruits are the Garden. So when He admits them to the Garden, He has given them an inheritance from their piety, just as an heir takes the property of the deceased.

Four: The meaning of *man kana taqiyyan* (whoever was devout) is one who holds fast to guarding against his disobediences and makes it his habit, and who guards against neglecting the obligations. Al-Qadi said: In this there is an indication that the Garden is reserved for those who were devout, and that a wrongdoer who commits major sins is not described by that. The answer: The verse indicates that the devout one enters it, and there is no indication in it that one who is not devout does not enter it. Furthermore, the one who commits a major sin is devout with regard to disbelief (*kufr*), and whoever is truly described as devout with regard to disbelief is truly described as devout, because the concept of "devout" is part of our statement "devout with regard to disbelief." Since the one who commits a major sin is truly described as devout, it is necessary that he be included under it. Therefore, the verse indicating that the one who commits a major sin enters the Garden is more fitting than the verse indicating that he does not enter it.

[Page 204]

The commentator said, regarding the words of the Most High:

﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us, what is behind us, and what is between that. And your Lord is never forgetful. Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, so worship Him and be steadfast in His worship. Do you know of anyone who shares His name?﴾

Know that there is a difficulty in the verse. The words ﴿That is the Garden which We cause to inherit from Our servants those who were righteous﴾ are the speech of God, while the words ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ are the speech of someone other than God. So how is it permissible to join this to what comes before it without any separation?

The answer is that when the indication is clear, it is not objectionable. Just as His words, glorified is He, ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 47] are the speech of God, and His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord﴾ [Maryam: 36] are the speech of someone other than God, and one of them is joined to the other.

Know also that the apparent meaning of the words of the Most High ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ is an address from a group to one person, and that is only fitting for the angels who descend upon the Messenger. Regarding its cause, it is possible that it is what has been narrated: that Quraysh sent five men to the Jews of Madinah to ask them about the description of Muhammad ﷺ and whether they find him in their Book. They then asked the Christians, who claimed that they did not know him. The Jews said: "We find him in our Book, and this is his time. We have asked the Rahman of al-Yamamah about three characteristics, and he did not know them. So ask him about them. If he informs you of two of them, then follow him. Ask him about the youths of the Cave, about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and about the Spirit." They came and asked him about these, and he did not know how to answer. He promised them that he would answer them later, and he did not say, "If Allah wills." So revelation was withheld from him for forty days, and it is said fifteen days. This was very hard on him, and the polytheists said: "His Lord has forsaken him and has come to hate him." Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, descended, and the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "You were slow to come to me until my thoughts became bad, and I longed for you." He said: "I was more eager, but I am a servant who is commanded. When I am sent, I descend, and when I am held back, I am held back." So Allah the Most High revealed this verse, and He revealed His words: (﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,﴾ ﴿unless Allah wills﴾) [al-Kahf: 23–24], and the Surah of al-Duha.

Then they confirmed that by their words: ﴿To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us﴾, meaning: He is the one who manages our affairs at all times, the past and the future, and what is between them, or the world and the Hereafter and what is between them. For He knows the correct management, in the future and in the past, and what is between them. The point is that our affair is entrusted to Allah the Most High. He disposes of us according to His will, His purpose, and His wisdom, and no one has any objection to Him in this.

Abu Muslim said: His words ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ may be the speech of the people of the Garden, and the meaning is: "We do not descend to the Garden except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us," meaning what is in the Garden in the future, "and what is behind us," meaning what was in the world, "and what is between that," meaning what is between the two times. "And your Lord is never forgetful," meaning regarding anything He has created, so that He would leave off its restoration, because He is the Knower of the unseen, from whom not even the weight of an atom is hidden. His words ﴿And your Lord is never forgetful﴾ are the beginning of a statement from Him, may He be exalted, addressing the Messenger ﷺ, and it is connected to it: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: rather, He is ﴿the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, so worship Him﴾.

The qadi said: This is contrary to the apparent meaning in several respects.

The first: the apparent meaning of descent (tanzil) is the descent of the angels to the Messenger ﷺ, because of His words "by the command of your Lord," and the apparent meaning of command fits the state of moral responsibility (taklif) better.

The second: it is an address from a group to one person, and that is not fitting for the address of some of them to others in the Garden.

The third: what comes in its context, His words ﴿And your Lord is never forgetful﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾, is only fitting for the state of moral responsibility, and it is not attributed to the Messenger ﷺ. So it is as if they said to the Messenger: "And your Lord, O Muhammad, is not forgetful, so that forgetfulness could be permitted for Him, to the point that our delay in descending to you would harm you, and similar things."

Then there are several discussions here.

The first discussion: the author of al-Kashshaf said: tanzil has two meanings:

One of them: descent gradually (ʿala mahal).

The second: in the general sense of descent. The evidence for this is that it is the intransitive form of nazzala, and nazzala can mean anzala and can mean gradual progression. What is fitting for a context like this is descent gradually, and the meaning is that our descent at times, time after time, is only by the command of Allah the Most High.

The second discussion: they mentioned in His words ﴿what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that﴾ several interpretations:

One of them: to Him belongs what is in front of us, behind us, and in the directions in which we are, so we cannot move from one direction to another or from one place to another except by His command and will. So it is not for us to turn from the sky to the earth except by His command.

The second: to Him belongs what is before us, namely what has passed of the affairs of the world, and what is behind us, namely what will come of the affairs of the Hereafter, and what is between that, which is between the two blasts of the Trumpet, and that is forty years.

The third: our past lifetimes, what remains of them, and the state in which we are now.

The fourth: what came before our existence and what comes after our passing away.

The fifth: the earth that is before us when we descend, the sky that is behind us, and what is between the sky and the earth. Under all these interpretations, the intended meaning is that He encompasses everything, nothing is hidden from Him, and not even the weight of an atom escapes Him. So how could we proceed with an action except by His command and decree?

The third discussion: His words ﴿And your Lord is never forgetful﴾ mean: one who abandons you, like His words ﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He come to hate you﴾ [al-Duha: 3]. That is, the withholding of descent was only because the command to descend was withheld, and it was not because of Allah's abandoning you or leaving you. As for His words ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾, the meaning is that the one who is Lord of all of them cannot be subject to forgetfulness, since He must keep them in existence moment by moment, otherwise the affair concerning them and concerning whoever disposes of them would be void.

Our companions (the Ash'aris) used this verse as evidence that the act of the servant is the creation of Allah the Most High, because the act of the servant takes place between the heaven and the earth, and the verse indicates that He is the Lord of everything that takes place between them.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿your Lord﴾, and it is permissible that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. ﴿So worship Him and be steadfast in His worship﴾: this is a command to the Messenger ﷺ to worship and to persevere through the hardships of the obligations in conveying and delivering the message, and in what concerns his own worship.

If it is asked: why did He not say "be steadfast in His worship" (with ʿala), but said "be steadfast for His worship" (with li)? We answer: because worship has been made like the opponent (qirn) in your saying to a warrior, "Be steadfast against your opponent," meaning: hold firm against him in what he brings against you of his assaults. The meaning is that worship brings hardships and difficulties upon you, so hold firm in them, and do not weaken, and do not let your chest be constrained by the People of the Book's fabrication of lies to you, nor by the delay of revelation from you for a period, nor by the mockery of the polytheists against you.

As for His words, the Most High, ﴿Do you know of anyone who shares His name?﴾: the apparent meaning indicates that the Most High made the reason for the command to worship and the command to persevere in it that He has no namesake. The closest interpretation is that He is the bestower of the roots and branches of blessings, namely the creation of bodies, life, intellect, and others, since no one other than Him, glorified is He, is able to do that. So when He has bestowed upon you the utmost favor, it is obligatory that you exalt Him with the utmost exaltation, which is worship.

Some people said: the meaning is that He, glorified is He, has no partner in His name. They explained this in two ways:

The first: although they used the word "god" (ilah) for an idol, they did not use the word "Allah" for anything other than Him. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that none is named "al-Rahman" other than Him.

The second: do you know anyone who was named with His name in truth rather than in falsehood? Because naming in falsehood, in terms of it not being counted, is like no naming at all.

The first statement is the correct one, and Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 19, verses 66–70**

God's words: ﴿And man says, "When I die, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?"﴾ ﴿Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾ ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them, and the devils too, then We will surely bring them around Hell on their knees.﴾ ﴿Then We will surely draw out from every group whichever of them is most insolent toward the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿Then We know best those who most deserve to burn therein.﴾

Know that when God commanded worship and steadfastness in it, it was as if a questioner asked: "These acts of worship have no benefit in this world, and as for the Hereafter, a people have denied it. So there must be a mention of the proof for the doctrine of resurrection, so that it becomes clear that devoting oneself to worship is beneficial." For this reason God related the statement of those who deny the resurrection, saying: ﴿And man says, "When I die, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?"﴾ They said this in denial and as a way of deeming it far-fetched. Regarding "man" (al-insan) there are two interpretations:

The first: that it refers to the whole species. If it is objected that not all of them say this, how is the statement valid? We answer with two points:

The first: since this statement exists among a part of their kind, it is valid to attribute it to all of them, as one says, "The sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," when the killer was in fact only one man among them.

The second: this far-fetchedness is initially present in the natural disposition of everyone, but some of them set it aside, the far-fetchedness being based on mere disposition, through the decisive proof that established the validity of the doctrine.

The second interpretation: that "man" refers to a specific individual. It has been said that he is Abu Jahl; it has been said that he is Ubayy ibn Khalaf; and it has been said that the reference is to the category of disbelievers who deny resurrection. Then God established the proof for the validity of resurrection through His words: ﴿Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾ All the readers recite "yadhdhakkaru" with the doubled letter (shaddah), except Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim, who read it without the doubling. That is, "Does man not remember (yatadhakkaru) that We created him before?" When it is read as "awa la yadhdhakkaru," it is closer to the intended meaning, since the purpose is reflection and consideration: that one who was created before, from nothing, is capable of being restored a second time.

Some scholars said: "If all creatures gathered to produce an argument for resurrection in this brevity, they would not be able to do so, for there is no doubt that restoration a second time is easier than initial creation." A parallel to this is His words: ﴿Say, "He who produced them the first time will give them life"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 79], and His words: ﴿It is He who originates creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27]. Our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) used this verse as evidence that the non-existent is not a thing, but this is weak, because "man" is a term for a collection of composed substances in which accidents subsist, and this collection was not a thing before. But why do you say that each of those parts was not a thing before its existence?

If it is asked: how did God command man to "remember" when remembering is knowing what one already knew before, and forgetfulness has intervened between the two? We answer: the intended meaning is "Does he not reflect so that he knows?" especially when read as "awa la yadhdhakkaru al-insan" with the doubling. As for when it is read as "awa la yadhkuru" without the doubling, the meaning is "Does he not know this from the state of his own self? For everyone knows that he was not alive in this world and then became alive."

Then, once God had established the required matter through proof, He followed it with a threat in several respects:

The first: His words: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them, and the devils too﴾. The purpose of the oath is twofold:

One: it is customary to emphasize a statement with an oath.

Two: in God's swearing by His name joined to the name of His Messenger (ﷺ), there is an exalting of his station (ﷺ) and an elevation of his status, just as He elevated the status of heaven and earth in His words: ﴿So by the Lord of heaven and earth, it is indeed the truth﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 23]. The "wa" in ﴿and the devils﴾ may be conjunctive, or it may mean "together with" (ma'a), which is the more fitting sense. The meaning is that they will be gathered together with their companions among the devils who led them astray; every disbeliever will be bound with a devil in a chain.

The second: His words: ﴿Then We will surely bring them around Hell on their knees﴾. This bringing will occur before they are cast into Hell. Then, once God had established the required matter through proof, He followed it with a threat in several respects:

The first: His words: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them, and the devils too﴾. The purpose of the oath is twofold:

One: it is customary to emphasize a statement with an oath.

Two: in God's swearing by His name joined to the name of His Messenger (ﷺ), there is an exalting of his station (ﷺ) and an elevation of his status, just as He elevated the status of heaven and earth in His words: ﴿So by the Lord of heaven and earth, it is indeed the truth﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 23]. The "wa" in ﴿and the devils﴾ may be conjunctive, or it may mean "together with" (ma'a), which is the more fitting sense. The meaning is that they will be gathered together with their companions among the devils who led them astray; every disbeliever will be bound with a devil in a chain.

The second: His words: ﴿Then We will surely bring them around Hell on their knees﴾. This bringing will occur before they are cast into Hell. God brings them in the most humiliated form, as His words ﴿on their knees﴾ indicate, for one who kneels on his knees resembles the abject or the helpless. If it is objected that this condition applies to everyone, as evidenced by His words: ﴿And you will see every nation kneeling﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 28], and the reason for this is the custom that people, in situations of accountability before kings, kneel upon their knees out of anxiety and apprehension, or because of the severity of a matter which overwhelms them so that they cannot stand on their feet, then how does it indicate greater humiliation for the disbelievers? We answer: perhaps the meaning is that they will remain in this state from the time of gathering until the time of standing in the place of account, and this entails greater humiliation for them.

The third: His words: ﴿Then We will surely draw out from every group whichever of them is most insolent toward the Most Merciful﴾. The word "shi'ah" is of the form "fi'lah," like "firqah" and "fi'ah," and means a group that follows, that is, a company that follows a misguided one among the misguided. God said: ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects﴾ [al-An'am: 159]. The meaning is that God first brings them around Hell on their knees, then distinguishes some from others. Whoever was most rebellious in his disbelief is singled out for a greater punishment, because the punishment of the misguider who misguides others must be above the punishment of one who goes astray following another. The punishment of one who rebels and acts arrogantly is not like the punishment of the mere imitator, and the punishment of one who presents doubts in falsehood is not like that of one who follows him while heedless. God said: ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of God, We will add to their punishment a punishment upon punishment for what they used to corrupt﴾ [al-Nahl: 88], and He said: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13]. Thus God made clear that He draws out from every group the one who is most insolent and most rebellious, so that it may be known that his punishment is the more severe. The benefit of this distinction is singling out for greater severity of punishment, not singling out for the very fact of punishment. For this reason He said regarding all of them: ﴿Then We know best those who most deserve to burn therein﴾, and "awla" is used only when the people share in the punishment.

They differed over the grammatical case (i'rab, inflection of the final sound) of "ayyuhum" (which of them). According to al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad), it is in the nominative on the basis of quotation, its implied sense being: "We will surely draw out those of whom it is said: which of them is most insolent." Sibawayh held that it is built on the dammah (a fixed vowel) because the first part of the clause that serves as its relative complement has been dropped; were it stated, it would be inflected. It has also been said: "Ayyuhum huwa ashaddu" (which of them is the most insolent).

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 19, verses 71–72:**

Allah's words: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it. That is ever, with your Lord, a decree [that must be] carried out.﴾ ﴿Then We shall save those who feared Allah, and leave the wrongdoers therein, kneeling.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, said earlier, ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them and the devils,﴾ and then said, ﴿Then We will surely bring them forth around Hell, kneeling,﴾ He followed it with His words, ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it,﴾ meaning Hell. The scholars differed. Some said that what is meant is the disbelievers previously mentioned. He first referred to them with the kinaya (indirect allusion) of the third person, then addressed them directly. They said: it is not permissible for the believers to pass over the Fire. This is indicated by several matters:

The first: Allah's words, ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best [reward] has preceded from Us, those will be kept far away from it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 101]. One who is kept far away from it is not described as passing over it.

The second: His words, ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound﴾ [al-Anbiya: 102]. If they had passed over Hell, they would have heard its faintest sound.

The third: His words, ﴿and they will be safe from terror that Day﴾ [al-Naml: 89]. Most scholars said that this is general, covering every believer and disbeliever, because of Allah's words, ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it,﴾ where He did not specify. This address is a new beginning, different from the first address. This is indicated by His words, ﴿Then We save those who feared Allah,﴾ meaning from among those who pass over, those who feared Allah. And it is not permissible to say, ﴿Then We save those who feared Allah, and leave the wrongdoers therein, kneeling,﴾ unless all of them are passing over. The narrations reported support this view.

Then these people differed about the interpretation of "passing over" (al-warud). Some said: al-warud means drawing near to Hell, and that they will be around it, which is the place of reckoning. They argued that warud may mean nearness, by Allah's words, ﴿So they sent their water-carrier﴾ [Yusuf: 19], where it is known that this water-carrier did not enter the water. And Allah said, ﴿And when he came to the water of Madyan, he found on it a group of people watering [their flocks]﴾ [al-Qasas: 23], and by it He meant nearness. It is said, "The caravan came to the town (waridat al-qafilah al-baldah)," even though it did not enter it. Accordingly, the meaning of the verse is that the jinn and mankind will be present around

[Page 208]

Hell: ﴿That is ever, with your Lord, a decree [that must be] carried out﴾, meaning obligatory, settled by the judgment of the threat (wa'id, the divine threat of punishment). ﴿Then We save﴾, meaning We remove those who feared Allah far from Hell, and this is what is meant by His words, ﴿those will be kept far away from it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 101]. What supports this view is what is reported: the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "No one who was present at Badr and al-Hudaybiyah will enter the Fire." Hafsah said, "Did not Allah say, ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾?" He (peace be upon him) said, "Enough! ﴿Then We save those who feared Allah.﴾" Had warud meant entering, Hafsah's question would have been compelling.

The second view: warud is entering. This is indicated by the verse and the report. As for the verse, it is His words, ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell; you will be entering it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98], and He said, ﴿So He will lead them to the Fire, and wretched is the place of arrival (wird) to which they are led﴾ [Hud: 98]. It is indicated by His words, ﴿those will be kept far away from it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 101], and the one who is kept far away is one who, were it not for the keeping away, would be near. This only happens if they are in the Fire. Then He keeps them far from it, and this is indicated by His words, ﴿and leave the wrongdoers therein, kneeling﴾, which shows that they remain in the place they came to, and they remain only in the Fire. So they must have entered the Fire. As for the report, it is that Abdullah ibn Rawahah said, "Allah has informed of the warud and did not inform of the sudur (departure/exit)." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said, "O son of Rawahah, read what follows it: ﴿Then We save those who feared Allah.﴾" This indicates that Ibn Rawahah understood warud as entering, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not reject this from him. And from Jabir: he was asked about this verse and said, "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Warud is entering. No one, righteous or wicked, will fail to enter it. It will be cool and safe for the believers, to the extent that people will cry out because of its coolness.'"

Those who hold this view say: the believers enter the Fire without any fear or harm whatsoever, rather with joy and delight. This is because Allah informed of them that ﴿the greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ [al-Anbiya: 103]. And because the Hereafter is the abode of recompense, not the abode of obligation, and inflicting distress and grief is permissible only in the abode of obligation. And because it is authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The angels give good news in the grave to whoever is among the people of reward, of Paradise, until he sees his place in Paradise and knows it." The same applies to the state of direct witnessing. How then could they pass over the Resurrection while they are in doubt about their state? These conditions only affect the people of the Fire, because they do not know that they are among the people of the Fire and of punishment.

Then they differed about how the harm of the Fire is averted from them. Some said: the area called Hell may contain, within it, parts where there is no fire, and these may be among the places through which one passes to the levels of Hell. If so, it is not impossible that all of them enter Hell: the believers will be in those empty places free of fire, and the disbelievers will be in the midst of the Fire.

The second: Allah extinguishes the Fire, and the believers cross it, while it collapses on others. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said, "They pass over it as if it were melted fat (ihalah)." And from Jabir ibn Abdullah: he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said, "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, some of them will say to others, 'Did not our Lord promise us that we would pass over the Fire?' It will be said to them, 'You have passed over it, and it was extinguished.'"

The third: the heat of the Fire is not by its nature. Allah makes the parts touching the bodies of the disbelievers burning and harmful to them, and makes the parts touching the bodies of the believers cool and safe for them, as in the case of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Just as a single vessel of water is drunk by a Copt and becomes blood for him, and drunk by an Israelite and becomes sweet water. Know that one of these aspects must apply to the angels appointed over the punishment, so that they will be in the Fire together with those being punished. If it is said: if there is no punishment for the believers in their entering the Fire, then what is the benefit of that entering? We say: there are several aspects to this:

[Page 209]

The first: that this increases their joy when they know they are delivered from it.

The second: that it causes greater grief for the people of the Fire, since they see the believers, who were their enemies, being delivered from it while they remain in it.

The third: that it causes greater grief for the people of the Fire, in that their disgrace becomes apparent before the believers, and even before the close friends, and before those who used to warn them of the Fire but whom they did not heed.

The fourth: that when the believers are with them in the Fire, they rebuke them, which increases the grief of the disbelievers and the joy of the believers.

The fifth: that the believers used to warn them of the gathering and resurrection and establish for them the soundness of the proofs, but they did not accept those proofs. So when they enter Hell with them, they show them that they had been truthful in what they said, and that those who denied the gathering and resurrection had been lying.

The sixth: that when they witness that punishment, it becomes a cause of greater delight in them with the bliss of Paradise, as the poet said:

*"And by their opposites are things made clear."*

As for those who cling to Allah's words, ﴿those will be kept far away from it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 101], we have already shown that this is one of the things that indicates entering Hell. Moreover, what is meant is being kept far from its punishment. The same applies to His words, ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound﴾ [al-Anbiya: 102]. If it is asked: Has it been established by reports how the entering of the Fire occurs, and then the emergence of the God-fearing from it to Paradise? We say: It has been established by reports that the reckoning will take place on the earth, or wherever the earth was. This is also indicated by His words, ﴿On the Day when the earth will be replaced by another earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 48]. Hell is close to the earth, and Paradise is in the heaven. So at the place of reckoning there will be the gathering, and they will enter Hell from that place. Then Allah will raise up the people of Paradise, deliver them, and push the people of the Fire into it.

As for His words, ﴿That is ever, with your Lord, a decree [that must be] carried out,﴾ al-hatm is the verbal noun of "hatama al-amr," meaning he made it obligatory. So what is made obligatory is called al-hatm, as in the expressions "khalq Allah" (the creation of Allah) and "darb al-asir" (the striking of the captive). Those who hold that punishment is obligatory by reason argued: His words, ﴿That is ever, with your Lord, a decree,﴾ indicate the obligation of what came by way of the threat and the reports, because the particle "ʿala" (upon) indicates obligation, and what is established merely by report is not called obligatory. The answer is that when Allah's promise is impossible to be broken, it takes the status of what is obligatory.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿Then We save those who feared Allah and leave the wrongdoers﴾, it has been read as nunajji and nunjī and yunajjā (in the passive, with no named agent). Al-Qadi said: the verse supports our view on the threat (wa'id), because Allah, exalted is He, made clear that all of them pass over it, then He described the one who is saved, namely the God-fearing, and the wicked is not God-fearing. Then He made clear that whoever is other than the God-fearing, He leaves in it kneeling. So it is established that the wicked will remain in the Fire forever. Ibn Abbas said: the God-fearing is one who guards against shirk by saying "There is no god but Allah." Know that what Ibn Abbas said is the truth, which the proof testifies to its soundness. For whoever believes in Allah and His messengers, it is correct to say that he is one who guards against shirk. And whoever is truly described as guarding against shirk is truly described as God-fearing, because the God-fearing (muttaqi) is a part of the one who guards against shirk. And whoever the compound description applies to, the simple description applies to. So it is established that the person who commits a major sin is God-fearing. When that is established, it is necessary that he exits the Fire, because of the generality of His words, ﴿Then We save those who feared Allah.﴾ Thus this verse, which they imagined to be evidence for their view, becomes one of the strongest proofs against their position.

Al-Qadi said: the verse also indicates the invalidity of the view of those who say that some of the accountable people will be neither in Paradise nor in the Fire. We say: this is weak, because the verse indicates that Allah saves those who feared Him, and there is nothing in it indicating that He saves them to Paradise. Even if we grant that it indicates that, the verse indicates that the God-fearing will be in Paradise and the wrongdoers will remain in the Fire. Then there remains a third category outside the two: the one whose obedience and disobedience are equal, so each cancels out the other, and he remains neither obedient nor disobedient. If this category is invalid, it is invalid only by something other than this verse, so this verse does not indicate the restriction he claims.

Among the Mu'tazilah, some held onto the threat by His words:

[Page 210]

﴿and leave the wrongdoers therein, kneeling.﴾ The word "al-zalimin" (the wrongdoers) is a plural word with the definite article, so it implies generality. And the discussion of holding to the forms of generality has already passed many times in this book.

As for His words, ﴿kneeling﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: His words, ﴿and leave the wrongdoers therein, kneeling,﴾ are evidence that what is meant by warud is kneeling around it, and that the believers part from the disbelievers toward Paradise after their deliverance, while the disbelievers remain in their place, kneeling.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 73–74:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieved say to those who believed: "Which of the two groups is better in station and finer in assembly?"﴾ ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed before them, who were better in wealth and in appearance?﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had established the proof against the polytheists of Quraysh who denied the Resurrection, He followed it with a warning concerning what has been mentioned of them: that they opposed the proof of God with speech. They said: "If you were upon the truth and we were upon falsehood, your condition in this world would be better and finer than ours, because it does not befit the Wise to place His loyal friends in punishment and humiliation while placing His enemies, who turn away from His service, in might and ease." Since the matter was the reverse, the disbelievers being in blessing, ease and dominance, while the believers at that time were in fear and humiliation, this indicated that the truth is not with the believers. This is the essence of their doubt in this matter. A parallel to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 11]. It is related that they used to comb their hair, anoint themselves, perfume themselves, and adorn themselves with splendid adornment, then they would boast over the poor among the Muslims, claiming that they were more honored by God than them. Two investigations remain:

The first: His saying ﴿Our verses, clear﴾ may have several meanings:

One of them: they are well-arranged in wording and clear in meaning, whether muhkamat (decisive) or mutashabihat (ambiguous); their clarification has followed, either through the decisive verses or through the Messenger's clarification, by word or by deed.

The second: they are manifestly miraculous, and they were challenged with them, yet they were unable to oppose them.

The third: the meaning of their being clear verses is that they are evident and manifest proofs upon which no question or objection can be directed, like His saying, exalted is He, in establishing the validity of the Gathering: ﴿Does not man remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾ [Maryam: 67].

The second investigation: Ibn Kathir read (muqaman) with a damma, which is the place of dwelling and abode, while the rest read it with a fatha, which is the place of standing. By al-nadi is meant the assembly; it is said nadiyy and nad, and its plural is al-andiyah. From it is His saying: ﴿And you commit in your assembly the evil﴾ [al-Ankabut: 29], and He said: ﴿Then let him call his assembly﴾ [al-Alaq: 17]. It is said: "I gathered the people (nadawtu al-qawm, andu-hum) when I assembled them in the council," and from it is Dar al-Nadwa in Mecca, which was the gathering place of the people.

Then God, exalted is He, answered this doubt with His saying: ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed before them, who were better in wealth and in appearance?﴾

The explanation of this answer is to say: whoever had greater blessing than you in this world, God, exalted is He, has destroyed and annihilated them. So if the attainment of worldly blessings by a person indicated that he is beloved of God, exalted is He, it would necessarily follow that the beloved of God should not be made to suffer any grief in this world, and it would necessarily follow that He should not destroy any of those given luxury in the abode of this world. Since He destroyed them, this indicates either the invalidity of the first premise, namely that whoever finds the world is beloved of God, exalted is He, or the invalidity of the second premise, namely that God does not bring grief upon the beloved of God. On either assumption, what you have mentioned as doubt is invalid. The remaining investigation concerns the explanation of the words. We say: the people of every age are a qarn (generation) for those after them, because they precede them. And (hum ahsanu) is in the accusative position as an attribute of (lakum). Do you not see that if you omitted hum, you would have no choice but to put (ahsanu) in the accusative as a descriptive? Athath is the furniture of the house. As for ri'an, it has been read in five ways, because it is either read with the ra' which has no dot above it, or with the zay which has a dot above it. As for the first, it is either combined with a hamza and a ya', or with the ya' alone. When combined with a hamza and a ya', there are two possibilities:

One of them: with a silent hamza followed by a ya', and it means appearance and form, a noun in the sense of a passive participle from ra'aytu ri'an.

The second: ri'an, by inversion (qalb), like their saying ra'in for ra'an.

As for when we suffice with the ya' alone: sometimes with a doubled ya', by converting the hamza into a ya' and assimilating; or it is from al-riyy, which is abundance and luxury, from their saying: rayyan min al-na'im (saturated with blessing).

The second: with the ya' by dropping the hamza altogether. Its basis is that the inverted form, which is ri'an, is lightened by dropping the hamza and transferring its vowel onto the silent ya' before it. As for zayyan with a dotted zay from above, its derivation is from al-zayy, which is gathering, because al-zayy is beautiful qualities gathered together, and the meaning is "better than these," and God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 75–76:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say: Whoever is in error, let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension, until, when they see what they are promised, either the punishment or the Hour, then they will know who is worse in position and weaker in soldiers.﴾ ﴿And Allah increases those who are guided in guidance; and the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in return.﴾

Know that this is the second answer to that doubt. Its explanation: let us suppose that this wrongdoer, who enjoys luxury in this world, has been granted by Allah a long life and a lengthy respite, so that a long duration is added to the great blessing. Then he must end up in a punishment in this world, or a punishment in the Hereafter after that. They will know that the blessings of this world did not save them from that punishment. So His saying ﴿then they will know who is worse in position﴾ is mentioned in contrast to their saying ﴿better in station﴾ [Maryam: 73], and ﴿and weaker in soldiers﴾ is in contrast to their saying ﴿and better in assembly﴾ [Maryam: 73]. Thus He made clear that although they supposed at present that their position was superior, since Allah had favoured them with station and assembly, they will later know that the matter is the opposite of that, and that they are worse in position, for there is no position worse than the Fire and the strict reckoning. ﴿And weaker in soldiers﴾: they used to think, while in this world, that their gathering would benefit them; but when they see that they have no helper in the Hereafter, they then recognise that in this world they were falsifiers in what they claimed.

The discussion of the words remains, and it has several aspects:

First: ﴿let the Most Merciful extend for him﴾ means He gives him respite and lets him continue in life. It is expressed in the form of a command, to indicate that this is obligatory and will certainly happen, like one commanded who complies, in order to cut off the excuses of the wrongdoer. And it will be said to him on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Did We not give you life long enough for whoever would take heed to take heed in it?﴾ [Fatir: 37], and like their saying: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran].

Second: His saying ﴿either the punishment or the Hour﴾ indicates that the punishment meant is one that occurs before the Day of Resurrection, since ﴿or the Hour﴾ refers to the Day of Resurrection. Then the punishment that occurs before the Day of Resurrection may be the punishment of the grave, or it may be the punishment that will take place at the time of direct witnessing, since at that time they will know what they deserve. It may also be that the meaning is the change of their conditions in this world from honour to humiliation, from wealth to poverty, from health to sickness, from security to fear. It may also be that the meaning is the empowering of the believers over them. It may also be that the meaning is what befell them on the day of Badr. All these aspects are mentioned.

Know that He, the Exalted, then made clear that just as He deals with the disbelievers in the manner He mentioned, so He increases the believers who are guided in guidance. Know that we explain the possibility of this according to reason: it is not improbable that some kinds of guidance are conditional upon others, for the outcome of guidance returns to knowledge, and there is no impossibility in some knowledge being conditional upon other knowledge. Whoever is guided by the guidance which is the condition comes to a state in which it is not impossible that he be given the guidance which is the conditioned. So His saying is sound: ﴿And Allah increases those who are guided in guidance.﴾ An example: faith is guidance, and sincerity in faith is an increase in guidance, and sincerity cannot be attained except after attaining faith; so whoever is guided by faith, Allah increases him in guidance by sincerity. This is if we apply the word guidance to its apparent meaning. Some people have understood the increase in guidance to mean reward, i.e. ﴿And Allah increases those who are guided in reward for that guidance﴾; and some have explained this increase as the acts of worship that follow from faith. The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿yazid﴾ is coordinated with the place of ﴿falyamdud﴾, because it stands in the position of a predicate, and its implied sense is: whoever is in error, the Most Merciful extends for him an extension, and He increases, i.e. He increases the errant in their error by abandoning them through that extension, and He increases the guided in guidance by His granting them success. Then He, the Exalted, made clear that what the guided are upon is what benefits in the end, so He said: ﴿And the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward﴾. That is because what the guided are upon is a small, finite harm which is followed by a great, infinite benefit, whereas what the errant are upon is a small, finite benefit which is followed by a great, infinite harm; and everyone knows by necessity that the first is preferable. By this route the doubt on which they relied falls away.

They differed regarding the meaning of ﴿the enduring good deeds﴾. The scholars who investigate said it is faith and righteous deeds; He called them enduring because their benefit lasts and does not perish. Others said the meaning is some acts of worship; perhaps they mentioned what is greatest in reward, so some mentioned the prayers and some mentioned tasbih. It is narrated from Abu al-Darda', who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sat one day and took a dry stick and removed its leaves, then said: Indeed, the saying 'there is no god but Allah', 'Allah is greatest', and 'Glory be to Allah' erases sins, erasing them as the wind erases the leaves of this tree. . . Take them, O Abu al-Darda', before you are prevented from them; they are the enduring good deeds, and they are among the treasures of Paradise." Abu al-Darda' used to say: "I shall teach them and shall use them much, until when an ignorant person sees me he thinks I am mad."

The first view is preferable, because Allah described them as enduring righteous deeds only in respect of their reward lasting and not ceasing. Some acts of worship, although less in reward than others, share in lasting, so all of them together are enduring and righteous in view of their effects, which are the reward. Then He, the Exalted, informed that they are ﴿better with your Lord in reward and better in return﴾. It is not permissible to say "this is better" except that what is meant is that it is better than something else; so what is meant is that they are better than what the disbelievers supposed by their saying: ﴿better in station and better in assembly﴾ [Maryam: 73].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 77–80:

﴿Never! We shall record what he says and extend for him the punishment, extending it (for him).﴾ ﴿And We shall inherit from him what he says, and he will come to Us alone.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"? Has he attained the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?﴾ ﴿Never! We shall record what he says and extend for him the punishment, extending it (for him). And We shall inherit from him what he says, and he will come to Us alone.﴾

Know that when Almighty God first mentioned the proofs for the validity of resurrection, and then presented the doubt of the deniers and answered it, He now presents what they said by way of mockery, as a criticism of the doctrine of resurrection, saying: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wuldan" (وُلْدًا), which is the plural of "walad" like "usd" for "asad," or with the meaning of "walad" (child) like "al-'urb" for "al-'arab." From Yahya ibn Ya'mar it is read "wildan" with a kasra. From al-Hasan: the verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, but the well-known view is that it was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: "He owed me a debt, so I demanded it from him. He said, 'No, by God, not until you disbelieve in Muhammad.' I said, 'No, by God, I will not disbelieve in Muhammad ﷺ, neither while alive nor dead, nor when you are resurrected.' He said, 'Indeed, when I die I will be resurrected?' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'When I am resurrected and come to you, there will be wealth and children for me there, and I will pay you then.'" It is also said: Khabbab made jewelry for him, then demanded payment, and he said, "You claim that you will be resurrected, and that in Paradise there is gold, silver and silk; I will pay you there, for I will be given wealth and children then." Then God, exalted, answered his words with His saying: ﴿Has he attained the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?﴾

The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Ittala'a al-ghayb" comes from the expression "ittala'a al-jabal," meaning he ascended to its top; and it is said "marra mutti'alan li-dhalika al-amr," meaning dominating it and possessing it. The preferred way to render this expression is: "Has he reached such greatness that he has ascended to knowledge of the unseen, which the One, the Subduer, has made exclusive to Himself?" The meaning is that the one who claims that what he wishes will be his cannot attain it except by one of two matters: either knowledge of the unseen, or a covenant from the Knower of the unseen. So by which of these two did he attain it? It has also been said concerning "covenant" that it is the statement of the testimony (kalimat al-shahadah). From Qatadah: "Does he have a righteous deed that he sent ahead, so that he hopes by it for what he says?"

Then, glorified is He, He showed the opposite of what he claimed about his state, saying: ﴿Never!﴾ and it is a word of reprimand and warning about error, meaning: he is mistaken in what he says and wishes. If it is asked, why did He say ﴿We shall record what he says﴾ with the sin of future tense (sin al-taswif), while, as it has been said, it is recorded without delay? He, exalted, said: ﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is an observer ready [to record]﴾ [Qaf: 18]. We say that there are two answers:

The first: It will become apparent to him, and he will know that We have recorded it.

The second: The one who threatens says to the criminal, "I will surely take revenge on you," even though he is not currently taking revenge, and his purpose from this speech is pure threat. So it is likewise here.

As for His saying: ﴿and We shall extend for him the punishment, extending it﴾, meaning: We will lengthen for him of the punishment what befits him, and increase for him of the punishment, and multiply for him of the extension. It is said "madda-hu" and "amadda-hu" with the same meaning, and the reading of Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, supports this: "wa-numiddu lahu" with a damma.

As for His saying: ﴿And We shall inherit from him what he says﴾, meaning: what he promised of wealth and children will be removed from him and will not return, just as an inheritance does not return to the one who left it behind. When that is taken from him in the Hereafter, he will remain alone; therefore He said: ﴿and he will come to Us alone﴾. It is not valid that he would be alone in the Hereafter with wealth and children: ﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾ [al-An'am: 94]. And God knows best.

I said, 'No, by God, I will not disbelieve in Muhammad ﷺ, neither while alive nor dead, nor when you are resurrected.' He said, 'Indeed, when I die I will be resurrected?' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'When I am resurrected and come to you, there will be wealth and children for me there, and I will pay you then.'" It is also said: Khabbab made jewelry for him, then demanded payment, and he said, "You claim that you will be resurrected, and that in Paradise there is gold, silver and silk; I will pay you there, for I will be given wealth and children then." Then God, exalted, answered his words with His saying: ﴿Has he attained the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?﴾

The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Ittala'a al-ghayb" comes from the expression "ittala'a al-jabal," meaning he ascended to its top; and it is said "marra mutti'alan li-dhalika al-amr," meaning dominating it and possessing it. The preferred way to render this expression is: "Has he reached such greatness that he has ascended to knowledge of the unseen, which the One, the Subduer, has made exclusive to Himself?" The meaning is that the one who claims that what he wishes will be his cannot attain it except by one of two matters: either knowledge of the unseen, or a covenant from the Knower of the unseen. So by which of these two did he attain it? It has also been said concerning "covenant" that it is the statement of the testimony (kalimat al-shahadah). From Qatadah: "Does he have a righteous deed that he sent ahead, so that he hopes by it for what he says?"

Then, glorified is He, He showed the opposite of what he claimed about his state, saying: ﴿Never!﴾ and it is a word of reprimand and warning about error, meaning: he is mistaken in what he says and wishes. If it is asked, why did He say ﴿We shall record what he says﴾ with the sin of future tense (sin al-taswif), while, as it has been said, it is recorded without delay? He, exalted, said: ﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is an observer ready [to record]﴾ [Qaf: 18]. We say that there are two answers:

The first: It will become apparent to him, and he will know that We have recorded it.

The second: The one who threatens says to the criminal, "I will surely take revenge on you," even though he is not currently taking revenge, and his purpose from this speech is pure threat. So it is likewise here.

As for His saying: ﴿and We shall extend for him the punishment, extending it﴾, meaning: We will lengthen for him of the punishment what befits him, and increase for him of the punishment, and multiply for him of the extension. It is said "madda-hu" and "amadda-hu" with the same meaning, and the reading of Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, supports this: "wa-numiddu lahu" with a damma.

As for His saying: ﴿And We shall inherit from him what he says﴾, meaning: what he promised of wealth and children will be removed from him and will not return, just as an inheritance does not return to the one who left it behind. When that is taken from him in the Hereafter, he will remain alone; therefore He said: ﴿and he will come to Us alone﴾. It is not valid that he would be alone in the Hereafter with wealth and children: ﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾ [al-An'am: 94]. And God knows best.

[Page 214]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah, that they may be a source of honour for them.﴾ ﴿No! They will deny their worship of them, and will become opponents to them.﴾ ﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement?﴾ ﴿So do not be hasty against them. We are only counting out their days for them.﴾ ﴿On the Day We gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation,﴾ ﴿and drive the criminals to Hell like thirsty cattle,﴾ ﴿they will not have the power of intercession, except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful.﴾

Know that when Allah the Exalted had spoken about the matter of the Gathering and the Resurrection, He now spoke in refutation of the idol-worshippers. He related of them that they had taken gods only for themselves, so that they would be a source of honour for them, in that these gods would be intercessors and helpers for them with Allah, rescuing them from destruction. Then Allah the Exalted replied with His words: ﴿No!﴾, which is a rebuke to them and a denial of their being honoured through the gods.

Ibn Nuhayk recited: "Kullan sayakfuruna bi-'ibadatihim" (every one of them will deny their worship), meaning: all of them will deny the worship of these idols. In the *Muhtasab* of Ibn Jinni, it is read as "kallan" with a fatha on the kaf and tanwin, and he claimed its meaning is "all this belief and opinion is void." The author of the *Kashshaf* said: If this reading is authentic, then it is the *kalla* that signifies rebuke, and the one who pauses on it converts its alif into a nun, as in *qawarira*.

They differed over whether the pronoun in His words ﴿sayakfuruna﴾ refers to the worshipped or to the worshippers. Some said it refers to the worshipped. Then some of them said: He meant by this the angels, since in the Hereafter they will deny their worship, disown them and dispute with them, and this is what is meant by His words: ﴿Did these people worship you?﴾ [Saba': 40]. Others said: Allah will give life to the idols on the Day of Resurrection so that they may rebuke their worshippers and disown them, and that will be greater in their regret. Among the people, some said the pronoun refers to the worshippers, meaning that these polytheists on the Day of Resurrection will deny that they worshipped idols. Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then their only argument will be to say: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ [al-An'am: 23].

As for His words ﴿and will become opponents to them﴾, it is mentioned in contrast to His words ﴿a source of honour for them﴾. What is meant is the opposite of honour, which is humiliation and disgrace, i.e., they will be opposed to them in what they intended and sought, as if it were said: they will be a humiliation for them and not an honour; or it means they will be a helper against them. *Didd* means helper, as one says: "one of your *didd*," i.e., one of your helpers. It seems that a helper is called *didd* because he opposes your enemy and contradicts him by helping you against him. If it is asked: why did He use the singular? We say: He used the singular in the manner of the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying: "They are one hand against whoever is other than them," because of the unity of their word, for they are like a single thing due to their complete cohesion and agreement. The meaning of the gods being a help against them is that they are the fuel of the Fire and the pebbles of Hell, and because they were punished on account of worshipping them.

Know that when Allah the Exalted mentioned the condition of these disbelievers with the idols in the Hereafter, He then mentioned their condition with the devils in this world, for they ask them and submit to them. So He said: ﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement?﴾ and in this there are issues:

**First issue:** Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued from this verse that Allah the Exalted wills all existing things. They said: the statement of the speaker "I sent so-and-so upon so-and-so" is established in the language to convey that he empowered him over him, with the intention that he should gain dominion over him. He (peace be upon him) said: "Say the name of Allah and send your dog upon it." If this is established, then His words ﴿We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers﴾ convey that He empowered them over them, intending that they should gain dominion over them, and this conveys the intended meaning. Then this is confirmed by His words ﴿inciting them with incitement﴾, for its meaning is: We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers so that they incite them with incitement. And it is further confirmed by His words: ﴿And stir up whoever you can among them﴾ [al-Isra': 64].

The judge (al-Qadi, i.e., 'Abd al-Jabbar) said: The literal sense of the word requires that Allah the Exalted sent the devils to the disbelievers as He sent the prophets, by entrusting them with a message to deliver to them. [Page 215] Then in that message there can be nothing except what the devils were sent with, namely seduction. So the disbelievers would have to be obedient to the devils by accepting from them, and that would be disbelief on the part of the one who says it. Moreover, it is strange that the Predestinarians (al-Mujabbira) cling to this, since in their view the misguidance of the disbelievers comes from Him, the Exalted, in that He created disbelief in them and decreed disbelief, so the devil has no effect in what occurs. When the literal meaning is rejected, interpretation becomes necessary, so we take it to mean that Allah the Exalted left the devils and the disbelievers free to meet, and did not prevent them from seducing them. This leaving free is called "sending" in the broad sense of the language, as when a man does not restrain his dog from entering his neighbour's house, one says: he sent his dog against him, even if he does not repel the harm of the people. Although this leaving free involves intensifying the trial for them, they are able not to accept from them, and their reward for refusing to accept will be greater. The evidence for this is His words: ﴿I had no authority over you except that I called you and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]. This is the end of his words.

We say: We do not concede that it is impossible to take it according to its apparent meaning. For if the words "[We have sent] the devils" meant that Allah sent them to the disbelievers, the disbelievers would be obedient to Him by accepting the words of the devils. We say: Allah did not send the devils to the disbelievers, but rather sent them *upon* them, and sending upon them is empowering, with the intention that it should become dominant over them. How is this related to sending *to* them? As to the saying that the misguidance of the disbeliever is from Allah the Exalted, then what effect does the devil have on it? We say: Why should it not be said that the devil's whispering that suggestion to him creates that misguidance in his heart, on condition that the listener's understanding is sound, since the speech of the devil is part of Allah the Exalted's creation? Thus that misguidance arising in the heart of the disbeliever is attributed both to the devil and to Allah the Exalted, from these two aspects.

If it is said: why can it not be that the meaning of sending is leaving free? We say: Just as He left free between the devil and the disbelievers, He also left free between them and the prophets. Then He specifically singled out the disbeliever by saying that He sent the devil upon him, so there must be an additional benefit here. Also, His words ﴿inciting them with incitement﴾, i.e., stirring them with a powerful stirring, are like the purpose of that sending, so it is necessary that the incitement be what Allah intends, and that the purpose of it be achieved. This is what there is at this point, and Allah knows best.

**Second issue:** Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿inciting them with incitement﴾ means: He disturbs them in acts of disobedience with a strong disturbing. It was revealed concerning those who mocked the Qur'an, and they were five men. The author of the *Kashshaf* said: *al-azz*, *al-hazz* and *al-istifza'* are siblings in meaning, signifying agitation and intensity of disturbance; i.e., they urge them to acts of disobedience, goad them and stir them up to these with whisperings and enticements. As for His words ﴿So do not be hasty against them. We are only counting out their days for them﴾: it is said, "I hastened against him with such and such" when you urged him to it; i.e., do not be hasty against them by wishing that they perish or are destroyed, until you and the Muslims find rest from their evils. For between you and what you seek of their destruction there are only limited days and counted breaths. Its parallel is His words: ﴿Do not seek to hasten for them. On the day they see what they are promised, it will be as though they had not remained except an hour of a day. A proclamation﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that when he recited it he would weep and say: "The last of the count is the going out of your soul; the last of the count is the entering of your grave; the last of the count is parting from your family." It is also related from Ibn al-Sammak, may God have mercy on him, that he was with al-Ma'mun and recited it, and he said: "When breaths are counted and have no replenishment, how quickly they are spent!"

They mentioned two further explanations of His words ﴿We are only counting out their days for them﴾:

The first: We count their breaths and their deeds, and then We requite them for their few and many.

The second: We count the times until the time of the appointed term for each person, which admits no increase or decrease.

Then Glorified is He explained what will become apparent on that Day of the distinction between the God-fearing and the criminals in the manner of the Gathering, and said: ﴿On the Day We gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾. The author of the *Kashshaf* said: *yawma* (the day) is governed by an implied verb, i.e., "on the day We gather and drive, We will do to the two groups what no description can encompass," or "remember the day We gather." It may also be governed by "they will not have the power" (of intercession). From 'Ali (peace be upon him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, when the God-fearing come out of their graves they will be met with white she-camels that have wings, upon which are saddles of gold," and then he recited this verse. In it there are issues:

[Page 216]

**First issue:** The judge (al-Qadi) said: This verse is one of the things that shows the terrors of the Day of Resurrection are specific to the criminals, for the God-fearing from the beginning are gathered in this kind of honour, so they are safe from fear. How could terrors reach them?

**Second issue:** The Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists) argued from the verse, saying: His words ﴿to the Most Merciful﴾ indicate that the end of their movement will be at the Most Merciful. The People of Tawhid (monotheists) say the meaning is: on the day We gather the God-fearing to the place of the honour of the Most Merciful.

**Third issue:** A heretic (mulhid) criticised it, saying: His words ﴿On the Day We gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾ only hold if the one who gathers is other than the Most Merciful; but if the one who gathers is the Most Merciful, then this statement does not hold together. The Muslims replied that the implied meaning is: On the day We gather the God-fearing to the honour of the Most Merciful. As for His words ﴿and drive the criminals to Hell like thirsty cattle﴾: His words ﴿We drive﴾ show that they are driven to the Fire with humiliation and contempt, as if they were thirsty cattle driven to water. *Al-wird* is a name for thirst, because one who comes to water only comes to it out of thirst. The reality of *al-wurud* is going to the water, and the ones who come are called *al-waridun*.

As for His words ﴿they will not have the power of intercession﴾, i.e., it will not be theirs. The apparent meaning is that what is meant is their interceding for others, or others interceding for them, and therefore they differed. Some said: they do not have the power to intercede for others as the believers do. Others said: rather, what is meant is that no one else has the power to intercede for them. This second view is better, for to take the verse in the first sense would be explaining what is already obvious. And if this is established, the verse indicates that intercession is attainable for the people of major sins, since He said after it: ﴿except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾. The implication is that these people do not deserve that anyone should intercede for them unless they have taken a covenant of monotheism and prophethood with the Most Merciful, so it must be that this falls under that. Among the things that confirm our view is what Ibn Mas'ud related: that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said to his companions one day: "Is one of you unable to take a covenant with Allah every morning and evening?" They said: "How is that?" He said: "He says every morning and evening: O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen, I bear witness to You that I bear witness that there is no god but You alone, without partner, and that Muhammad is Your servant and Messenger. If You leave me to myself, You bring me near to evil and far from good, and I trust only in Your mercy. So grant me a covenant that You will fulfil for me on the Day of Resurrection, for You do not break the promise." When he says that, Allah seals it with a seal and it is placed beneath the Throne. When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call out: 'Where are those who have a covenant with the Most Merciful?' and they will enter Paradise." By this hadith it becomes clear that what is meant by the covenant is the word of testimony, and the way the verse indicates intercession for the people of major sins became clear. The judge (al-Qadi) said: the verse supports his school. It has become clear that the verse is strong in its indication for our view, and Allah knows best.

As for His words ﴿and will become opponents to them﴾, it is mentioned in contrast to His words ﴿a source of honour for them﴾. What is meant is the opposite of honour, which is humiliation and disgrace, i.e., they will be opposed to them in what they intended and sought, as if it were said: they will be a humiliation for them and not an honour; or it means they will be a helper against them. *Didd* means helper, as one says: "one of your *didd*," i.e., one of your helpers. We say: He used the singular in the manner of the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying: "They are one hand against whoever is other than them," because of the unity of their word, for they are like a single thing due to their complete cohesion and agreement. The meaning of the gods being a help against them is that they are the fuel of the Fire and the pebbles of Hell, and because they were punished on account of worshipping them.

Know that when Allah the Exalted mentioned the condition of these disbelievers with the idols in the Hereafter, He then mentioned their condition with the devils in this world, for they ask them and submit to them. So He said: ﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement?﴾ and in this there are issues:

They said: the statement of the speaker "I sent so-and-so upon so-and-so" is established in the language to convey that he empowered him over him, with the intention that he should gain dominion over him. He (peace be upon him) said: "Say the name of Allah and send your dog upon it." If this is established, then His words ﴿We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers﴾ convey that He empowered them over them, intending that they should gain dominion over them, and this conveys the intended meaning. Then this is confirmed by His words ﴿inciting them with incitement﴾, for its meaning is: We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers so that they incite them with incitement. And it is further confirmed by His words: ﴿And stir up whoever you can among them﴾ [al-Isra': 64].

The judge (al-Qadi, i.e., 'Abd al-Jabbar) said: The literal sense of the word requires that Allah the Exalted sent the devils to the disbelievers as He sent the prophets, by entrusting them with a message to deliver to them. [Page 215] Then in that message there can be nothing except what the devils were sent with, namely seduction. So the disbelievers would have to be obedient to the devils by accepting from them, and that would be disbelief on the part of the one who says it. When the literal meaning is rejected, interpretation becomes necessary, so we take it to mean that Allah the Exalted left the devils and the disbelievers free to meet, and did not prevent them from seducing them. This leaving free is called "sending" in the broad sense of the language, as when a man does not restrain his dog from entering his neighbour's house, one says: he sent his dog against him, even if he does not repel the harm of the people. Although this leaving free involves intensifying the trial for them, they are able not to accept from them, and their reward for refusing to accept will be greater. The evidence for this is His words: ﴿I had no authority over you except that I called you and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]. This is the end of his words.

We say: We do not concede that it is impossible to take it according to its apparent meaning. How is this related to sending *to* them? As to the saying that the misguidance of the disbeliever is from Allah the Exalted, then what effect does the devil have on it? We say: Why should it not be said that the devil's whispering that suggestion to him creates that misguidance in his heart, on condition that the listener's understanding is sound, since the speech of the devil is part of Allah the Exalted's creation? Thus that misguidance arising in the heart of the disbeliever is attributed both to the devil and to Allah the Exalted, from these two aspects.

If it is said: why can it not be that the meaning of sending is leaving free? We say: Just as He left free between the devil and the disbelievers, He also left free between them and the prophets. Then He specifically singled out the disbeliever by saying that He sent the devil upon him, so there must be an additional benefit here. Also, His words ﴿inciting them with incitement﴾, i.e., stirring them with a powerful stirring, are like the purpose of that sending, so it is necessary that the incitement be what Allah intends, and that the purpose of it be achieved. This is what there is at this point, and Allah knows best.

The author of the *Kashshaf* said: *al-azz*, *al-hazz* and *al-istifza'* are siblings in meaning, signifying agitation and intensity of disturbance; i.e., they urge them to acts of disobedience, goad them and stir them up to these with whisperings and enticements. As for His words ﴿So do not be hasty against them. We are only counting out their days for them﴾: it is said, "I hastened against him with such and such" when you urged him to it; i.e., do not be hasty against them by wishing that they perish or are destroyed, until you and the Muslims find rest from their evils. The first: We count their breaths and their deeds, and then We requite them for their few and many.

In it there are issues:

**Second issue:** The Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists) argued from the verse, saying: His words ﴿to the Most Merciful﴾ indicate that the end of their movement will be at the Most Merciful. The People of Tawhid (monotheists) say the meaning is: on the day We gather the God-fearing to the place of the honour of the Most Merciful.

Then this is confirmed by His words ﴿inciting them with incitement﴾, for its meaning is: We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers so that they incite them with incitement. And it is further confirmed by His words: ﴿And stir up whoever you can among them﴾ [al-Isra': 64].
