So the disbelievers would have to be obedient to the devils by accepting from them, and that would be disbelief on the part of the one who says it. Moreover, it is strange that the Predestinarians (al-Mujabbira) cling to this, since in their view the misguidance of the disbelievers comes from Him, the Exalted, in that He created disbelief in them and decreed disbelief, so the devil has no effect in what occurs. When the literal meaning is rejected, interpretation becomes necessary, so we take it to mean that Allah the Exalted left the devils and the disbelievers free to meet, and did not prevent them from seducing them. This leaving free is called "sending" in the broad sense of the language, as when a man does not restrain his dog from entering his neighbour's house, one says: he sent his dog against him, even if he does not repel the harm of the people. Although this leaving free involves intensifying the trial for them, they are able not to accept from them, and their reward for refusing to accept will be greater. The evidence for this is His words: ﴿I had no authority over you except that I called you and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]. This is the end of his words.

We say: We do not concede that it is impossible to take it according to its apparent meaning. For if the words "[We have sent] the devils" meant that Allah sent them to the disbelievers, the disbelievers would be obedient to Him by accepting the words of the devils. We say: Allah did not send the devils to the disbelievers, but rather sent them *upon* them, and sending upon them is empowering, with the intention that it should become dominant over them. How is this related to sending *to* them? As to the saying that the misguidance of the disbeliever is from Allah the Exalted, then what effect does the devil have on it? We say: Why should it not be said that the devil's whispering that suggestion to him creates that misguidance in his heart, on condition that the listener's understanding is sound, since the speech of the devil is part of Allah the Exalted's creation? Thus that misguidance arising in the heart of the disbeliever is attributed both to the devil and to Allah the Exalted, from these two aspects.

If it is said: why can it not be that the meaning of sending is leaving free? We say: Just as He left free between the devil and the disbelievers, He also left free between them and the prophets. Then He specifically singled out the disbeliever by saying that He sent the devil upon him, so there must be an additional benefit here. They mentioned two further explanations of His words ﴿We are only counting out their days for them﴾:

The first: We count their breaths and their deeds, and then We requite them for their few and many.

The second: We count the times until the time of the appointed term for each person, which admits no increase or decrease.

From 'Ali (peace be upon him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, when the God-fearing come out of their graves they will be met with white she-camels that have wings, upon which are saddles of gold," and then he recited this verse. In it there are issues:

**Second issue:** The Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists) argued from the verse, saying: His words ﴿to the Most Merciful﴾ indicate that the end of their movement will be at the Most Merciful. The People of Tawhid (monotheists) say the meaning is: on the day We gather the God-fearing to the place of the honour of the Most Merciful.

**Third issue:** A heretic (mulhid) criticised it, saying: His words ﴿On the Day We gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾ only hold if the one who gathers is other than the Most Merciful; but if the one who gathers is the Most Merciful, then this statement does not hold together. The judge (al-Qadi) said: the verse supports his school. It has become clear that the verse is strong in its indication for our view, and Allah knows best.

Although this leaving free involves intensifying the trial for them, they are able not to accept from them, and their reward for refusing to accept will be greater. The evidence for this is His words: ﴿I had no authority over you except that I called you and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]. This is the end of his words.

We say: We do not concede that it is impossible to take it according to its apparent meaning. For if the words "[We have sent] the devils" meant that Allah sent them to the disbelievers, the disbelievers would be obedient to Him by accepting the words of the devils. We say: Allah did not send the devils to the disbelievers, but rather sent them *upon* them, and sending upon them is empowering, with the intention that it should become dominant over them. How is this related to sending *to* them? As to the saying that the misguidance of the disbeliever is from Allah the Exalted, then what effect does the devil have on it? We say: Why should it not be said that the devil's whispering that suggestion to him creates that misguidance in his heart, on condition that the listener's understanding is sound, since the speech of the devil is part of Allah the Exalted's creation? Thus that misguidance arising in the heart of the disbeliever is attributed both to the devil and to Allah the Exalted, from these two aspects.

If it is said: why can it not be that the meaning of sending is leaving free? We say: Just as He left free between the devil and the disbelievers, He also left free between them and the prophets. Then He specifically singled out the disbeliever by saying that He sent the devil upon him, so there must be an additional benefit here. Also, His words ﴿inciting them with incitement﴾, i.e., stirring them with a powerful stirring, are like the purpose of that sending, so it is necessary that the incitement be what Allah intends, and that the purpose of it be achieved. This is what there is at this point, and Allah knows best.

**Second issue:** Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿inciting them with incitement﴾ means: He disturbs them in acts of disobedience with a strong disturbing. It was revealed concerning those who mocked the Qur'an, and they were five men. The author of the *Kashshaf* said: *al-azz*, *al-hazz* and *al-istifza'* are siblings in meaning, signifying agitation and intensity of disturbance; i.e., they urge them to acts of disobedience, goad them and stir them up to these with whisperings and enticements. As for His words ﴿So do not be hasty against them. We are only counting out their days for them﴾: it is said, "I hastened against him with such and such" when you urged him to it; i.e., do not be hasty against them by wishing that they perish or are destroyed, until you and the Muslims find rest from their evils. For between you and what you seek of their destruction there are only limited days and counted breaths. Its parallel is His words: ﴿Do not seek to hasten for them. On the day they see what they are promised, it will be as though they had not remained except an hour of a day. A proclamation﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that when he recited it he would weep and say: "The last of the count is the going out of your soul; the last of the count is the entering of your grave; the last of the count is parting from your family." It is also related from Ibn al-Sammak, may God have mercy on him, that he was with al-Ma'mun and recited it, and he said: "When breaths are counted and have no replenishment, how quickly they are spent!"

They mentioned two further explanations of His words ﴿We are only counting out their days for them﴾:

The first: We count their breaths and their deeds, and then We requite them for their few and many.

The second: We count the times until the time of the appointed term for each person, which admits no increase or decrease.

Then Glorified is He explained what will become apparent on that Day of the distinction between the God-fearing and the criminals in the manner of the Gathering, and said: ﴿On the Day We gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾. The author of the *Kashshaf* said: *yawma* (the day) is governed by an implied verb, i.e., "on the day We gather and drive, We will do to the two groups what no description can encompass," or "remember the day We gather." It may also be governed by "they will not have the power" (of intercession). From 'Ali (peace be upon him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, when the God-fearing come out of their graves they will be met with white she-camels that have wings, upon which are saddles of gold," and then he recited this verse. In it there are issues:

[Page 216]

**First issue:** The judge (al-Qadi) said: This verse is one of the things that shows the terrors of the Day of Resurrection are specific to the criminals, for the God-fearing from the beginning are gathered in this kind of honour, so they are safe from fear. How could terrors reach them?

**Second issue:** The Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists) argued from the verse, saying: His words ﴿to the Most Merciful﴾ indicate that the end of their movement will be at the Most Merciful. The People of Tawhid (monotheists) say the meaning is: on the day We gather the God-fearing to the place of the honour of the Most Merciful.

**Third issue:** A heretic (mulhid) criticised it, saying: His words ﴿On the Day We gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾ only hold if the one who gathers is other than the Most Merciful; but if the one who gathers is the Most Merciful, then this statement does not hold together. The Muslims replied that the implied meaning is: On the day We gather the God-fearing to the honour of the Most Merciful. As for His words ﴿and drive the criminals to Hell like thirsty cattle﴾: His words ﴿We drive﴾ show that they are driven to the Fire with humiliation and contempt, as if they were thirsty cattle driven to water. *Al-wird* is a name for thirst, because one who comes to water only comes to it out of thirst. The reality of *al-wurud* is going to the water, and the ones who come are called *al-waridun*.

As for His words ﴿they will not have the power of intercession﴾, i.e., it will not be theirs. The apparent meaning is that what is meant is their interceding for others, or others interceding for them, and therefore they differed. Some said: they do not have the power to intercede for others as the believers do. Others said: rather, what is meant is that no one else has the power to intercede for them. This second view is better, for to take the verse in the first sense would be explaining what is already obvious. And if this is established, the verse indicates that intercession is attainable for the people of major sins, since He said after it: ﴿except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾. The implication is that these people do not deserve that anyone should intercede for them unless they have taken a covenant of monotheism and prophethood with the Most Merciful, so it must be that this falls under that. Among the things that confirm our view is what Ibn Mas'ud related: that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said to his companions one day: "Is one of you unable to take a covenant with Allah every morning and evening?" They said: "How is that?" He said: "He says every morning and evening: O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen, I bear witness to You that I bear witness that there is no god but You alone, without partner, and that Muhammad is Your servant and Messenger. If You leave me to myself, You bring me near to evil and far from good, and I trust only in Your mercy. So grant me a covenant that You will fulfil for me on the Day of Resurrection, for You do not break the promise." When he says that, Allah seals it with a seal and it is placed beneath the Throne. When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call out: 'Where are those who have a covenant with the Most Merciful?' and they will enter Paradise." By this hadith it becomes clear that what is meant by the covenant is the word of testimony, and the way the verse indicates intercession for the people of major sins became clear. The judge (al-Qadi) said: the verse supports his school. It has become clear that the verse is strong in its indication for our view, and Allah knows best.

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, had refuted the worshippers of idols, He returned to refute those who attributed offspring to Him. ﴿They say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ ﴿Indeed, you have brought forth a monstrous thing.﴾ ﴿The heavens are almost torn apart from it, the earth is split open, and the mountains collapse in ruin,﴾ ﴿because they ascribe a son to the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿It is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant.﴾ ﴿He has counted them and numbered them precisely.﴾ ﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone.﴾

Some say that the Exalted's words, "And the Jews say, 'Ezra is the son of Allah,' and the Christians say, 'The Messiah is the son of Allah'" [At-Tawbah: 30], and the Arabs' saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah, all fall within this verse. Others restrict it to the Arabs who asserted that the angels are the daughters of Allah, because the refutation of the Christians came earlier, at the beginning of the surah. As for now, since He has refuted the Arabs who worshipped idols, He speaks about corrupting the view of those who worshipped the angels on the ground that they are the daughters of Allah.

As for His words, ﴿indeed, you have brought forth a monstrous thing (shay'an idda)﴾, the word idda is read with a kasra and with a fatha. Ibn Khalawayh said: al-idd and al-add mean "a wonder," and it is said they mean "a great abomination." Al-adda means "severity," and adda ʿalayya al-amr and ādanī al-amr mean "the matter weighed heavily upon me."

The word yatafaṭṭarna is read with a tā' after the yā' (that is, the dotted letter below it). They differed about yakādu: some read it with a dotted yā' below, and others with a tā' above. The verb infiṭār comes from faṭaraho, meaning he split it, and tafaṭṭur comes from faṭṭaraho, meaning he split it into pieces, repeating the action in it. Ibn Masʿud read yatasaddaʿna (they would be cleft).

As for His words, ﴿and the mountains collapse in ruin (hadda)﴾, the meaning is that they are crushed to pieces (tuhaddu haddan), or they are crushed (mahdūdah), or it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu, the accusative of cause), meaning because they are crushed. The meaning is that they fall with the utmost violence, some collapsing onto others.

If it is asked: how does the assertion that Allah has a son lead to the splitting of the heavens, the cleaving of the earth, and the collapse of the mountains? We say there are several answers.

First: Allah, glory be to Him, says, "I shall do this to the heavens, the earth, and the mountains when this word is uttered, out of anger at the one who utters it, were it not for My forbearance and that I do not hasten to punish, as He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; and if they should cease, none could hold them after Him. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving﴾ [Fatir: 41]."

Second: that this is to magnify the word, to express its enormity, and to depict its effect on the religion and its destruction of its pillars and foundations.

Third: that the heavens, the earth, and the mountains would almost do this if they had understanding, because of the grossness of this utterance. This is the interpretation of Abu Muslim.

Fourth: that the heavens, the earth, and the mountains were free of all defects, but when the children of Adam uttered this word, defects appeared in them.

As for His words, ﴿that they ascribe to the Most Merciful a son (an daʿaw lil-Raḥmān waladan)﴾, there are several issues.

The first issue concerns its i'rab (grammatical analysis), which has three possibilities:

One: it may be in the genitive as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in minhu (from Him), or in the accusative by supposing the removal of the preposition lām and the transitivity of the verb, meaning "for this, because they ascribed..." Or it may be in the nominative as the subject of haddan, meaning that the calling of a son for the Most Merciful crushed them. The sum is that He, the Exalted, made clear that the cause of those great events is this utterance.

The second issue: He repeated the name al-Raḥmān several times to draw attention to the fact that He alone is the Most Merciful, because the roots and branches of all blessings come from Him alone.

The third issue: His words, ﴿da'aw lil-Raḥmān (ascribe to the Most Merciful)﴾, come from daʿā meaning "to name," which is transitive to two objects, of which only the second is mentioned, seeking generality and comprehensiveness, so as to include everyone who ascribes a son to Him. Or it comes from daʿā meaning "to attribute to," which is its intransitive counterpart (muṭāwiʿ), as in the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever claims kinship to other than his masters..." The poet said:

"We, the sons of Nahshal, do not claim (nadda'ī) to a father,"

meaning we do not attribute ourselves to him.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿It is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾, meaning it is impossible. As for ordinary begetting, there is no dispute about its impossibility. As for adoption, a child must resemble its parent, and Allah, the Exalted, has no likeness. Also, taking a son happens for purposes that cannot apply to Allah, such as joy in him, seeking his help, or gaining good renown, and all of these are unbefitting to Him.

Then He said: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾. The meaning is that there is no one they worship in the heavens and the earth, among the angels or the people, but that he comes to the Most Merciful, that is, he takes refuge in Him and seeks shelter in His lordship, as a servant who is submissive, obedient, humble, and hopeful, as servants do. Some have interpreted it as referring to the Day of Resurrection alone, but the first interpretation is preferable because there is no restriction in it.

As for His words, ﴿He has counted them and numbered them precisely﴾, the meaning is that they are all under His command, governance, subjugation, and power. He, glory be to Him, encompasses them. He knows their affairs in general and in detail, and nothing of their circumstances escapes Him. Each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone, with none of these polytheists with him, and they will disown them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 19, verses 96–98:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds - the Most Merciful will endow them with affection.﴾ ﴿So We have only made it easy in your tongue that you may give good tidings thereby to the righteous and warn thereby a people contentious.﴾ ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed before them? Do you perceive from them anyone or hear from them a whisper?﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, had refuted the categories of disbelievers and elaborated on their conditions in this world and the Hereafter, He concluded the surah by mentioning the conditions of the believers, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds - the Most Merciful will endow them with affection.﴾ The exegetes differ regarding His saying ﴿wudd﴾ (affection) into two opinions:

The first opinion, which is the view of the majority, is that He, may He be exalted, will create affection for them in hearts and plant it in them without any seeking of it on their part, and without any pursuit of the causes by which people acquire affection in hearts, such as kinship, friendship, doing favours, or other things. Rather, it is an invention from Him, may He be exalted, and an initiation, singling out His allies with this honour, just as He casts awe and dread into the hearts of their enemies, magnifying them and exalting their station. The sin in ﴿sa-yaj'alu﴾ (will make) is either because the surah is Meccan, and the believers at that time were despised among the disbelievers, so Allah promised them this when Islam would come; or it may be that this will occur on the Day of Resurrection, when He makes them beloved to His creation by what He displays of their good deeds and spreads from the register of their deeds. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding this verse: "When Allah loves a servant, He calls Gabriel: 'I have loved so-and-so, so love him.' Then Gabriel calls out to that effect in the heavens and the earth. And when He hates a servant, it is similar to that."

And from Ka'b, who said: "It is written in the Torah and the Gospel that there is no love for anyone on earth until its origin is from Allah, the Exalted; He sends it down to the people of heaven, then to the people of earth. And the confirmation of this in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿the Most Merciful will endow them with affection.﴾"

The second opinion, which is the choice of Abu Muslim: the meaning of ﴿the Most Merciful will endow them with affection﴾ is that He will grant them what they love. Wudd and mahabbah (love) are the same; it is said: "I gave so-and-so his love," and "He made for them what they love," and "I made for him his wudd." From their speech: "He wishes (yawaddu) that it were so," and "I wished (waddidtu) that it were so," meaning "I loved." The meaning is: the Most Merciful will give them their wudd, that is, what they love, in Paradise.

The first opinion is preferable, because taking love to mean the beloved is a metaphor, and because we have mentioned that the Messenger (ﷺ) recited this verse and explained it in that way, so that is more preferable. Abu Muslim said: rather, the second opinion is preferable, for several reasons:

Page 219
The first: How can the first opinion be valid when we know that the righteous Muslim is hated by the disbelievers, and many Muslims also hate him?

The second: Such love may be found among disbelievers and sinners even more, so how can it be considered a favour toward the believers?

The third: Their love in hearts is from their own action, not something Allah, may He be exalted, did; so interpreting the verse as giving the otherworldly benefits is more preferable.

The answer to the first is that the intended meaning is: the Most Merciful will create love for them among the angels and the prophets. And it is related from him (peace be upon him) that he related from his Lord, mighty and majestic, that He said: "If My believing servant remembers Me in his self, I remember him in My self; and if he remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better and more excellent than them." This is the answer to the second point, because the disbeliever and the sinner are not like this.

The answer to the third is that it is to be understood as the bestowing of kindnesses and the creation of the motive to honour him in their hearts. As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We have only made it easy in your tongue that you may give good tidings thereby to the righteous﴾, it is a resumed statement by which He explains the great significance of this surah, because it contains tawhid, prophethood, resurrection and gathering, and refutation of the groups of misguided falsifiers. So He explains that He made this easy by His tongue, so that he may give good tidings with it and warn. Had Allah not transferred their stories into the Arabic language, this would not have been easy for the Messenger (ﷺ). As for the Qur'an including the good tidings for the righteous and the warning for those among them who deviate, this is clear; but when He mentioned that it gives good tidings to the righteous, He mentioned in contrast one who is more eloquent in opposing piety, and the most eloquent of them is the ﴿alad﴾ (contentious), who clings to falsehood, argues about it and is intransigent, and this is the meaning of ﴿luddan﴾.

Then He concluded the surah with an eloquent admonition, saying: ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed before them?﴾ Because when they reflect and know that there must be the passing away of the world and the arrival at death, they fear that, and they also fear the evil end in the Hereafter, so they are closer to avoiding sins. Then He emphasised this further, saying: ﴿Do you perceive from them anyone?﴾ Because if the Messenger, peace be upon him, does not perceive any of them by sight, perception or sensing, and does not hear from them a ﴿rikz﴾ (whisper) - which is a faint sound, from which comes "rakaza al-rumh" when one buries its tip in the ground, and "al-rikaz" meaning buried wealth - this indicates their extinction and total annihilation.

The closer meaning of His saying ﴿We destroyed﴾ is that what is intended is their passing away by death, although some exegetes have taken it to mean hastened punishment in this world. And Allah knows best the truth, and to Him is the return and the final place. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah send blessings upon our master Muhammad, the unlettered Prophet, and upon his family and companions, and grant them peace.

From their speech: "He wishes (yawaddu) that it were so," and "I wished (waddidtu) that it were so," meaning "I loved." The meaning is: the Most Merciful will give them their wudd, that is, what they love, in Paradise.

The first opinion is preferable, because taking love to mean the beloved is a metaphor, and because we have mentioned that the Messenger (ﷺ) recited this verse and explained it in that way, so that is more preferable. Abu Muslim said: rather, the second opinion is preferable, for several reasons:

Page 219
The first: How can the first opinion be valid when we know that the righteous Muslim is hated by the disbelievers, and many Muslims also hate him?

The second: Such love may be found among disbelievers and sinners even more, so how can it be considered a favour toward the believers?

The third: Their love in hearts is from their own action, not something Allah, may He be exalted, did; so interpreting the verse as giving the otherworldly benefits is more preferable.

The answer to the first is that the intended meaning is: the Most Merciful will create love for them among the angels and the prophets. And it is related from him (peace be upon him) that he related from his Lord, mighty and majestic, that He said: "If My believing servant remembers Me in his self, I remember him in My self; and if he remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better and more excellent than them." This is the answer to the second point, because the disbeliever and the sinner are not like this.

The answer to the third is that it is to be understood as the bestowing of kindnesses and the creation of the motive to honour him in their hearts. As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We have only made it easy in your tongue that you may give good tidings thereby to the righteous﴾, it is a resumed statement by which He explains the great significance of this surah, because it contains tawhid, prophethood, resurrection and gathering, and refutation of the groups of misguided falsifiers. So He explains that He made this easy by His tongue, so that he may give good tidings with it and warn. Had Allah not transferred their stories into the Arabic language, this would not have been easy for the Messenger (ﷺ). As for the Qur'an including the good tidings for the righteous and the warning for those among them who deviate, this is clear; but when He mentioned that it gives good tidings to the righteous, He mentioned in contrast one who is more eloquent in opposing piety, and the most eloquent of them is the ﴿alad﴾ (contentious), who clings to falsehood, argues about it and is intransigent, and this is the meaning of ﴿luddan﴾.

Then He concluded the surah with an eloquent admonition, saying: ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed before them?﴾ Because when they reflect and know that there must be the passing away of the world and the arrival at death, they fear that, and they also fear the evil end in the Hereafter, so they are closer to avoiding sins. Then He emphasised this further, saying: ﴿Do you perceive from them anyone?﴾ Because if the Messenger, peace be upon him, does not perceive any of them by sight, perception or sensing, and does not hear from them a ﴿rikz﴾ (whisper) - which is a faint sound, from which comes "rakaza al-rumh" when one buries its tip in the ground, and "al-rikaz" meaning buried wealth - this indicates their extinction and total annihilation.

The closer meaning of His saying ﴿We destroyed﴾ is that what is intended is their passing away by death, although some exegetes have taken it to mean hastened punishment in this world. And Allah knows best the truth, and to Him is the return and the final place. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah send blessings upon our master Muhammad, the unlettered Prophet, and upon his family and companions, and grant them peace.
